This area is fairly new and should develop into a fairly good section and eventually a better class of home is expected to be built have as the adjacent B-3 and B-4 are very good neighborhoods. Rents should advance. Very conservative mortgage loans are made here. The future is promising.
St. Edwards Catholic School is south of 15th and west of the Chicago and North Western Railroad. Good transportation, schools, churches, and business center.
North Shore Railroad to the west.

This section is part of what is known as West Racine. Has mostly 5 and 6 room bungalows and is very popular as a residential section. Prices are well maintained and the only sales being made are forced ones. The section from Cleveland Ave. to Lathrop Ave. to the west is sparsely settled. From 16 St. to the north and to the North Shore Railroad to east and Lanthrop Ave. west, values are somewhat lower due to proximity to D-9 to south where properties and houses are very poorly and cheaply constructed.
Level and high east of West Blvd. with ravines to north and east of area. East of West Blvd. and north of West Blvd. very low ravines.
Picturesque setting. Very well treed, winding roads, good schools, transportation and churches.
Catholic cemetery to the east and the North Shore Railroad.

West section of area is sparsely settled and is also high ground -- not platted. South section is level with homes well kept -- great pride in ownership. Money is learned very conservatively. The east section is sparsely settled and very low. Along Harvey Drive, West Blvd, and Shelley Drive there are several fine homes -- this section is quite desirable.
High and level with ravine to north of Mohr Avenue.
Good transportation, schools, church, close to business center to east.
Catholic cemetery to west and Mound Cemetery to south. (However, both are very well kept up)

Danes comprise the majority of inhabitants. From Chicago Ave. to to Kinsie there is a slight slope of 5 blocks to the east. The streets are well lighted and all are paved. Properties are very well kept. Fine park facilities to the southeast. McKinley Junior High School is immediately north of area.
Level, sloping on west toward the Root River.
Good school, church, and adjacent to business section. Good transportation. Jefferson School is located in this area.
None, except stagnant water in the river during summer months.
One apartment named "Will Manor" of 20 units

The Root River overflows every spring to the north of the W. 6th St. Bridge to extreme north of area. The land is low from Cliff Avenue to the river. There is the Washington Park Golf links to the southwest point of area which adds to property value adjacent thereto. Close to industry. That section of area on extreme southwest contains an apartment building named "Will Manor" of 20 units consisting of 3 - 4 rooms. This building is of brick and concrete construction, is about 10 years old, and is situated on the corner of Lafayette and W. 6th St. Directly east of the apartment is the Old Peoples Home -- very well kept.
Good schools, transportation, business center, Lincoln School is east of area and adjoining. Open Air School is located north of this area. Sacred Heart Catholic School is just north of area.
Isolation Hospital (called the Lincoln Hospital) is to the south.
Good - few for rent, if any

The area is situated on a plateau and on the west from Jefferson there is an abrupt drop to the river of 45 feet. On the extreme south there is approximately a 50 - 60 foot drop. A park has recently been made by W. P. A. on the south which is an asset to the area. The inhabitants work in various factories within easy walking distance.

Good schools, transportation, parks, churches, playgrounds, a new field house recently completed by W. P. A. is at Union (Lincoln) Park on northwest section. St. Johns Neponuk Catholic School is south of Yout and west of St. Clair. The Horlick Senior High School is located outside on the west of area. Trinity English Lutheran School is south of Goold and west of Marquette.
Industry along the railroad to west.

On the extreme west and northwest from Lincoln School on south to Ronayne Ave. on north, property averages in age from 15 - 20 years. From Douglas Ave. on west to Goold on north to the Lake on the east to Hagerer St. on south, the area is about similar to the foregoing west and northwest description - property is well kept and same age. The German element in whole area is thrifty and properties are well kept. The greater portion of population works in the Case (Main Works) and also in the Bell City Malleable and Iron Company and Hamilton Beach Manufacturing Co. and various other factories within walking distance from their homes. The two blocks from Carliale St. on west north from High St. to Yout St. have very fine homes. The land (undeveloped) west of here is owned by Horlicks and today probably worth $1200-$1500 per acre. When developed of this land takes place it should be of high order.
Good school, transportation, and business section.
A foreign settlement, poor maintenance, railroad, and surrounded by factories in which these residents work. Some negroes. An undesirable area.
High and low (a drop of approximately 60 feet occurs from Chicago and North Western Railroad west to the river).
A greater portion of area is low and sometimes known as "Frogtown".
Any mortgage loans made here would be ultra-conservative. A foreign settlement with colored element. Spotted throughout. All factory laborers. An undesirable area, 2/3 of it being low land.
Good high school and park systems in south and west section of area.

Values have always been stable here because of the adjacency of the Washington Park Senior High School to the southwest. Streets are all paved and well lighted and properties taken care of. Very heavy traffic on 12th St., a thoroughfare through the center area.
Washington Park is to the north, good transportation, churches, schools and Taylor Avenue business section. The Gilbery Knapp School is on the south and the Howell School is located on northeast.
St. Paul Railroad to south and North Shore Railroad to west.

That section east of Taylor Avenue is a newer one and average 18 years in age. The majority of inhabitants in this area work in the North factory to the southeast. Streets are well paved, property well kept. Popular place for mechanics and laborers to reside. 16th Street is spotted with business. In the northwest section from Dean Blvd. to 16th Street to Washington Street, many business and professional men reside and the property values here are somewhat better. Gilbert Knapp School is in the southern portion of area.
Surrounded by industry - smoke - noise, etc.
Very conservative loans for home purchase are made here. A good rental area. Many rooming houses. Prices have maintained stability fairly well.
Many shacks consisting of 1 to 5 rooms.
A very undesirable plat with no tendency to grow. Unimproved roads, no sewerage system, lights, transportation, etc. Quite a distance from employment

Spotted area. Good homes in the area suffer by the many poorly constructed ones with no basements, etc. Southwestern section is very low with stagnant water every spring. South of the Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad and west of West Lawn is outside the city limits.
"The new Mitchell Junior High School is in this area. Churches, good transportation, and business section to north on Taylor Avenue.
Dairy -- early hours of rising, wagons, etc. This dairy is located south of Durand Avenue.

Comparatively new area. Very thrifty people and they show an exceptional desire for home ownership. Most of the inhabitants work in the J. I. Case Company South Works on the east. Area has all modern utilities. The extreme southwest section of area has a better class of bungalow homes ranging between $7,000 and $7,500 and has between 20 and 35 of these good homes. This section is outside city limits. *This new high school was constructed in 1936 by W. P. A. progress.
None except adjacent to B-5; church, school and transportation O.K.
Railroad to north, also factories to north and east. Quite smoky and dirty.

The northwest section has many 1 1/2 story single homes of 5 and 6 rooms. The southwest section consists mostly of single homes of the bungalow type with the exception of Taylor Avenue which has several apartments -- it is also a business street. A large apartment building on Meachem and Taylor Avenue is now owned by the First National Bank. The adjacency to Nash Motors keeps rentals and property values steady.
Colored element and industry, railroads, smoke, etc.

Colored element is located from Philly Avenue to Kearney Avenue on DeKoven Avenue. Homes from 20th Street to 21st Avenue are newer and of the bungalow type. Convenient to industry. No upward trend expected for many years, if any.
Very sparsely settled. The two sections south of Durand are outside city limits.
Center of western section is low, otherwise area is level.
Good school. Transportation is about 4 blocks to the north (the Taylor Avenue bus line).

Very much spotted with homes ranging from $8,000 to $12,000 and some from $5,500. Vacant land is steady and commands good prices along Taylor Avenue, otherwise area is sparsely settled. Outside city limits.
Poor transportation. No churches. Schools are at a distance. Poor business center.
No paving or sewerage. Factories, smoke, etc.
Sparsely settled area - not a desirable one for residential purposes. Residents mostly work in J. I. Case Company South Works.
Level - except a small decline from Center Street and Washington Avenue to 13th Street to the south, to the Chicago Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad to the west.
Good schools, transportation, church, business center. The Vocational school is located in extreme north of area, also Franklin Junior High School.

The area from 13th Street south to 17th Street and west to Racine Street is level. Also the section from 17th to 21st on Mead Street west on 21st to the Chicago and North Western Railroad and north to 17th is level. The only time a demand for rents exists here is when (as is now) there is a shortage of homes for rent. The section south of 17th consists entirely of a factory district and is very undesirable. Along the Chicago Milwaukee and St. Paul Railroad to  the east is popular.

Everything necessary. St. Catherine's High School is south of 12th St. and west of Park Ave. St. Mary's Catholic School is in business center just north of area. St. Rose Catholic School is north of 11th St. and west of Grand. Holy Name Catholic School is just south of 15th St. and west of Park. The Vocationa; School and Franklin Jr. High School are located on northwest of area in D-5. Winslow School is in center of area.
Interurban line running north and south through area -- very noisy and annoying at night.

There are 6 apartments ranging from 15 - 40 units on the west side of Main Street from 7th to 15th Streets. From 7th to 12th Streets there is a mixture of single homes of 6 - 9 rooms, and from 14th to 16th Streets there are single homes of 8 - 9 rooms of substantial value; from DeKoven Avenue north to 14th on Park Avenue and east to the lake there are many homes from $12,000 to $20,000. This area is one where land values will remain good and probably increase due to the desirability for location of high grade apartment houses. There are several exceptionally fine homes on DeKoven near the lake. Some of the old homes in this area cost up to $50,000 but after these old families die off these homes will be of little value, although the value of the ground.

St. John's Lutheran School is south of St. Patrick Street and west of N. Wisconsin. Garfield School is on southwest corner. St. Patrick's School is east of center of area. Close to industry and business.
Railroad to west and industry all around area.

20% Jews along railroad (junk yards) to west. Only foreign element will buy any property in this area. This is one of the oldest sections in the city. Homes are old and hard to maintain. A very undesirable area rapidly on deline - north to High Street. St. Joseph's Catholic School is south of St. Patrick Street and east of Erie Street. Washington Junior High is in north center of area. Janes School is on east - north of Barker Street.
Transportation, schools and churches excellent. Neighboring stores good. (Roosevelt School is in center of area)
White-collar & business men with small % of factory workers
This area is well supplied with all conveniences. It will continue to be a popular area for residential homes.
None (except adjacency to A1 and B1 on east)
Schools far away, no close churches, poor transportation.

Notwithstanding adjacency to A1 and B1, this area does not warrant a "B" rating. The reason for this is the element residing in the west in D1 which is the lower class of foreigners (Italians predominating) and the very poor shack-like construction of homes in D1. Also, in D1 the land is low and swampy. Any chance of A1 expanding to the west is well taken care of by the 2 blacks west of N. Main Street which is mostly vacant land.
Level but slanting approximately 4 to 6 feet from road on west to 6th Avenue; and about 2 feet from Green Street on east to 6th Avenue on west.
None, except good school on north.
Very low and many shacks -- low class Italians -- transportation poor

In that section south of North Street to Seymour the lots are 30 feet wide only. The section north of North Street to the city limits is not platted. This area has no future for a long time. Poor class of residents. In the northwest section of area the North Racine School is located.
Level. Severe drop to Lake Michigan - about 70 degree angle. (This drop starts at from 80 to 100 feet from the water's edge.)
Bus line runs north to Augusta Avenue and north Main Street. Good country grammar school outside city limits on north end.
No business center, no churches, and no transportation north of August Avenue.
Very limited (Only a very few buyers for this class of property.)

A portion of this area on extreme north is outside the city limits. This is the most desirable section of Racine in which to live. There is no particular demand for homes here due to the limited number of business and professional men who can buy homes in this area. Very well restricted and very few, if any homes for sale. They have been built for owners and not for sale. The 2 blocks west of N. Main Street are very sparsely settled and unlikely to expand due to the undesirable elements to west in the C1 and D1. These 2 blocks will be used as a bumper to protext A1, the prices of this vacant land being held high enough to prevent the encroachment of this foreign element. Few, if any, rentable properties.
None, except adjacency to Racine County Club.

One resident, the Janes estate, worth approximately $15,000 and another house of 8 rooms worth $8,0000 are the outstanding homes; otherwise the area is stagnant, very sparsely settled, and with very little future.
About 1 1/2 miles from good school to the east. Area well timbered with oak trees.
None, except tavern recently built to the north.
Single 6 rm. bungalows 2 story 7 rm. & 1 1/2 story
Outside city limits. Garrety's Grove. Mostly vacant property. The Lots are large sized and area was developed because of oak trees. It is about 3 miles west of the city on Trunk Highway "K" and 38.
Golf course to the east. Good school.
None, except the inconvenience of getting to town in winter
Some in southern section of area

Eventually this area should develop. The section to the south is largely comprised of laborers seeking cheaper grade of home (spotted). The professional class lives in the northern section of area. In the southern section of area, the grade of home runs from $3,500 to $5,000 frame, 1 1/2 story, 5-room bungalows and frame cottages. Both section of area are 85 - 90% vacant.
Good schools, transportation, churches, parks and close to business section of Taylor Avenue.
Close to North Shore, R. R. on west and St. Paul R. R. to the north.
Accessible to Nash Motor factory on east. About 60% of the inhabitants work there.
Good schools - near DeKoven Academy on east. Stephen Bull School is in this area. Churches (Polish) and Racine Street business section to the west.
To the south of J. I. Case South Works is Lakeside with salons, night clubs, colored element, etc.

This is a Polish settlement - about 80% of the foreigners are Poles. These Poles are considered of the better or best class in the city. Most of the inhabitants are employed at J. I. Case South Works and Nash Motors, also the LAkeside Malleable Casting Company. Employment at the Case factory has been steady except for strike periods of 2 - 3 months. Nash Motors are idle generally from September to March yearly. South of this area is vacant park land and Racine Sewerage Disposal Plant now under construction. This no considered detrimental.
Workers on mountain - clerks - lower income white collar workers

This is a small area located on Signal Mountain, with benefit of high elevation. This development was originally for summer homes and construction was not substantial - hence improvement has ceased and there is hardly any promise for future improvement. Area is about 60% improved, schools, church, and community stores are convenient, and transportation is by gasoline bus and is adequate. Type of population and type of construction make it a third grade area.
Professional Men, executives, white collar workers
During past 3 years there has been some infiltration of people with more moderate incomes.

The area is located on Signal Mountain, a separate municipality about 7 miles from the Chattanooga business center. It has good grade school, community stores and adequate transportation by means of gasoline bus which runs from the mountain top to the center of Chattanooga on regular schedule. The mountain was developed by a wealthy Chattanooga man and formerly was used almost exclusively during the summer months by the moderately wealthy to wealthier Chattanooga residents. With very few exceptions type of houses built have been very substantial, some very costly, and residents now make the mountain their home for the entire year. A golf and country club is located on the mountain.     What formerly was a summer resort hotel was three years ago sold to the Alexian Brotherhood, a Catholic Organization, for use somewhat as a religious retreat and sanatorium. Some residents on the mountain claim that this has had no effect on the area from the standpoint of residential desirability, but the fact remains that there has been no new building in this area during the past three years, and while there is only one vacant house (Not including about 4 which are being repaired) rentals are only about 65% of what they were 3 years ago and the only sales made have been at very low prices. With its high altitude, easy accessibility to the city, good type of population and good type of construction, it is still a very desirable place to live and will continue so, but the trend towards new building has veered to Lookout Mountain.

This area lies outside city limits, is a level section, about 1/4 mile wide, lying between ridges on the east and west. Improvement on the east is largely concentrated to lots fronting Dayton Blvd. and is very scattered and of cheap construction towards the ridge on the east. Improvement on the west is more substantial and extends a distance of what would equal about 2 blocks away from Dayton Blvd. Between the city limits line and the southern boundary line of this beer taverns, some of which have a rather shady reputation.     On Dayton Blvd., just north of Midvale St., have recently been erected about 10 small 3 room houses, resembling tourist camps, all having the same appearance, on small lots that are about 3 feet below street elevation. Other new construction scattered throughout area but is not of any great proportion and is all in the low price class. Area has city water and electric lights but no gas or public sewerage.
White collar workers, minor executives, skilled mechanics.

This area located in Red Bank, outside Chattanooga city limits. It is in a valley with high ridges on both east and west sides. Both grade and high schools are located in the area, community business center is located on Dayton Boulevard and easily accessible to all parts of area. Transportation is by gasoline bus and is adequate. The center of the area (along Dayton Boulevard) is level with gradual rise to ridges to both east and west. Most substantial construction is along Dayton Boulevard and the section between the Boulevard and Lamar Avenue and Crisman and Morrison Springs Road. To the north of this area (not shown on the map) two subdivisions have been opened within past year and about 30 new homes built in price range $3000-4000. Being outside city limits, it is not burdened with city taxes but fire insurance rates are higher. Recent agitation has been started to create fire district to serve this area and Area C-2 just south of it in order to reduce fire insurance rates and provide better protection.

The area if from rolling to hilly and only about 40% improved - the southern part (inside the city limits) is the more thickly populated. The eastern part overlooks the Tennessee River, and it is in this section that the majority of the very high priced homes are located. The lower priced homes are located in the western part. Lots are large, well wooded and lawns well maintained, and as a rule homes are well designed.     The northern part (outside city limits) is sparsely improved. On Haywood Avenue, in the northwest corner of the area, a new subdivision has just been opened; 10 new homes have just been completed to sell for $5250-$5750. This building done by a speculative builder and his success with the first ten will govern his activity in the remainder of the subdivision which has approximately 100 lots. Part inside city limits served by bus - grade and junior high school are fairly convenient.     The extreme northern point of the area is only about 15 minutes by automobile from the central retail business section.
White collar workers - skilled mechanics - some few professional men and minor executives

This area located in North Chattanooga just across the river from the principal business center of the city proper. Its contour is from rolling to very steep. On the south it joins a large community business center, has all utilities, schools and churches are convenient, and it has adequate transportation by gasoline bus. It is about the oldest section of North Chattanooga.     Age of properties, very hilly terrain, lower grade area on west and proximity to business center are features which adversely affect the desirability of the area, while on the contrary, its easy accessibility to the principal business center of the city proper is in its favor. Some properties are well maintained, others only fair and still others poorly maintained. The area is definitely on the down-grade and for this reason rates third class.
White collar workers - skilled mechanics, professional men

This area lies in North Chattanooga, across the river from Chattanooga proper and principal business district, but has all utilities and adequate transportation by gasoline bus. Grade and Jr. High School located in the area and a large community business center is located conveniently close. The area lies from rolling to hilly, maintenance of homes generally indicates pride of ownership. It is about 80% improved - receives a beneficial influence from the higher grade area to the north and east. Construction as a rule fairly substantial but some cheaper homes indicate lack of restrictions or failure to enforce them, especially in the section around Federal and Dartmouth Streets.
Low income industrial workers - mechanics and laborers

This area is rolling to hilly, one of the oldest sections in North Chattanooga. It has adequate transportation and school facilities and is convenient to the community business center of the section. There are several industrial plants south of the area, between it and the river.     It is an area of old cheaply built small houses, some shacks, and all very poorly maintained. Mixed type of low income population and cheapness and condition of properties make this a fourth grade area.

The area is level to rolling, most of it outside city limits. Nearest transportation is about 4 blocks from the eastern line of the area. Houses are cheap, flimsy structures, very poorly maintained. It does not have either lights, water or sewerage. Colored school located in southern part of area. Some distance to central part of city and transportation not convenient.
Hosiery Mill workers - mechanics - wage earners - laborers

The area lies level to rolling and hilly on the northern and eastern side which extends to Missionary Ridge. Has all utilities, grade and junior high school located in it, also churches and community business center. One of the larger hosiery mills of the city is located in this area and formerly provided employment to many of the inhabitants of the area, but a change in management of the mill has occurred in recent years and its activity has declined quite a bit. It now uses only about 60% of employees formerly used. As a whole the area is composed of cheaper constructed houses with little indication of any pride of home ownership.     Northern part of area not far from Chickamanga Dam and during construction of this dam, many of the workers resided in this area and it did not feel the effects of lessened activity of the hosiery mill. However, the dam is about complete and employment now is only about 40% of peak, and this will undoubtedly adversely affect this area within the next 6 months.
Business & professional men - white collar workers - salesmen
Old houses made into 2-4 fam. apts. 3-5 rms

This area is located in what is known as "Cameron Hill" a very high bluff overlooking the Tennessee River. It is within walking distance of the principal business center. Population in this area includes many Jews. It has all utilities, grade school is close as are churches and stores. Transportation is by gasoline bus and adequate.     This is a very old section, surrounded by lower grade areas on all sides, home ownership is declining yearly, many of the older inhabitants of the area moving to other sections.     Area is about 98% improved. The northern part is very hilly and southern part very rolling.
Laborers, domestics, low wage earners, some clerical
Some better class negro mechanics and also lower class negro laborers - domestics - some white clerical and wage earners

This area is level on the eastern side adjoining the main business district to rolling on the western side. White population is largely concentrated adjacent to area C-4, north of W. 9th St., and the greatest negro concentration is in the southeast and southwest part of the area. A colored low-rent housing project has been started on Main St. at College but will not be completed for about 12 months. It will contain 497 units.     The area as a whole consists of old, dilapidated houses, badly in need of repair, some few fairly good apartment houses. Schools and churches are in area and it adjoins principal business center.     Age of properties, lack of proper maintenance, type of population are such to make this a fourth grade area. Properties vary all the way from cheapest shacks occupied by negroes to large old brick houses now used as cheap rooming houses, some for white and some for colored.     About 5% of structures in this area are apartment houses containing 8-12 units of 2 to 4 rooms renting at about $15-$25 per month. They are old and not well maintained but proximity to principal business center keeps rental demand good.
Mechanics - white collar workers - wage earners
Gradual shifting to lower income group and rooming and boarding houses

Area is from level to steeply rolling, about 98% improved, within easy walking distance of central business district, has all utilities, both street car and gasoline bus transportation, grade school in it and city high school at northeast corner. At the northwest corner on Bluff View are located about 10 large expensive homes still occupied by original owners, who are people of wealth and built these houses at this point because of the scenic view of the Tennessee River and the high elevation, but they are certainly misplaced. That part of the area east of Palmetto and from Oak St. to Fort Wood St. also contains some very large expensive homes, but the owners are trying to sell and can find no buyers. North, east and south are negro areas. Southern part of the area, Vine St., Oak St., and McCallis Avenue are filled with rooming and boarding houses (some good and some not so good) and also many apartment houses. It is just an old area, formerly occupied by people of means most all of whom have moved to other sections and left their large, fine old homes to be used as boarding or rooming houses or converted into apartments.

Part of the area north of McCallie is all negro except on McCallie and Oak east of Central Avenue. Some better negro properties on 5th St. off Central Avenue. Remainder of this part contains all kinds of negro properties with the bad predominating. Negro park at the northern corner of area. Railroad yards from the east boundary and noise and smoke is a nuisance. In that part of area south of McCallie, whites live in about 4 blocks from western side on 8th St. and negroes in other part of 8th to Central Ave. The principal negro business district of the city is located on E. 9th St. and negroes reside on it to Magnolia where whites reside on to Central Ave.     It is a mixed area of old houses, mixed population, poor maintenance, contour from rolling to hilly and about only thing in its favor is that it is within easy walking distance of main business center.     Schools, churches and stores are located in the area.     Sales activity almost exclusively in negro properties.
Common laborers - wage earners - factory workers - all low income

This area is level to rolling with mixed population. Railroad belt line runs through eastern part and railroad yards join it in west. Some small industrial plants located on western side. Transportation and school facilities are adequate and negro high school located in area. Stores are also scattered through the area. Warner Park, largest in the city, joins at the southwest corner. There are some very nice small homes scattered throughout the area but the predominance is the cheap, poorly maintained type. About half of the properties in the area have outside toilets, no bathrooms.     Sales activity is almost entirely in negro properties and is fair for them - but there is no demand for white properties.
White collar workers - skilled mechanics, tradesmen
Infiltration of lower income group and exodus of former original owners of better income

This area is known as Highland Park, is level to rolling, has all utilities, grade and high schools located in it and also community stores especially along McCallie Avenue which is dotted with beer taverns, filling stations, and stores of every description. It is one of the older residential sections and one of the first suburban developments of original Chattanooga. It is convenient to the principal business district and transportation facilities are excellent. It is about 95% improved. The better part of the area is between Holly and Beech Streets, east and west, and Duveau and Kirby, north and south.     During depression years foreclosures were probably more in this section than anywhere else in the city and this fact together with infiltration of people of lower income has been the cause of declining prices. Accessibility to principal business section, proximity to Jackson Park and Warner Park, combine to make rental demand good in this area.
Factory workers, mechanics, white collar workers

This area is composed of Audubon Blvd., Versailles Blvd., and Fontainebleau Dr., between Short and Versailles. Audubon Blvd. contains the older properties but they are the substantial type and have been well maintained. Fontainebleau Dr. also contains older properties and the lower priced properties of the area. Versailles Blvd. contains the more recently built properties.      

Residential desirability in this area is of the highest. Audubon and Versailles Blvd. restricted to single family. Wealth of shade trees throughout area. Transportation by street car on S. Claiborne Ave. and gasoline bus on Fontainebleau and is adequate, also electric bus crossing Fontainbloau at Broadway. It is very close to Tulane, Sophie Newcomb and Loyola Universities. Grade and high schools, churches and community stores near. Easy access to central business center by S. Claiborne.     

Area about 90% improved and generally accepted as good as any from the standpoint of residential desirability.     

Conveyance records for 1937 show 2 sales of vacant lots at about $45 and $60 per front foot, and 8 single family houses and 1 duplex, ranging from $7100 to $15,000; for 1938, 3 vacant lots and 6 single family houses.

This area is fairly level except on the eastern side which goes into the side of Missionary Ridge where it is rolling and hilly. It is composed of small single family homes occupied by people of lower incomes. Several industrial plants are located on Dodds Avenue between 23rd and 31st Streets. That part of the area west of 4th Avenue is low and subject to overflow from Chattanooga Creek in flood seasons. Transportation and school facilities are ample and stores are scattered throughout the area. Cheap construction, low income of population, and age of properties make this a third grade area. It is about 75% improved.     Bids have been received for the construction of a low-cost housing project in this area, located on 4th Avenue between 23rd and 28th Streets. It is to be constructed on a vacant tract of ground containing 35 acres and when completed will cost about $1,500,000, and provide about 437 new units.     Feger Place, consisting of Morningside Drive and Eveningside Drive, located in northwest corner of area, is a small subdivision containing about 25 homes originally costing $10,000 to $15,000. However, this has proved to be a misplaced development, the subdivision has lost its desirability due to unfavorable surroundings and properties can hardly be sold for in excess of 40% of original cost.
Forest Place - East Lake, Chattanooga, Tenn.
Low income industrial workers - mechanics and laborers

The entire area is level to rolling, the part north of 23rd Avenue being the most heavily populated and the section in which most of the negro population resides. Transportation and school facilities are adequate and this part of the area is easily accessible to the business district. Years ago it was occupied by railroad workers, firemen and policemen but in recent years an undesirable element of very low income people has gradually taken it over.     On 23rd St., east of Montague Park, is a tract of 16 acres on which is to be constructed a new National Guard Armory costing about $200,000. Work is expected to begin on this in the near future.     That part of the area south of 23rd St. is level, extending on both sides of Rossville Boulevard, the principal street leading out of the city to the south. Many beer taverns, filling stations, junk yards and other undesirable places are located on Rossville Blvd. It is also low and subject to overflow from water of Chattanooga Creek during high flood seasons.     Houses are small singles of every description, badly maintained, population is largely of the shiftless type. There are a few fairly good houses in the area, most of them widely scattered, with Crescent Circle and Clifton Terrace (in Clifton Hills) having the better houses.
Professional, business men, executives, capitalists, some white collar workers
Gradual infiltration of people of more moderate income when original owners die or move away

This area is the southern part of Missionary Ridge - located on the top of the Ridge with an elevation several hundred feet higher than the city proper. It is rolling, lots are rather large and well wooded. The northern 2/3 of the area contains the most expensive homes occupied by some of the wealthier citizens of the city. It has all utilities but no stores are located on the Ridge. All but about the southern 1/3 is served by street car. The northern 2/3 is about 90% improved while the southern 1/3 is only about 60% improved - the Ridge widens out at the southern end and there is more ground available for improvement than in the northern part. It is a delightful place on which to live but apparently reached the height of its popularity some time ago and while still desirable and will continue so for many years, the trend is away from it.
Professional men - executives - salesmen - white collar workers

This area known as the Glenwood Subdivision was opened about 15 years ago, was well planned and laid out with curving roadways. Construction at the outset was of a rather high type but in more recent years some cheaper homes were built. It is level except towards the east which is rolling and extends into Missionary Ridge, but there are only a few improved lots on this side. Grade school located in area and only short distance to high school. Area has all utilities and adequate bus transportation - it is also only about 10 minutes drive to the principal business center. Generally, homes are well kept and there are indications of pride of ownership. Area only about 50% improved. For some reason it has stopped growing.
Professional men - executives - better income bracket
Present trend is to persons of more moderate income

This area is the northern part of Missionary Ridge. It has a very high elevation, is only wide enough on top for one street which in some parts has houses on both sides and in others the street runs along the side of the ridge and houses are therefore only on one side of the street. The sides of the ridge, except in a few spots, are too steep for building purposes. Area has all utilities, adequate street car transportation, grade school, but no stores are located on the ridge, but are not far distant. It is about 4 miles from the principal business center. Major portion of construction has been of the very expensive type but no new homes have recently been constructed. Originally it was occupied by the wealthier citizens of the city but in recent years they have been moving away and their homes are either being rented or sold at sacrifice prices. Available building sites are about 70% improved.
Business & professional men - executives - white collar workers, skilled mechanics and some wage earners.

This area lies east of Missionary Ridge and is reached by a tunnel through the ridge. It consists of East Highlands and a part of the Brainerd Section. It is rolling to hilly, is thickly wooded, lots are wide, schools and churches are located in the area, and there is quite an extensive community business center on Brainerd Road just after passing through the tunnel under the Ridge. Brainerd Road is dotted with tourist homes, filling stations, taverns, and is gradually going to business although there are some very substantial homes located on it but mostly towards the eastern end. Area has all utilities and adequate transportation by gasoline bus.     The East Highlands section is all outside the city limits and while it has all utilities and adequate transportation, type of construction is not as substantial as in the remainder of the area, and it is in this part of the area that the lower period properties are located and the lower income group of people live. Area as a whole is about 75% improved.
Professional men and executives with good incomes

This area is rolling, lots are wide, well maintained and well wooded. Construction is uniform and homes well designed. It is well restricted and restrictions have been more rigidly enforced than in any other section of the city. It is located outside the city limits but is served by gasoline bus and has city fire protection. The area is about 40% improved. Convenient to community business center on Brainerd Road.     Type of construction is good and maintenance of homes and lawns indicates high type of home ownership. The subdivision is so laid out to add charm and appeal. Northern part of area along Shallowford Road slopes rather steeply and this slope continues across the road, making building sites not as desirable, and no restrictions as to building are in effect - hence the jump from 1st to 3rd grade.

The area is very rolling, about 40% improved, but is handicapped by lack of uniformity. There are some very cheap properties located in it especially in the southern part. It has adequate transportation facilities. Schools are convenient as well as stores but churches somewhat distant.     Presence of cheap construction and poor maintenance and mixture of type of population make this a third grade area.
Professional men - executives, white collar workers

The eastern part of the area is level to rolling and the western and southern part rolling to hilly. Transportation is by gasoline bus and is adequate. Houses are well constructed and well maintained. Schools are convenient, community business center not far distant and municipal golf course is very close to the northeast corner of the area. Area is about 50% improved. The area is in line with present development and because of relatively low land values, new construction activity has been very pronounced.
Low income, industrial workers - mechanics - laborers

This is one of the very old sections of the city, level and about 80% improved. Many industrial plants are located west of Broad St. and just south of the area. Transportation and school facilities are adequate and stores of every description abound on Broad St., the western boundary, and Main Street, the northern boundary. Age of properties, lack of maintenance, mixture and type of population make this a fourth grade area.
White collar workers - employees of Chattanooga Medicine Company, mechanics

This section is known as St. Elmo. It is located at the base of Lookout Mountain and contour generally is from rolling to very hilly. Community business center is located in the north end of the area. Transportation and school facilities are adequate. Plant of Chattanooga Medicine Company located at north end of area provides employment to many residents of the area.     It is one of the older communities and its residents do not often move out of it, and on the contrary, it does not attract residents from other communities. It is some distance from the principal business center and the approach to the center of the city is through one of the worst sections of the city.

This is a level area, formerly Alton Park. Before it was annexed to Chattanooga every street in it was paved with concrete. Nearby and in the area are located plants of Armour & Company, Wilson & Company, a brick yard, and Chattanooga Glass Factory, which provide employment for many residents of the area.     Transportation and school facilities are adequate and several small stores are located in the area. Some distance to principal business center.     Area about 60% improved.     Presence of railroad tracks through area, industrial plants, cheap construction and low income of residents make this a third grade area.
Professional men, executives, some white collar workers

This area is located on top of Lookout Mountain, a separate municipality about 6 miles from the center of Chattanooga. It is served by 2 paved highways, also by an Incline Railway and gasoline bus from the railway terminus on top of the mountain. It has an elevation of 2200 feet and is especially delightful in the summer. This area is on the "inside" and does not include the sites overlooking the brow on either side, and therefore does not have the scenic advantages of the brow sites. For this reason, homes as a whole are not as expensive as those located in the brow sites and construction is not quite as substantial.     Terrain is rolling, lots are large and well wooded. Schools, churches, and stores are located in the area. Presence of small negro population is caused by the fact that they were brought to the mountain to work as domestics for the white population. There are about forty of these negro houses, mostly owned by the occupants, they range in value from $1000 to $2000 and of course, are not worthy of second grade, but these houses are somewhat scattered and there are not sufficient of them in one spot to make a separate area.

This area is located on Lookout Mountain and includes both East Brow and West Brow, which overlook the country for miles around, and on which many beautiful and costly homes have been built. Formerly the mountain was used almost entirely for summer homes for wealthy people of Chattanooga, but in later years most of the inhabitants have been staying on the mountain the entire year. While some of the houses were built as summer homes the great majority are of good construction, well planned and well maintained.     It is a separate municipality, about 6 miles from Chattanooga business center. There are two principal highways from Chattanooga to the top of the mountain and it is also served by an Incline Railway (in use about 40 years) from the base to the top, and gasoline bus also serves the locality on top of the mountain. Its elevation is about 2200 feet, which is about 1600 feet higher than Chattanooga proper, and it is a delightful place in which to live. It also has quite a historic background.     Its popularity has increased considerably during the past three years. The present trend to the mountain, the type of population, construction of majority of homes, and its desirability as a residential spot make it a first grade area.
INDIANAPOLIS Mars Hill and Surrounding territory
Lack of city facilities. Poor transportation. Cheap class of property and citizens.
Cheap subdivision developments west and south-west of Indianapolis. A moderate number of good type homes scattered thru area on which local institutions will lend.
Indianapolis National & Rockville Road Suburban Section.
Section of moderate priced houses, not far from the City Center
Lack of city facilities. Poor transportation. Passing thru blighted area on way to City Center.

Outlying section of better class laboring and mechanic type occupancy, desiring newer design of small house. Business development, most of inferior class, along Washington (National Road) Several cheap additions, but many fairly good houses in this section.
Small suburban town, incorporated. Near manufacturing plants.
Lack of proper sewage system. This is being corrected by new sewer. Limited school facilities also, which are being being corrected by additional building.

A small section not greatly affected by the depression in which prices remained very stable and will continue to improve as city facilities in this section are bettered. Building combination single house and bungalow types.
Close to factories for working people
RR yards, Stockyards, Factories. West part affected by overflow water from Eagle Creek
Native white - Laboring and white collar classes

Section immediately around Rhodious Park developed with some newer type bungalows. Section along Blaine from McCarthy and Morris and on the other streets west to Belmont and south Howard are best parts of this section, partially developed with newer type houses. Majority are home owners. Other sections affected by very low class native whites. Section from Howard to Minnesota and from Richmond to Hiatt - negro.
Catholic church and school on Warman Avenue.
State Insane Hospital -- Factories, RR tracks and switching yards.
Local institutions will lend on moderate riced residences in northern section and along Warman Avenue.
Proximity to RR yards and factories where most people in this district are employed.
In center portion of district, older type of houses. Northern portion lacks good transportation.

South portion: older type, rentable and salable to better laboring class. North and west portion: newer type with foreign classes and their descendants employed as mechanics in shops and with RRs. Good demand for sale and rental when factories are operating.
Lack of city facilities. Cheap construction. Small lots.
Cheap subdivision. Oversold in very small lots.
Proximity to new High School, near RR shops and yards and factory districts.
Surrounding cheap territory; State Insane Hospital to the west. Grade crossing of RR and blighted district on way to City Center.
Section occupied by RR and shop men and mechanics. New High School (one only in the west side of the city) creates demand for sales and rentals in this section.
Section north of 10th and section on Elder, Lynn and Traub north of Michigan: greater part negro, balance low standard whites.

North portion from Blake to Lacke and north to Indiana recently completed low-cost apartments for negroes. There is possibility that balance of this territory west of Blake and north of Michigan may be taken over by City, County and state for development as Park, overlooking hospital development on the west.
Level to rolling, with hilly land along the River and Creek.
Number of estates developed particularly along Eagle Creek branches in the extreme northwest
Number of cheaper type subdivisions developed; lack of city facilities; lack of transportation
Frame and Br Veneer from large Bungalows

A very spotty section. Some parts in particular near Creeks and rolling land --  developed into large estates with prospect of continuing development of such types. Along Michigan Road a number of cheap subdivisions with non-modern type houses on average to large lots. Section west of Broadmoor Ave -- attempted development along new Blvd. which failed, -- somewhat over developed -- considerable time for an active demand in this particular section. Small section called "Spring Hills, Inc." is subdivision on high land above the River, north of Riverside Park -- an attempted likewise section in which several years ago an amount of extreme wealthy attempted to develop into large estates, building houses from 150,000 to 300,000 with no demand for such types today. Immediately west of Riverside Park is abuilt-up section with some good and some cheaper type houses.
Level to rolling. Small restricted section known as "Golden Hill"
Small restricted section of large lots and small estate tracts
Cheap section south. Cemetery to east.
Attractive location for property known as "small estates," yet not far from city center.
Native white - Laboring and Mechanic classes
Small section of high land overlooking White River. Developed into medium to large estates.
Lack of city facilities, also transportation.
Small large-estate section. Particularly popular to a certain social group. Generally find buyer available if the present owner must sell.
Near good section of the City and Schools
Near cemetery. Several older type houses. Number of negro families of better grade.

Narrow strip - 42nd to 43rd Sts. from Boulevard Place west: solid white section but affected by several negro families in section south of 42nd St. From Maple Road to 42nd St. a number of negro families of the better type the majority is a white neighborhood. "East: Crown Hill and 32nd St. to Maple Road and Salem Street West, a number of older type homes. Several apartments on west side, particularly Boulevard Place -- in which a few negro families reside.
Site of Butler University in west portion. All city facilities.
Native white; executive and other white-collar type

West of Illinois Street: Influenced by Butler University. 42nd & Central: New Catholic Church and School where such families with good incomes desire their children to attend grade schools. Other section north of this, newer type houses, mostly brick veneer, built within last ten years.
South portion near best High school. good schools -- Churches of all denominations. Transportation excellent. All sections enjoy all city facilities.
South portion: number of two-family houses and four to sixteen family apartments. Section along east edge near Monon RR tracks.
Frame & Br. Veneer singles, duplexes; Br. Apartments

Section along Meridian Street: to large high class apartments. Along 28th, trend is to business and apartments. Extreme east section, along both sides of Winthrop Avenue, affected by Monon RR tracks. Along Pennsylvania Street and north of 38th: large older type good homes. Small section in extreme north east: cheaper type bungalows and some older type frame houses.
Near good schools and churches of all denominations. Short distance from City Center.
Older type houses. some very large -- used for rooming house purposes

In section from 19th to 22nd Sts and from west side of Delaware to west side of Central Ave known as "Martin's Place" - large older type well built residences, some converted into apartments and 2-fam. units, still in good rental and fair sales demand. Section from 22nd st. north to Fall Creek and from west side of park to east side of Broadway, large older type houses of fairly good construction, good rental and fair sale. Section north of Fall Creek from Penn St. east to College older type single family and 2-fam. units, still desirable rental, with fair sales demand. Section east of Fall Creek, north of 28th St. mixed 1 & 2 Fam. units, fair rental section, but very poor sales. SEction along Illinois St. -- mixed with old type one-two fam. singles, business property and apartments, fair rental but very poor sale. Balance of section mixed with large old, fine residences, to cheap older type frames, declining, except for possible development of apartments on Delaware, Pennsylvania, Central, Park and Broadway.
Portion is desirable residential neighborhood for better class negroes.
Generally down except for better negro portion.

North of 24th St. to 29th and from west side of Capitol Ave. to Clifton (except for small section south of Roache) and west of Northwestern Ave -- a former good white section in which better class negroes now reside. However, there still remain a number of white families scattered thru this district. South of 25th, east of Northwestern and south of Roache, west of Northwestern, --  older and cheaper negro houses. Section along 29th and 30th: white neighborhood affected by negro infiltration. Section along Grayson Avenue-Capitol Avenue, also affected by negro infiltration. Section along Kenwood and Illinois -- are larger 1-2 fam. old houses occupied by lower class whites and are used partly for rooming houses. Local lending institutions will lend mortgage money to negroes of better class. Extreme northeast section is a small addition built up of very cheap houses across from Crown Hill Cemetery.
Poor transportation, thru blighted area to City Center. RR tracks.
South portion: majority white. North portion: East of Harding -- decided infiltration of negroes. Local institutions will make loans on better class properties in this section.
Very old type houses becoming occupied on the east portion by negroes. New RR tracks and switching yards.

Section along Bellefountaine, Guilford and Winthrop, south of 22nd now 80% of negro. Extreme north section along McPherson-white section, mostly rentals. Number of these houses have been remodeled into cheap small apartments.
Negro Park and Municipal Golf Course.
Older type houses. RR tracks and factories. Part of section occupied by lower type negroes.
South and center portion older white neighborhood now occupied 100% by negroes. East portion cheap to fair newer type houses. Section around Douglas Park and north of 30th -- better class negroes
Very old. Some remodeled into cheap apartments and rooming houses. Part is factory district.
Very old section. Alleys occupied by negroes. Some factories scattered thru the district.
Indianapolis Old section near Arsenal High School.
Arsenal Technical High School. Good Transportation. Large Catholic Church in south portion.
Very old type houses. Factories and RR tracks.
Extreme north section: negroes. Center portion: poor sale but fair rental-- near car barns and high school. South portion: large older type houses. In an old Catholic Parish
Indianapolis Woodruff Place and surrounding territory
Number of schools and churches. Good transportation-short distance-to City Center.
Older type houses. Number of 2-family units. Women's Prison affects rent and sales on Randolph and Hamilton Avenue from New York to Michigan only.

Section known as "Woodruff Place" small incorporated town. Enjoys all city facilities and police protection. This section at one time was high class residential, now being remodeled into small apartments and very desirable rental for that class. Section: east side of Randolph and east side of Hendrick place,-- development about 20 years old of good type singles and two family units. Good rental and fair sales. Other parts, older types and somewhat depreciated.
Largest Catholic Parish. Close to good Public High School.
Several older type houses, but mixed with majority of better type.
This section good because of desire of families of depreciated sections to move into this part of City particularly because of High School and Church influence.
Large well developed city park and parkways along small creek. Number of grade schools and Protestant Churches.
Except fro 10th Street, -- poor transportation. Number of older type houses particularly in west end. Extreme northwest side borders on colored section.

Best residential section: from Oxford St. east to east side of Tuxedo and along south side to Brookside Parkway. Several newer type houses mixed with some of the older types; very good rental; fair sales section; however, an over development along both sides of Brookside Park. Extreme west and northwest: older type houses; only fair rental and sales.
Indianapolis East Section near Belt RR
Near RR switching tracks; coal and lumber yards.
Native white- Laboring and white collar
Small section, eastern part of city, with many old and new type houses. Always has been fair rental, but slow sale. Affected by RR tracks.
Indianapolis Tuxedo Park and Section north
Good transportation, except in north section. Varied number of schools and churches.
Proximity to Belt RR tracks. Some small factories along said tracks. Number of older type houses from Washington to Michigan. Number of cheaper class properties in extreme north section.

Section from Michigan to 10th Street on Denny and Chester and part of Grant Street, sales and rent very active. These are the three very desirable streets in this section. Section from Washington to Michigan; older type, cottages, singles and doubles; fair sale and good rental. Extreme north section: Number of cheaply built, though quite modern, homes.
Near new Catholic Church and School; also good grade school and Protestant Churches.
Poor transportation -- bus service to downtown
Small section built around new Catholic Church and School. Very desirable to young couples of ordinary means.
Eastern part of the City -- mostly level lots and streets
Boulevard along creek. All city facilities. Near public park. Newer development of good type house, fairly well restricted.
Section along 10th Street -- transportation not good and far from Schools; "Hower" School is to be built in this Section. Other parts excellent transportation and school facilities.

Best residential section east part of Indianapolis. Section along Pleasant Run Parkway, east of Emerson Avenue, developed with good type frame and brick veneer singles from new to 20 years old. All well kept. Section from Ritter east and south of 10th -- developed with frame and brick veneer bungalows and singles, from new to 15 years old. Section from 10th north of 12th Street and from Emerson Avenue to and including Hawthorne Lane, newer type frame and brick veneer bungalows. Section along north side of 10th Arlington -- not built up but next in line for eastern section of City. Section from west side of Kenmore Road to Edmondson and from Washington Street to south line of Shelby St. -- brick veneer and frame bungalows and singles. West part of which is built up nearly 100% and east part being developed. Section east of Emerson to Pleasant Run Boulevard and from Michigan St. north to said Boulevard, 100% built up, good type frame and brick veneer singles and bungalows from 8 to 18 years old. A very excellent sale section.
Lack of city facilities and transportation in most parts. Bordering on RR tracks.
Native white- Laboring and white- collar clerical

Small section west of Emerson between RR tracks, very poor sale and rental. Section east end of Irvington, south of Washington on Webster, Cutherwood and Sheridan, negro. Also scattered along east side Arlington Avenue. Greenfield Ave. extreme south end of Ritter and east part of Burgess Avenue, also scattered negro. Section north of Minnesota on both ways from Emerson, built up chiefly with non-modern cheap houses
Older but good section of former fine residential section of Irvington. New stores, churches and schools.

Good old section of Irvington. A former very good residential suburb. Older -- but good single houses mixed with two-family doubles more recently constructed. Along Washington Street: apartments, business and family units.
Lack of city facilities in most of territory. Poor transportation. RR grade crossing at Madison Avenue on way to reach City Center.

Section developed with small semi-modern and modern type houses-- section only partially developed, bordered by good and cheaper sections. Considerable spotty possible development along Madison Avenue not of good type which affects the entire neighborhood.
Near factories and shops for laboring and mechanic classes.
Lack of transportation in most part. Near RR tracks

Four negro sections: one west from Sherman Drive and south of Prospect-- heavy. Extreme west end from Lawton to Calhoun, Shelly to Draper. From Keystone to St. Paul, north of Woodlawn and along Pleasant Street-- scattered. East of Keystone to Perkins from Reformers Avenue to RR tracks -- heavy. Section bordering Southeastern Avenue from Trowbridge east to LaSalle -- mortgage money for home purchase available from local institutions.
Near Center of City. Factories for working classes.
Very old houses. RR switching yards and industry
A very old section. Spotted with factories. Tax Assessments
Indianapolis Section East of Fountain Square
Short distance to City Center. Number of Churches: several Protestant--2 Lutheran and schools, and one Catholic and school.

Section occupied by mechanics and white collar type and also business men having stores within a short distance. Desirable section also for laboring and RR type of employee. In extreme southeast section number of newer type modern small bungalows.
Number of older German Type citizens near Lutheran Churches and Schools.
Older type houses; bordered by cheaper old class -- thru very old part of city to City Center
Old but good section. Nearly all home owners of German Lutheran type, desiring to be near to their Churches and Schools.
North portion, large German Catholic Church. South portion, number of newer type houses. Good school and Protestant Churches.
North section: older type houses. South section: factories along belt RR and grade crossing of two RR tracks.

North portion: Number of German Catholic families willing to maintain residences near large Catholic Church. South portion: Somewhat improved by development of Boulevard at Pleasant Run and elevation of Belt RR at Meridian Street recently completed.
Near Large Park. Good Transportation. Good grade of schools. Several Protestant and one Catholic Church and School.
Bordered by cheaper and older sections. Grade crossing - RR Tracks - to city Center.
Will remain good for several years

Section of south of Southern Avenue, newer type frame and brick veneer singles and bungalows in demand. Mechanics to white-collar type. Section east of Garfield Park to Shelby Street, and south of Raymond is beste residential section of South Side. Neighborhood business and professional men. Section east of Shelby Street around Catholic Church. Mostly mechanics. In thru this part are scattered about ten negro families -- better class, all home owners. West of Garfield Park not fully built up being developed with frame and semi-modern and modern bungalows -- mechanics and white collar type occupancy.
INDIANAPOLIS Older part of South Side
Very old especially in northern portion. Factories and RR tracks. Cheap construction in southern portion.
Fairly close-in section from truck gardens and greenhouses.
Poor transportation and lack of city facilities. Cheap additions developed in this area.

Section developed mostly by gardeners with vegetable and flower greenhouses. Above sales and rental ranges do not include greenhouses which represent additional investments of from $7000 to $25000. The low grade additions in the area are shown in RED. Section west of the I.C. RR. : low and subject to high water
INDIANAPOLIS St. Rock German Catholic Church Section
New German-Catholic Church and School (Branch of large old German -Catholic Parish) Not far from City Center
Lack of city facilities and improved streets

Section being developed by younger citizens of German descent, will greatly improve during the next several years. Large lots to acreage tracts. Number of truck green houses scattered thruout the section
Large city Park. Number of Protestant Churches. One Catholic Church and School.
Distance from transportation in east portion and several negro families. In west portion, several older type houses.
Influence of Garfield Park, Churches, etc. in this section creates a good demand for mechanic and laboring classes, as well as lower bracket of white-collar class.
Near city Park and factories. Fairly good transportation.
Older type houses. Near RR tracks.
Native White - Laboring and white collar
Section developed in the cheap-to-fair houses. Desirable for laboring classes.
Indianapolis Churchman Avenue and outlying sections.
Proximity to RR shops at Beech Grove-- near factory district in southeast Indianapolis.
Lack of complete city facilities in most of this territory. Poor transportation.
Section developed with cheap to fair type houses on small lots to acre tracts for mechanic and laboring classes. Golf course shown on plat has no influences on the section.
Flat terrain. Contiguous to Indianapolis on the south. Inhabited chiefly by employees of CCC, St. Louis RR shops.
Convenience to employment in RR shops
Static -- depending no employment in RR shops
Best part of RR shop district. Excellent rental and sale section of small houses when RR shops are in operation.
Adjacence to Big Four RR shops
Poor transportation. Lack of city facilities in most parts.

East part of Beech Grove, older type non-modern houses close to RR shops. Other part of this section, sparsely built up with cheap to fair type single family homes. Mortgage money is available in this territory from local institutions.
Small section near small College (Indiana Central) at southern edge of the city.
Unimproved streets - distance to grade and high school. RR Tracks.
College will develop some, and increase demand. Streets will be improved and grade school facilities bettered.
Suburban section not far from city center. Good transportation.
Lack of city facilities --  number of cheaper type houses. Few restrictions in most additions.

Section not far out, where working men and mechanics can have small additional ground for gardening purposes in addition to homes. A number of very good frame and brick veneer homes in this section. Most purchasers buy or build non-modern homes and improve and modernize as finances permit.
Lack of transportation and city facilities
This territory developed from cheap houses to good small estates. In a number of cases-over-development.
Proximity to Beech Grove Big 4 RR shops. Extreme southeast to Five Points, lots and tracts sufficient for gardening purposes. Luthern section with Church and School.
Lack of city facilities; transportation; number of cheap additions developed in and near this section.

Five Points: German Luteran settlement, with church and school, except for cheap addition immediately to the east which is being poorly developed because of lack of drainage. Southeastern Avenue: developed with cheap frame to good brick veneer singles. Large tracts, mostly un-platted. This piece of ground comprising 120 acres which was formerly a Catholic Protectory was recently purchased by the Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. of New York. Development of the tract is expected to begin in July of this year with the construction of a low cost housing project. Plans under consideration call for the expenditure of $100,000,000 over the next few years in the completion of the development. The location is not likely to attract better than middle class tenants, but the intention of the owners is to keep out anyone who might be considered undesirable for various and sundry reasons. Proceedings on the the thought of being as selective of occupants as is consistent with maximum occupancy, restrictions will undoubtedly be modified should the response of the public be apathetic. It is, therefore, too early to predict with any degree of accuracy exactly what grade the area will become. The surrounding neighborhoods are all third class, today, housing a large percentage of Russian (some with Communistic tendencies) and Italians. It is very probable that much of the demand for quarters in this development will come from this class whose rents are from $10-15 per room.

Rooland, opened a year ago by the Charles E. Vawter Investment Company. Forty-six houses had been built in the fall of 1938, financed on a blanket FHA loan (under Section 210) with the release clause. At the end of January 1939, 22 of the 46 houses had been sold. They are a variety of brick, stone and frame bungalows, 1 1/2 and 2-story structures selling from $4500 to $7200, the big majority at about $6000. It is a "high pressure area" as to sales promotion situated in a rural neighborhood, surrounded by farms, with a cheaper residential section adjoining on the west. Sales are made to wage earners, minor executives and small business men, some of whom borrow on life insurance policies to make the 10% down payment. Some houses are offered at no down payment, but amortized at larger monthly payments until the equivalent of a 10% down payment accrues. It is graded "A" because it is now, restricted, not entirely built up. The construction is not as substantial as that in other newer sections, including Country Club. The area has all utilities except sewers. Public utility transportation is inadequate. School children are transported by bus to nearby schools. Shawnee Mission High School is to the southwest about two miles. Taxes will run from $40 to $55 a year on the various properties. Application was made in January for another blanket loan to finance 34 houses of the same type and size to be built in 1939. Some lenders, including Prudential, will lend here only because of the insured mortgage feature.

The growth of this subdivision has been sufficient to warrant the establishment of a Post Office there, which was authorized in April 1939. While a good many FHA loans have been made in the area there are loans which are not FHA but made by the building and loan associations in Kansas City, Kansas and other points in Kansas, as well as the Federal savings and loan associations of Kansas City, Missouri. The Home Building & Loan Association of Ottowa, Kansas is quite active in this area. Building and loan association loans other than FHA are usually made up to 75% of the market value.

The outer fringe of the community on all sides stretches into farm land. The town has a wide variety of types of construction, all singles with one-story houses predominating to about 75%. About one-dozen houses built during the last twelve months, (financed on FHA plan) have sold readily. There is very little demand and activity for other houses selling for more than $4000. The community has good schools, utilities, as well as electric interurban transportation to Kansas City. there is also a rather active business center adequately serving the community.

Mission Highlands, a development begun by Mission Hill Investment Co., 10 years ago, designed to house an "average" class of people. It is a bungalow area, houses uniform in size but many have no basements. The developer is advertising new houses for $3750 to $6500. The area is about 50% built up on reasonably level to slightly rolling ground. All streets are oiled. The area is served with gas, water and lights. Public transportation is inadequate and the long distance from stores is another handicap. School children are transported by bus. This area is occupied by a moderate income group of wage earners and clerks who work in Kansas City. Construction of 7 houses in the $4000-5000 class was begun in April 1939. The area gas been sluggish as to demand for 3 to 4 years.

Fieldston, another J.C. Nichols development, begun about fifteen years ago built up between 52nd and 55th Streets with large houses, mostly frame, several brick. Lots are advertised at $20 per foot. Houses herein are larger in size than those of A-1 and A-2 and attract a higher income group. That portion of the area south of 55th Street, sparsely built up, is a most attractive wooded neighborhood attractively landscaped and intended for large country estates. There are probably 15 to 20 houses built therin, all 2 or 2 1/2 story houses. That includes Bryant-wood. The area is restricted and has all utilities. Demand for property in this area has been slow, this being another high priced area.

This is Fairway, a J.C. Nichols subdivision, begun in April 1938. In April 1939, 87 houses had been built and 15 were under construction, or contracted for. Several Kansas City builders were operating in the area. Construction runs from 5-room bungalows to 8-room houses, selling at from $5500 to $8000, vacant lots advertised at $20 per front foot. About 75% are frame houses attractively painted white, the balance a mixture of brick, brick and stone, and a few stucco. This area is restricted, served by a community sewer and all other utilities. Children are transported by bus to a school a mile to the northwest. Nearby golf clubs are an attraction; also the suburban atmosphere, freedom from smoke and low taxes. Nearly all of the houses have been financed on FHA plans. The annual tax averages $55 per year. An area with more "tone" than A-1, A-4, or A-7, other new developments in Johnson county. Persons with a $175-225 monthly income are buying in this area.

An area begun shortly after the advent of FHA, wherein several builders have erected houses selling at $5500 to $8000 with a few at $10,000 in the Swatzell Addition on 50th Street between Belinder and Hudson. About 80% of the houses are frames attractively painted white, 20% brick. The ground is slightly rolling. The area has all utilities including a community sewer. Chas. E. Vawter Investment Company has made application for a FHA loan to finance 30 new houses in the Swatzell addition. The area has attracted moderate income people, some business and professional, from Kansas City, Missouri and Kansas City, Kansas. Virtually all the houses have been FHA financed. It is something of a high-pressure area as to sales. Public utility transportation is only fair. School children are transported by bus, although the Shawnee Mission School is almost within walking distance.
Mission Township Johnson County Kansas City, Kansas
Not a rent area, only few available

Westwood Hills, a J. C. Nichols development opened in 1923, which had built up 80% ten years ago. Houses are well built with much attention to architecture and position on the lots. It is an attractive neighborhood in rolling hills in style and quality quite similar to Westwood Park (B-11) adjoining on the Missouri side. It was something of a medium priced Country Club development. Adjoining the Kansas-Missouri state line, it has all the advantages of the Missouri metropolis, including all utilities, adequate transportation and school facilities, together with the suburban atmosphere of Johnson County and lower taxes. A very good second-grade section given a second grade because of its age, the fact that its houses do not have modern conveniences and the general reason that the district has reached its peak.

This is Westwood Park, one of the J.C. Nichols Country Club developments begun immediately after the World War. It has a substantial class of houses, intended for something of the middle-class business and professional people. The center of the area is on a hill running north and south, attractively laid out and well kept. It has all the conveniences of adequate transportation, close to the Plaza business district, the golf clubs of Johnson County, Kansas and other influences of being in the Country Club District. The fashionable County Day School is at the south edge. A good second-grade area.

This area embraces the best of the far-flung, nationally-known J.C. Nichols exclusive subdivisions. The northern portion to Westover Road is Sunset Hill. Between 75th and Mayer is Hampstead Gardens and between Meyer and 68th is Meyer Circle. Except for the northern portion the terrain is reasonable level between Wornall and Ward Parkway. Near the Kansas State Line the large mansions are artistically located in rolling hills. Mission Hills on the Kansas side is a continuation of this area as to type, style and quality of the home therein. Some of the wealthiest Kansas Citians live in this area. An encroachment of their gambling operations have adversely affected value during the last four years. The large homes in this area, some of which cost between $100,000 and $200,000, have dropped at least 60% in value since 1929, while the general run of houses costing between $25,000 and $60,000 suffered a 50% shrinkage. A large number of the mansions are on the market at low prices. Despite the fact that the area was begun eighteen years ago and is in some respects is declining, it continues to be the "gold coast" of Kansas City and with adjoining Mission Hills is one of the outstanding exclusive residential subdivisions of the United States. Although taxes on some of the large houses are high, this area like other parts of Country Club does not bear a fair proportion of the tax buren in relation to other parts of the city.

Mission Hills, one of the country's most attractive subdivisions. Highly restricted, it was built up of large homes distinctive in architecture, original costs ranging from $25,000 to $150,000. It was begun twenty years ago and began at once to attract (together with that party of Mission Hills lying in Kansas City, Missouri) the leading business and professional men of the city, drawn from older exclusive sections such as C-24, C-28, and C-30. Teh area lies in rolling hills, has charm, tone and appeal. Much attention is paid to landscaping the area as well as the position of the houses upon large lots. On the northwest the area is protected entirely by golf clubs and on the south by Indian Hills and a vacant tract destined to build up with a fine group of homes.
