Part of the old city, although development was slow. Eastern section not subdivided until 1910. Zoned for multi-family construction. Area, as a whole, conform fairly well as to type, and maintenance is better than would be expected in such an area. Financing limited as to property and individual. The few Negro families (two known) are said to affect values of only adjacent properties. Graded "low yellow".

Convenience to city center, transportation, schools, churches and trading centers. Development of district under supervision of competent sub-dividers has had an effect of establishing its pattern along distinctly favorable lines. Proximity to city's main high schools. Below city average in population density.
Proximity to business and lower grade areas. Some sales resistance to property abutting high school on account of noise and student car parking.
White collar workers, small business men.
Convenience to transportation, schools, churches, trading and recreational areas. General homogeneity of population and improvements High quality of upkeep.

This area consists of 7 subdivisions which were placed on market during period from 1913-27. Is zoned 2-family residential with exception of extreme northwestern section where multi-family dwellings are permitted. The area was developed under adequate & strictly enforced deed restrictions, which have generally expired. Improvements are 98% single-family dwellings of medium price range, which are well constructed and concorm to type. Population consists of moderate income group and is generally homogenous. Sales and rental demand is steady. Maintenance is of good quality. Is a well regarded, popular price area and is accorded a "low blue" grade.
Generally level with no construction hazards. City operates some large gravel pits in hatched portion of area, and this part would be unsuitable for residential sites.
Inadequate transportation, churches, and public utilities, including sewers and street improvements. Proximity to levee and Southern Pacific Railroad.
Too small an improved area to measure variations

Practically all the improvements in this area are in the 2 blocks between 64th & Park Streets which were subdivided in 1907. There are no deed restrictions, and zoning permits 2-family residences; however, improvements consist entirely of four and five-room, frame, single-family dwellings of below medium quality of construction. These are usually old and obsolete. The area is very largely unplatted, and land improvement is so small that is is difficult to classify. Owing to its distance from city center, lack of appeal, and detrimental influences noted, the area is accorded a "low red" grade.

Proximity to industrial district to the north. Planning Commission has designated McKinley Blvd. as a future major traffic arterial and H Street already somewhat affected by heavy traffic volume. Above average density of population in parts of area.
Professional & business men, skilled artisans, etc.
(33rd to D- North of McKinley 20 years.)

This area includes subdivisions platted in 1910,11,22,24,25,26,29 on 32nd and 33rd Streets, but pattern is well established. Zoned portion single-family; balance two-family. There is a steady sale and rental demand for property in this area, particularly on those streets abutting the park. The northwest section is somewhat lower grade, with some evidence of "Jerry building." The area as a whole is accorded a "high blue" grade.
Convenience to schools, churches, transportation, trading centers, and recreational areas. Nearness to city center, State Capitol Buildings and areas of industrial employment.
Proximity to railroad, industry, and business. Heterogeneity of population, type, size, and age of improvements, and quality of maintenance. High density of population in 2 southern tiers of blocks.

Population density considerably higher than city average. Encroachment of industry and commerce. Heterogeneous population. Age and obsolescence of residential structures. Western Pacific Railroads renders abutting residential properties practically unsaleable, except at a great discount.

Present housing predominantly 1-family but restrictions have expired and zoning permits multi-family except in northeast portion which is zoned 2-family Originally platted in 1850 with many lots 40x80. In eastern portion along 21st, 22nd, & 23rd streets are many old, mansion type houses, 25 years or more of age which still house original owners and which are well maintained. A few scattered blocks is better located would warrant a "blue" rating. However, the area is very mixed and warrants individual property consideration became of its lack of homogeneity. As a whole it is graded "medial yellow".
Level with favorable grade and no construction hazards.
Convenience to transportation, schools, churches, trading and recreational centers. Proximity to industrial employment. Population density below city's average.
Presence of levee and Southern Pacific Railroad. Excessive "hbo" traffic. Encroachment of business and industry.
Common & skilled laborers some white collar workers

An area without deed restrictions and, with exception of the extreme eastern portion, which is zoned 2-family, and the half-blocks on southern perimeter, zoned multi-family residential, zoning is "general commercial" and "heavy industrial." Improvements, are generally fairly well-maintained. Characteristics of area similar to those of ARea C-7. Population, while of the lower social and income levels, contains but few subversive elements. Residential improvements are largely confined to district south of the railroad. The area, on account of hazards mentioned and general lack of appeal, is accorded a "low red" grade.
Level with favorable grade and no construction hazards.
Proximity to industrial employment and trading centers. Adequate transportation and grade schools. Walking distance to city center.

Old area is without deed restrictions, and while zoned general commercial & multi-family residential, the improvements are predominantly single-family, five and six room, frame dwellings of cheap to medium quality construction. Those dwellings are, as a rule, quite old, but for a district of this kind have been well maintained. Population is very mixed. Italians predominate but with a sprinkling of Mexicans, Negroes, and Orientals. The subversive character of population constitutes the area's principal hazard. The area is accorded a "medial red" grade.

Transportation, schools of all grades, churches, trading and recreational areas conveniently available. Nearness to city center and State Office Buildings. In path of city's growth. Below city's average density of population.
Improvements somewhat heterogeneous as to age and architectural type in certain sections of area; this is overcome to a large extent by high quality of upkeep and maintenance.
Small business men, white collar workers, skilled artisans
Few 2-family dwellings, few larger, single family dwellings.

Maple Park Section (south of Markham) although platted in 1910 has only recently become popular. Deed restrictions are still effective. Zoning throughout is for 2-family houses but 1-family units predominate. Construction is good for price range and maintenance is above average. Architecture is fairly uniform except in portions of Maple Park. There are 3 negro families who own homes near the eastern perimeter  of Maple Park, but this influence does not warrant further penalizing of the area. In fact is is possible that some parts of the neighborhood will improve to better than its present medium blue rating.
Level with no construction hazards. There are some low spots in the hatched part of the area, which are flooded in times of heavy rain fall.

Adequate transportation, convenience to schools of all grades, including Junior College, churches, recreational, and trading areas. Beneficial affect of first-grade areas to the east. Homogeneous population and improvements.
Cemeteries on the north and industrial area on the west cause of some sales resistance to abutting properties.
Small business men, jr. executives, & white collar workers

This area was sub-divided in 1925 and is ample deed protected, only single-family dwellings being permitted, although zoning is 2-family residential. There is a steady demand for property in this area, both for rentals and sales. It is thought that the hatched portion of area will develop along same general lines when it is subdivided and marketed. Construction in the area is of generally good quality. The area is accorded a "medial blue" grade/
Level; no construction hazards in developed portion. Some places below grade in hatched part.
Adequate transportation, school, church, shopping and recreational facilities. In line of city's present development. Population density below city's average.
Proximity to Area D-7 which contains high river levee, upon which a railroad runs. Age and obsolescence of improvements, while not apparent upon casual inspection, are an actuality.
Common laborers to white collar workers

This area was subdivided and placed on the market in 1911 and 1912. Opened in 1911 and 1912. Now zoned for two-family houses, restrictions having expired. Houses are largely one-family units of cheap to medium quality, well maintained and of similar conformity. Population is homogeneous. The Negro family resides on the western perimeter and Japanese occupy leased garden tracts in the hatched part of the area. Although 7th & 8th Ave. properties appear good the possibility of infiltration of lower classes and the presence of above detrimental influences warrants only a "low yellow" grade for the section. The hatched portion is largely unplatted and under proper handling could develop into a moderate priced second grade area
Generally level. During periods of high water in the river there is danger of basement flooding from hydrostatic pressure. Land in western part near levee below grade.
Adequate transportation, schools, and trading centers. Proximity to Wm. Land Park, higher grade areas, and its ready accessibility.
Proximity to high river levee upon which are the tracks of two railroad lines. Presence of increasing number of Orientals. Heterogeneous improvements and population.
Very mixed - laborers to white collar workers

The southern part of this area was subdivided between 1909 and 1912, but deed restrictions have expired. The northern part is hatched and unplatted Zoning permits 2-family residences, but improvements consist wholely of small, frame, single-family dwellings of cheap to medium quality construction. Maintenance is remarkably good for this type of neighborhood. This is a border-line or buffer area, and location has little appeal. It is questionable whether hatched portion of area will ever be developed as a residential district. The area is accorded a "medial red" grade.
Level with favorable grades - no construction hazards.

Convenience to transportation, trading and recreational areas churches, etc. Particularly favored in being in close proximity to a junior college, high school, and grade schools. Nearness to downtown centers and to State Office Buildings.
None, fundamentally, but some evidence of a tendency toward heterogeneous architectural types.
Professional and business men-Sr. and Jr. executives

Development of area began in 1925, subsequent subdivisions being placed on the market in 1926-27-28-29-32-38, almost all carrying deed restrictions. 7th Ave. was dedicated in 1911, but abutting property was never platted. Is zoned 1 and 2-family residential, but over 95% improvements are single-family. Construction generally of good quality, homogeneity of social and income levels is fair to good. Including hatched portion of area, it is only about 25% developed. Is the fastest growing section of city, and when the hatched portion of area is developed, should be broken down and regarded. There is a high-grade, multi-family dwelling project in contemplation for this section. Under the circumstances, it is felt a provisional rating of low to medial green should be accorded. Is a keen competition for mortgages in area by all lending agencies, and bidding for loans is not uncommon. More than 25% of city's residential construction in 1937 was in this area.
Convenience to schools of all grades, including Junior College, churches, recreational and trading areas. Stabilizing effect of high grade areas to the east.
Inadequate transportation. Tendency toward heterogeneous population, which is mitigated and checked by better areas to east.
White collar workers, skilled artisans, etc.
None Mixture of Orientals, Mexicans, and low-class Italians.

This area was first subdivided in 1909, and was developed under deed restrictions, limiting improvements to single-family dwelling these restrictions have now expired, and zoning permits 2-family dwellings, but very few such dwellings have been constructed, and the area is predominantly single family dwellings of medium-grade construction, with high quality of maintenance. There are several families of Japanese on 8th Street in the "yellow" area to the west. The area is accorded a "low blue" grade.
Level with favorable grades, no construction hazards.
Convenience to transportation, schools, trading centers, churches, and recreational areas. Homogeneity of population and improvements.
There is evidence that 11th Avenue may become a main thoroughfare for heavy traffic.

This area, which is very sparsely settled, has adequate deed restrictions and is zoned single-family residential. The older portion east of Land Park Drive was subdivided in 1926 and the newer portion in 1938. Improvements generally conform both as to type and age, and construction is of the highest grade. This area enjoys a high degree of popularity and is accorded a "high green" grade.
College Tract and Land Park Tract
Washington - Yolo County Suburb of Sacramento
Generally level - some low areas near river. Subject to hydrostatic pressure due to high water in river would flood deep basements.
Adequate schools and trading center. Proximity to all classes of employment in Sacramento and in Rico Mills. Washington is an incorporated town with low tax burden.
Heterogeneous population and improvements. Inadequate transportation, public utilities, and street improvements. Pressure of subversive racial elements.
Laboring classes to white collar workers
Usually owner-occupied - no rental market for this purpose.

Comprises the incorporated town of Washington with a population of 2000 or more people. Construction ranges from very cheap to good and there are no restrictions or zoning laws. Maintenance is also spotty. The particular hazard is "racial"; 30% of the populace is foreign, including Orientals, Mexicans and low-class Italians. Although the section is heterogeneous with lodging houses, autotrailor camps, flats and dwelling units over stores its physical appearance is not as bad as might be expected. Graded a "medial red" area.
River bottom land protected from high water by levees. Subject to standing water in periods of excessive rainfall; possibility of hydrostic pressure aggravating this condition.
Good soil for subsistence homesteads. Accessibility by auto to industrial and commercial employment. Low taxes.
Inadequate transportation. Distance to schools and trading centers. Lack of sewers and paved streets. Heterogeneous population, improvements and maintenance.
Inadequate transportation. Being outside city limits, there is a lack of fire and police protection and no sewers. Proximity to low swamp lands to the south.

This outside, hatched area was subdivided some years ago as a substance homestead project, but its real development has only started in the past few years. There is no zoning nor deed restrictions. It is said to fill a community need and to hair fair prospects. With continued growth, many of the detrimental influences will be overcome. Property in the area is said to have a fairly ready market. It is hard to conceive of the area ever developing into a higher grade than the provisional "low yellow", which is assigned.
Generally level with no construction hazards. Western portion slopes toward Western Pacific Railroad.
Schools, churches, trading areas, and interurban transportation all available. Convenience to employment in Sacramento and new army air base.
Proximity to Western Pacific and Sacramento and new army air base.

Area has seemingly developed without direction. It has neither zoning nor deed restrictions and lacks homogeneity. There is said, however, to be a fair purchase and a good rental demand. It is understood that a zoning ordinance is in process of preparation for North Sacramento. There was a heavy default on local improvement bonds in this area, and a large amount of vacant lots was forfeited to the bondholders. This area has some possibilities, but present situation does not warrant a higher grade than "low yellow".
Level with no construction hazards. Hatched portion below grade of the developed parts of area.
Schools, churches and trading facilities adequate. Low tax burden. Charm of location. Highly deed restricted.

This is a new subdivision, located in natural oak grove. It is highly deed restricted but is without zoning. Improvements and population are homogenous, and construction is high class. There is a movement on foot to obtain a sewer system. This area has many of the qualities of a green area, but owing to detrimental influences set forth, it is deemed inadvisable to accord better than a high blue grade.
Convenience to schools, churches, and trading centers, Accessibility to Sacramento employment centers and new army base.
Heterogeneous population, improvements and maintenance. Proximity to Sacramento Northern Railroad on southern border. Inadequate transportation to Sacramento.
None (Some Portuguese & possibility 1 or 2 negro families eastern par

No zoning or deed restrictions, although zoning ordinance is said to be in preparation for North Sacramento. Improvements are mixed as to age but with a fair degree of conformity as to type. Construction is cheap to medium quality. This area is assigned a "medial yellow" grade.
Convenience to schools, churches, and trading centers. Proximity to Area B-1.
Some streets not improved. Mixed types and age of improvements. Proximity to railroad on the north.
Small business men, white collar workers, skilled artisans

No city zoning and very inadequate deed restrictions. In common with all areas in North Sacramento save B-1, this area shows the lack of direction in its development and presents a general heterogenous appearance, due largely to lack of uniformity in type and maintenance of improvements. Construction is of medium to good quality. Next to Area B-1, this is the best area in North Sacramento and is assigned a "high yellow" grade.
Convenience to schools, churches, trading centers, and interurban transportation. Readily accessible to employment centers in Sacramento and to new army air base.
Heterogenous improvements, both as to types and age, and spotted quality of maintenance. Proximity to two railroads in western and northwestern parts. Unimproved streets north of El Camino Avenue.
Laborers, white collar workers, small business men

A lower middle-class area, without zoning and deed restrictions. There were many defaults in Improvement District Bonds and much vacant property was forfeited to the bond holders. North Sacramento is said to have a zoning ordinance in preparation, but it is not yet effective. Construction ranges from cheap to medium quality. The northern part of area has a very low percent of land improvement, and it is possible that it may develop into a higher grade. The area as a whole is assigned a "medial yellow grade".
Convenience to schools, churches, trading centers, and industrial employment.
Proximity to business district on the north and low, swampy district to the south. Some streets unimproved.
Local business men, white collar workers, skilled artisans

No city zoning nor deed restrictions. This area has developed without direction, and improvements, consisting of single-family dwellings, are mixed as to type. Construction is generally of medium quality, and maintenance is spotted. Some homes in the area are of distinctly better type, and maintenance shows high pride of ownership. The area is assigned a "medial yellow" grade.

This is a substantial neighborhood with houses very well maintained.  Houses within Morrow Circle are the most desirable but the entire neighborhood is largely Polish and market is somewhat restricted.  Competition of new construction has affected prices on older properties because of lower payments, but this section should hold up fairly well because of proximity to Ford Motor Co. Transportation to Detroit is convenient and all other facilities are available.  Zoned for one family houses.   *See explanation sheet for Area Descriptions.
Water, gas, electric light, sewers. Remote from work. Adjoins negro area. Unpaved streets. Considerable foreclosure. 35% developed. Rates low 3rd grade or high 4th grade.

This is an area of substantially constructed brick houses which offers little promise of development in the near future; uniformity of type as well as a good grade of houses apparently costing up to $15,000 characterizes this small area. Curtiss Airport to the Northwest.

Located in Wauwatosa and Town of Greenfield. This area was platted with a view to development. There is a scattering of speculatively built houses. It is a typical outlying section with cheaper structures predominating. There are no restrictions, and modern conveniences are almost entirely lacking.
WAUWATOSA AND TOWN OF GREENFIELD WISCONSIN

Located in the Town of Greenville, an area of cheap houses occupied by persons desiring to escape higher city taxes. The area was begun with garage homes; today the area has bungalows under construction and all very cheap. The area has been swampy; a drainage development in the southern part of it promises to remedy this situation.
No utilities except gas and light
Somewhat low land, formerly flood hazard. Lack of restrictions. Distance from schools.

This is small area is situated in the center of the northwest sparsely settled section, and is reasonably well built up with a fair grade of houses. The area has a flood and drainage menace which has been partially but not entirely removed. Lack of restrictions and utilities is a distinct drawback to the area. It is occupied by working men entirely. This area is located in a part of Milwaukee County that may see considerable development at some time in the future. Spotty.
All utilities -- proximity to Smith Park and Silver Spring Park -- adequate schools -- transportation.
Mixed -- business, professional, skilled & common laborers

Parklawn, Government low-cost apartment project, is at the southwest of this area and is not a good influence. It is a typical working man's area with industry in several spots on the east. The area is made up of various types of construction, of many designs, with little conformity -- a spotty area.

A small area flanked on the southwest by industry and railroad tracks. It is occupied almost entirely by industrial workers - Russians predominating. It is one of the oldest sections of North Milwaukee.
Electricity -- gas -- metropolitan sewer facilities -- fair transportation only.
House of Correction to the west. Distance from schools. None other outstanding.

This neighborhood consists of various types of construction, mostly all jerry-build, including many garage bungalows. The development of the last three years is all a better grade of frame and some brick veneer, single family structures. There is a fair demand in this area for the cheaper type houses, presaging a good future. Rents are back to the 1929 level. Silver Spring Park and Smith Park nearby are advantages to the area.

Located in the Town of Greenfield; that portion of the area between Cedarburg Road and the railroad tracks is merely an extension of C-1 to the west which failed of development to any appreciable extent. That portion north of Silver Spring Road between the two railroad tracks is Crestwood, low-lying land. Although efforts were made to develop this section, up to this time it has failed to indicate an upward trend. Its future will lie entirely in a cheaper type of house. The railroad tracks on the northeast are graded to a height from fifteen to twenty feet, another adverse influence upon the neighborhood.
Proximity to Lincoln Park on the west and Estabrook Park on the southeast.
Railroad to north and industrial area. Distance from schools.

This area has an especial appeal to the laboring class because of proximity to manufacturing industries. Rapid transportation to downtown is available. Milwaukee River is to the south; riding academy to the north.
Lacks modern improvements -- no school in area.

This small section is occupied almost entirely by industrial workers from nearby industries which completely surrounded the area. Occupants are of the lower income groups. Low tax rates are a favorable influence. A heavy Polish infiltration has characterized this area during the last few years. It is on the down grade, much repair being needed. Along the railroad tracks which transverse the area, area a number of small industrial plants. It is entirely a wage earners' Section.

A few scattered houses in a platted subdivision similar in character to those in SB-1 west of railroad tracks. Fox Point Civic Center seen upon map to the east is platted but has not been developed. This area as well as SB-1 is in the River Hills section of Milwaukee County to which there is a trend as far as the better types of suburban homes. The largest and most expensive estates in the country are situated in the River Hills section and as such have a favorable reflection upon SB-1 and 2.

Railroad tracks traverse a portion of this area constituting a detrimental influence in its growth. Indications are that this section is due for development of a medium class of good houses. The better grade structures will be built near Lake Drive removed some distance from the railroad tracks. Fox Point Golf and Michiwaukee Golf Clubs add to the desirability of the section; also Doctor's Park and the lake shore to the east. Current values in this area range from $5,000 to $15,000. The area is located in Fox Point.

This small sparsely built section resembles the Fox Point Portion of A-1 as far as the type of security and occupants are concerned. Continued development will see this an excellent suburban residential district.
Level for the most part, with picturesque ravines through-out lake shore strip from northern extremity of area to Kensington.
Picturesque and wooded area -- lake shore influence -- parks -- adequate transportation -- school facilities -- all utilities.
Lack of uniformity in designs of some of the new houses, notably between Henry Clay and Silver Spring Drive, east of Shoreland to Hollywood -- no other major outstanding detrimental influences.
2-2 1/2, 7, 10 rms, brick & lannon stone; very few frame
Good - very few rent houses available.

This large area, extending from Fox Point on the north, to Kensington Avenue, embraces that portion of metropolitan Milwaukee that has witnessed the trend of the better and more expensive construction during the last 10 years. It includes the choicest residential parts of Fox Point, Whitefist Bay and most of Shorewood, all outside the city limits; therefore, having the advantage of slightly lower tax rates. The southern portion may be considered to be part of the "gold coast". Virtually all of the area is restricted as to price and type of structure. Ground values in the northern part shrunk 50% from 1929 but have returned to approximately 70% of that level. This area is picturesque, wooded and well kept and will undoubtedly continue to be the choice of higher income home owners. In the Fox Point portion there are estates with lots running from one-quarter acre to three acres.
SHOREWOOD, WHITEFISH BAY and FOX POINT
Adequate schools -- churches -- community center -- adequate transportation -- all utilities. Lincoln and Estabrook Parks to the southwest.

A very spotty area which is witnessing considerable new building, particularly west of Shoreland. The section west of Santa Monica lacks improvements such as storm sewers, paved streets, and street lighting. The portion between Henry Clay and Fairmount, Santa Monica and Lydell is almost all new and the trend will be upward despite the apparently unfavorable influence of the nearby railroad and industrial section. Sales activity has been best in northern portion of the area due to the lower price of properties there. The higher priced houses in the southern portion have been a drawback to sales. The area has a number of distressed building and loan-owned properties available at about 50% of 1929 prices. Its location in a choice part of the Milwaukee area presages an upward trend for this section.
Adequate schools -- adequate transportation -- all utilities -- churches -- community center.
Older and inferior type of security along Newhall & Bartlett, also Henry Clay to Fairmount, Santa Monica to Kimbark -- railroad and industrial section at the southwest
Singles, except few duplexes built before zoning ordinance became effective

That portion between Henry Clay and Fairmount, Santa Monica and Kimbark is a less desirable section bordering on third grade with cheaper and older houses. The same applies to Larkin and Newhall Streets. This area shares some of the favorable influence of its location in the Shorewood-Whitefish Bay Section. It is a spotty area with a good type of security along Cumberland and Ardmore between Hampton and Henry Clay. The sparsely built up section between Fairmount and Kensington should see a definite upward trend due to the amount of new building therein. Estabrook Park is to the southwest.
All utilities -- adequate transportation -- schools -- churches -- proximity to Milwaukee Downer College and Normal School; also high school.

A spotty area of substantial houses all located in the village of Capital Drive. These streets have several apartments. Estabrook Park to the west. Values in multi-family buildings were well maintained,

All utilities -- adequate schools, including Milwaukee Downer College and Normal School within area; also high school at Capital and Oakland -- churches -- influence of adjoining lake shore and "A" area -- adequate transportation.
Garbage incinerator west of Pinedale Court and railroad tracks to the west -- car barns near Edgewood and Oakland.

A spotty area wherein duplexes and multi-family dwellings predominate overwhelmingly due possibly to the influence of the exclusive girls' school, the seminary and normal school located within the area. The fact that it is not a great distance from the downtown business district also influenced apartment and duplex construction. Kern Park is to the west. From Oakland west, area is spotty and bad.

Adjoining Lake Park and nearby Lake Michigan -- restricted to 40 foot lots -- adequate transportation -- all utilities -- adequate schools including normal school, high school, exclusive girls' school and seminary nearby.

A "silk stocking" and high tax area adjoining and considered part of the "Gold Coast". It is typical of the exclusive and best section of 15 to 20 years ago. Lots are restricted to 40 feet. Despite the age of many of the properties, the area retains a degree of exclusiveness. South of Burleigh, recovery was not good. Values will be well maintained here on west end. Lake Park to the east. Riverside and Gordon Parks to the west.
All public utilities -- good schools -- highly restricted -- view property, Lake Park to the south; Downer College and Seminary to the west, also Milwaukee University School - both in B-3.
No rent in 1929. All home owners

This area embraces the southern part of Milwaukee's "gold coast" and probably it has reached its peak. The southern portion from Edgewood to Kenwood is the west side of Lake Drive due to traffic conditions and shortness of lots. The people who own homes here maintain the homes, lawns and shrubs in excellent condition. Property is strongly held and sales few.
All utilities -- adequate schools -- excellent transportation -- nearby Lake Park and Lake Michigan.
Nothing outstanding. Milwaukee River is to the west; also industrial area.
The cream of the apt. house district of Milwaukee
Almost all distressed apartment property owned by bondholders.

* No homes in this category for sale. Prospect Ave. in this area was Milwaukee's "Gold Coast" 40 and 50 years ago. The large mansions on this and nearby streets are developing into club rooms, better class rooming houses, and semi-apartments. There are many large apartments in the area located chiefly between North Ave. and Woodstock Pl.; among them some of the best apartments in the city, virtually owned and managed by bondholders. West of Oakland Ave. and south of Riverside Park are a poor grade of houses. In the eastern part of the area, with a good lake view, many of the old and substantial houses are occupied by the original owners. Trend in this area is to demolish old houses and replace by apartments. Riverside and Gordon Parks and Lake Michigan are decidedly favorable influences. The entire area is spotty, homes ranging from modest prices up to $60,000, many of the latter class costing about $200,000.
All utilities - Kern Park to the south and nearness to Lake Michigan on the east.
Surrounded by industry. A distance from schools.

This small area surrounded almost entirely by industrial ground is occupied by industrial workers. There are a few apartments on the west side of Humboldt Avenue. The area offers possibilities for future apartment house development because of favorable transportation to downtown and nearby industries. The low Milwaukee River bed is to the northeast. Kern Park at the south is a favorable influence.
All utilities -- fair transportation -- Lincoln Park to the east -- adequate schools.
Proximity to railroad -- electric line grade separation -- and industrial district.

A spotty area occupied entirely by working men. The eastern portion, now sparsely built up, will undoubtedly see some development of lower priced structures. It is a good rental area, rents being now back to the 1929 level.
All utilities -- adequate schools -- and transportation -- churches.
None outstanding. Industrial encroachment on west and east.

A spotty area occupied by a substantial class of wage earners, some smaller business men. That portion east of Green Bay Avenue is older than that west of Green Bay Avenue. Immediately south of B-7 are the newer houses of the section. On Atkinson Avenue are a number of apartments. This is a good third grade area.

Restricted to singles between 13th and 19th, Olive and Fiebrantz -- adequate schools include Rufus King High School in area -- adequate transportation -- close to shopping center -- all utilities -- churches.
Stadium at 19th and Fiebrantz -- car barns opposite stadium, 19th and Fiebrantz.

First development in this area was in 1926. The development is consistent with 40 foot lots. It is a highly competitive field for sales. Lots in 1929 sold for $3,000 a peice; today, $1200 - 1600. The area will undoubtedly extend north to W. Cornell.
All utilities -- schools -- churches -- adequate transportation.
Lack of restrictions as to price.
Business, professional white collared clerical; skilled labor.

This area has witnessed feverish building activity during the last 3 years, particularly since the advent of FHA, the majority of new homes having been financed through Title II loans. Most of the new structures are a substantial type of two-story brick, frame and lannon stone. The cemetery to the West, ordinarily a detrimental influence, appears to have little effect upon the desirability of the area, as houses are being erected to within one block of the eastern boundary of the cemetery. Park Lawn, a Government Housing Unit, is to the N.E., Sherman Park is S.E. The sparsely built up "c" areas to the west and north of this area have yet no adverse influence upon it.

This is a spotty area, but is a substantial neighborhood. There is a steady influx of Jews of a substantial class coming in from the yellow and red areas to the east, more especially along Center Street. Sherman Park to the north-east and Washington Park is to the southeast. The area is intersected with business streets and enjoys their adequate and quick transportation to downtown. The eastern portion and center of area are older sections.
All utilities -- adequate transportation -- adequate schools and churches.
Proximity to industrial plants to the east -- Parklawn is government low-cost housing project nearby on northwest.

A spotty area with a high proportion of 2-family dwellings.A fairly well paid class of working people are moving into the area. The last three years has seen considerable new buildings of brick and lannon stone houses, particularly in the northeast portion. Lots measuring 40 x 120 are selling at $750 to $1250. Sherman Park is to the south. South Burleigh is the older section of area.
Proximity to industry. However, this is favorable.

The A. O. Smith Plant, second largest in the Milwaukee area adjoins this area on the east. The area is occupied by a mixed substantial class of working people, also business and professional men. Sherman Park with Grant Boulevard leading into it from the south is favorable to the area. A good third grade area.
Good transportation -- good shopping districts -- schools -- all utilities.

25 years ago this was a good, middle class section of Milwaukee occupied by the second generation of Germans, Jews began to move in 20 years ago. That portion south of Lisbon is the oldest part of the area. It is now a wage earners' area with the advantages of being close in. It has a number of small industrial plants also 5 business streets. That portion north of North Avenue is slightly better than south of North Avenue, being not as old. The section west of 20th Street is better than that east of 20th. A good fourth grade area.
None outstanding. Union Cemetery in center of area.

This large area, while declining due to age, will sustain values for some time chiefly because of the conservative German influence. It is occupied by wage earners, Germans of the first, second, and third generation predominating overwhelmingly. Industry encroaches on the west. Union Cemetery in the middle of the area and Milwaukee Baseball Park on North 8th Street are adverse influences.
MILWAUKEE AREA FROM KEEFE SOUTH TO EAST CENTER
Polish infiltration. Industry on the north.

This neighborhood is on the down grade -- much repair is needed. Gordon Park is southeast, also Milwaukee River. A typical Polish district -- railroad runs diagonally through section. Many of these people would not live elsewhere.
All utilities -- schools -- adequate transportation -- Kern Park to the north and Gordon Park to the south.
Pumping plant in center of area.

A spotty area, flanked on the north and south by parks and on the east by a bluff leading to the river bed. In the northern one-half of this area there are some very good new houses occupied by business and professional people. A city pumping station in the middle of the area is a detrimental influence. There is an infiltration of the better class of Polish. Houses fronting on Humboldt Avenue are older and hardly warrant a second grade rating. However, they constitute a good buffer to the better class of houses to the east.
All utilities -- adjacent to downtown area and Lake Michigan -- adequate schools -- transportation -- proximity to Lake Shore Park.
Part of the original city first settled by Juneau -- a rooming house and old apartment section. Business district is to south and west; Milwaukee River to the northwest.
Cannot hazard what depreciation is, but extensive.
Widest possible range depending on the individual bldg & location 35-Few of these obtainable
A very speculative area with good land value for apts.

This is the part of original Milwaukee settled by Juneau. Some of the city's best apartments are located in the eastern part of the area. All single houses are very old. North of Ogden and west of Astor to river is an Italian section. East of Jefferson and south of Ogden is built up solidly with apartments interspersed with many rooming houses. Characterized by age of detached houses and many large apartments, it is a difficult area to grade. Land values in the southern part are well maintained because of the potential apartment and commercial use. Several large high-priced houses have been razed to avoid tax payment. It is doubtful if many of these properties could be sold at assessed values. Some of the wealthiest people of the city live in apartment houses in this area, some of the poorest in the detached houses. Ground values are the predominant factor in maintaining prices in the higher brackets.
Negro and slum area -- condemnation proceedings going on.

This is the Negro and slum area of Milwaukee. It is old and very ragged. Besides the colored people, a large number of lower type Jews are moving into the section. This section housed Milwaukee's wealthiest families seventy years ago.
All public utilities -- schools -- excellent transportation -- proximity to Washington Park -- and good shopping facilities.
Clerical, skilled, mechanical, and railroad men.

North of North Avenue the area is newer and almost solid flats. Many single family homes are around Washington Park and vicinity. The area is popular and will hold its own for some time. It is extremely desirable for those working in industry and handy to downtown.
All public utilities -- good transportation and schools.
Industry to the east and railroad tracks.

This area sets out as inferior to adjoining C-13. It is somewhat a continuation of D-6 to the east with industry and railroad tracks from its eastern boundary. It is a good rent section due to proximity to industry; a backward district as to sales.
All utilities -- fair transportation -- schools. Washington Park is to the northeast.
Industry to the south -- children going to school must cross heavy traffic in any direction.

That portion of this area south of Juneau Avenue is part of "Pigsville", the colloquial reference to the low river bed residential sections. This portion drops to a lower elevation. There are several apartments along West Martin Drive which follows the bluff. South of Juneau, also west of Washington Park, are a large portion of duplexes. Singles predominate north of Juneau to Washington Park, also north of Vliet east and west of Washington Park. Old clay pits in center of area are now being filled in by garbage and ashes.
Schools -- all public utilities -- transportation -- and churches.

This area was once the second largest German section of the city -- it has rapidly gone to a rooming house and light housekeeping area. It is a good rent section, being reasonably close to the business section. It has good potential land values for rooming houses and small apartments. Some flats on the west side of it sold in 1929 for as high as $27,500.
Level -- slight slope toward the east.
Walking distance to downtown area -- all public utilities -- good transportation and schools.

A fair "C" area, closed in, but suffering the adverse influence of adjoining D-6 and D-7. It is close to Marquette University on the southeast; it has good grade schools and a girls' technical high school. It is a rooming house area. Land values are accountable for recovery in big brackets.
Level to rolling along the valley, dropping to south.
All utilities -- ground values are holding and will maintain -- schools -- transportation.

Marquette University is in the southeastern part of this area and has contributed to its going into a rooming house and light housekeeping district. There are a number of large apartments on Wisconsin Avenue and southeast of 27th St, The area has more than an average number of small furnished apartments. There are also a number of sorority and fraternity houses in the area. Between 27th and 35th, south of Clybourn are the lower income industrial workers. The Vernon section on the west side is the poorest section of area. Ground values are well maintained and are a factor in holding prices up.
Level to rolling along the valley, dropping to south.
All utilities -- ground values are holding and will maintain -- schools -- transportation.

Marquette University is the southeastern part of this area and has contributed to its going into a rooming house and light housekeeping district. There are a number of large apartments on Wisconsin Avenue and southeast of 27th St. The area has more than an average number of small furnished apartments. There are also a number of sorority and fraternity houses in the area. Between 27th and 35th, south of Clybourn are the lower income industrial workers. The Vernon section on the west side is the poorest section of area. Ground values are well maintained and are a factor in holding prices up.
All utilities -- close to good schools -- good transportation.
Heavy traffic on Bluemound Road -- Calvary Cemetery to the west -- industry to the east -- smoke from the St. Paul Railroad Shops.

This is a substantial area. There is an encroachment of multiple family homes on Bluemound Road and Story Parkway, and there is heavy traffic on the Bluemound Artery. The area is very handy to downtown Milwaukee. It is also close to the industrial "valley" to the southeast. Bluff Park is to the southeast -- also the National Soldiers' Home is on the south. Woodlawn Court is a beautiful district.
Modern utilities including city and artesian well water -- good transportation along the Bluemound Road. -- schools.
Surrounded by industry -- Calvary Cemetery to the south.
There are a few stores, apartments, and multi-family units on Bluemound Road.

This area is on the edge of a hill falling away on the north to the river. It is spotted with some good homes on Wisconsin Avenue, along with the customary stores and apartments on Bluemound Road with some large apartments on Wisconsin Avenue. The area has a mixture of apartments, flats, with singles predominating. It is very handy to the downtown business section via Wisconsin Avenue. The Menomonee River is to the north.
Heavy traffic on Bluemound Road and Wisconsin Avenue.

This is an outstanding and substantial area, sufficiently to the south of industry as as to be unaffected by it. Quick transportation is provided to downtown areas. Artesian well drinking water is a decided benefit when compared with Milwaukee water. Sholes Park is to the north.
All utilities are available now -- this district was only taken into Milwaukee about 8 or 10 years ago -- schools.
Jugo, and S.E. Europeans, Germans, Austrians.

A sprinkling of old, two-story houses among newer also cheaper structures, make this a spotty area. The eastern and western portions are the poorest, the central one-half of the area being a reasonably substantial district. It is a working man's area. There has been some new building of good houses along Bluemound in the center of the area. Calvary Cemetery on the east is an adverse influence. It is a part of the Johnson's Woods Section. Mortgagors say that utility costs are now being carried by the city and are not levied against present mortgages owners; immediately, however, as mortgagors foreclose, the city assesses these costs against the property.
Railroad and industry to the south.

This is the original Johnson's Woods taken into the city 10 years ago after which several of the streets were graded. Some sections of the area are, therefore, below the street level. It is a working man's area entirely, with a variety of houses throughout; ragged in appearance. It is near the large Allis Chalmers plant, although railroad tracks separate the area from the industrial plant.
Level, slightly rolling toward the western boundary.
All utilities -- direct route to the heart of the city on both Wisconsin and Blue Mound Avenue -- restricted to single family houses -- adequate schools -- Honey Creek Parkway to north.
No rent houses in 1929 or at present time.

This area, embracing Jennings Subdivision west of 76th and Wellauer Subdivision east of 76th, holds its character very well despite the apparently adverse influence of the older area to the south. The developer has made it a policy of buying up distressed property. This was formerly a golf course and when abandoned was turned into an exclusive subdivision. Some speculative building in the price range of $18,000 to $25,000 has been carried on during the past four months. County institutions are to the northwest.
None outstanding, except traction line on the south. No schools.

This is known as the Henry W. Marx subdivision, a new one constructed of very substantial homes. This area is well developed, and the section of it west of 89th street which is sparsely populated will continue growing with home owners of a substantial nature. There is farm land to the immediate south, and to the north are the County Institutions. Good transportation to the downtown business area is available. Highly restricted -- homes up to $30,000 in this area.
All utilities -- artesian well water -- schools.
Transportation fair -- development to the west stopped by County Institutions.

The northeast corner of the main area was originally the Village of Wauwatosa; Honey Creek Parkway is being developed very nicely and attracting new homes. The east portion of area is substantially better than the west section; industry is to the northwest and northeast and County Institutions to the west. City Park is northeast and there is also park development on south of area. To the east of the eastern section is Sholes Park and the Menomonee River runs along the northern boundary. The area is spotty with considerable new building on the west side. One adverse influence is the location of the mental cases and old people's home of the County Institutions along north 84th Street.
Low land, railroad tracks,, industry to the east. Lack of schools.

This is a small neighborhood lying between double railroad tracks and the Menomonee River in the low riverbed strip. It is a noisy and dirty area. City Park to the west helps to offset adverse influences.
All utilities -- adequate transportation -- good schools.
Railroad to south and industry east and south.

City Park to the southwest now being developed. The area is situated on a bluff rising from State to Milwaukee Avenue and is not an outstanding area; but spotted throughout with many good homes especially on the east and north. Stone quarry to the southeast. A good "C" area.
Hilly to rolling; several ravines in area.
Highly protected and restricted -- adequate transportation -- all utilities -- adequate schools.

This is Washington Highlands, a highly restricted and exclusive area, slow in developing but substantial in character. Plans and specifications for new building must be approved by the Washington Highlands Building Committee which permits a wide latitude of discrimination in accepting residents into the neighborhood. That small portion of the area south of Milwaukee Avenue, joined on the east and west by "C" sections, is in a deep ravine. High ground along the southern boundary of this area fronting on Milwaukee Avenue forms a natural barrier so that C-17 on the south offers no adverse influence on this area.
Level, except the following portions -- southern boundary Wauwatosa Avenue to Menominee Drive is a bluff.
Adequate transportation -- utilities -- schools -- artesian well water.

This is a spotty area - one of the older sections of West Milwaukee with a substantial population - a very desirable place for people to commute from the City of Milwaukee. Throughout the area there are many very fine homes, but scattered throughout there are also many in the lower class brackets. The area as a whole is very well maintained. The better development is south of West North Avenue. The area is particularly attractive to those who do not particularly care for the East Side. Hoyt Park is to the southwest.
All utilities -- schools -- adequate transportation -- shopping center at 60th and Center Streets.
Spotty area of older houses to the north and east.

A small portion of this area, from 76th to 72nd, approximately 2/3 of the distance between Center and West Hadley, lies in Wauwatosa; the balance is in the City of Milwaukee. The area is another outgrowth of FHA financing and has been largely built up during the last three years. A rather substantial type of two-story structures predominate. There are a few two-family houses in the section. The area is similar to A-3 and A-5 in that it is a development not far from cemeteries with older and cheaper properties nearby. These influences seem to have little effect.
This section is in the southeastern part of the Shirley Park Subdivision. The area west to 92nd and north to West Burleigh promises to be a development with a trend toward a first-grade section.
Incline toward W. Center Street; formerly was a hill and never graded down.
Proximity to "A-5" on the west which is a new development.
Wauwatosa Cemetery in the center of area.
90-100 New building accounts for rising rent rate.

This small area suffers the adverse influence of Wauwatosa Cemetery in the center of it. The western portion adjoining A-5 is virtually undeveloped. It is a spotty area which has had some new construction during the last few years.
Level with slight rise from North Avenue to Center Street.
All utilities -- adequate schools -- Menomonee Parkway to the west -- artesian well water -- adequate transportation -- nearby, Blue Mound Country Club and an exclusive girls' college.

This area, situated in Wauwatose, offers much promise of being one of the better of the newly developed sections due to the suburban influence and the fine park system to the west. Virtually all of the houses herein have been built during the last three or four years, and financed chiefly through FHA loans. Despite the proximity to the cemetery and older section to the east, new houses have been built recently on both sides of 82nd Street. There is a distinct cleavage in the types of property midway between 81st and 82nd Streets in this area. The older section surrounding Wauwatose Cemetery seems to have had no deterring influence upon the eastern portion of this new area. Blue Mound Country Club to the northeast is an advantage; also Mount Mary College, an exclusive girls' school.

Located principally in the Town of Wauwatosa, the southwestern portion within the City of Milwaukee. This section offers promise of better suburban development than SC-3. The grade of homes scattered throughout the area are of a substantially good grade. As yet the section is largely an agricultural area with the exception of that portion within the City of Milwaukee lying between W. Lisbon Avenue and West Burleigh.

This area is located in the Town of Wauwatosa excepting that portion in the City of Milwaukee designated by the city limits. Continued development might have made this one of the exclusive areas of the city situated as it is in a rolling territory with the favorable influence of James Curry Park, Bluemont Country club, and Mount Mary College adjoining, and Menomonee River Parkway traversing the area. The economic  depression beginning in 1930 stopped development in the area. Any appreciable development in the area will be of the higher priced, better class of houses, and south development should make it an "A" section. It is well restricted, and every other influence is favorable to the area.
This section between the railroad tracks and two heavy highways offers little prospect of development. A second grade "B" -- very sparsely settled.
Located in the Town of Wauwatosa, a fair outlying neighborhood with an upward trend. To the west of this area in Waukosha County is a high grade development -- good possibilities.

A spotty rural area in rolling country which offers possibilities of good development. It is in a direct line to downtown Milwaukee with Wisconsin and Bluemound, both arterial highways having no natural barriers. The area is in the Town of Wauwatosa.
Adjoining Soldiers' Home with park influence -- all utilities -- schools -- adequate transportation
Industrial areas on east, south, and northwest.
Business, professional - better grade wage earners

That part of this area east of 56th Street lies in West Milwaukee and that portion west of 56th Street in West Allis. The West Allis portion of the area is the oldest section of that city. The area is spotty with a substantial number of good houses scattered among the older and poorer structures. Of the two-family flats referred to above, many are what is known as bungalow flats. The future of West Allis is encouraging.
Proximity to industry -- schools -- all utilities -- adequate transportation.
Odors, smoke and dirt from nearby factories -- predominating foreign element.

A typical factory workers' area. High percentage of the inhabitants are employed in the Allis-Chalmers factory which adjoins the area on the north. This is the largest single industry in the Milwaukee area. Between 1918 and 1927, many small houses were built in this area. The security is of a better grade in the extreme western part of the area than that in the eastern portion. The future of West Allis is good
Low taxes -- adequate transportation -- schools -- all utilities.
Boxed in on three sides with factories -- possibility of further industrial encroachment.

This is the most desirable section in West Milwaukee. It shares with other portions of West Milwaukee the advantage of low taxes inasmuch as industry practically maintains West Milwaukee. Compared to other parts of the Milwaukee metropolitan area, it is a fair second grade section.

A spotty area, wherein the great majority of houses are suited to the moderate income family, being close to industry, business district, and schools. Italians predominate from West Grant to Arthur. Juneau Highlands, immediately north and west of Grant and east of 68th, is a small concentration of very good houses deserving of an "A" or "B" grading if the district were larger. A fair third grade area.
Restrictions as to price -- all utilities -- schools -- adequate transportation.
Foreign element to the north -- railroad to the north and industrial section to the northeast.

This new area is the best spot in West Allis. The portion between 57th and 60th has built up during the last few years with a substantial type one and one-half and two story houses. Although a good section, it lacks the charm of other good residential sections of the Milwaukee area. Restricted area. The future of West Allis is good.
Close to shopping center -- schools -- all utilities -- adequate transportation.
Factories to the east and north.

Another very spotty section of old and reasonably new houses. A fair third grade section. State Fair Park is to the northwest. An exceptionally good rental section. Allis-Chalmers plant to the northeast.
Limited from factories -- new Junior High School at 86th & Lincoln -- other school facilities adequate -- all utilities -- adequate transportation except as noted under "c" below.
Transportation to industries not ample -- parts of area away from shopping center.
Frame, few brick, few lannon stone

A very spotty area. The northeastern part of the area is the oldest in West Allis. Scattered throughout the area are newer and substantial types of structures, also old houses suffering from obsolescence and lack of repair. Much of this area was formerly North Greenfield. Many homes without basements. In the west and southwest section there are many shacks.
Unrestricted -- poor transportation and school facilities -- unpaved streets -- no water or sewers -- no fire protection

This small area is located in the Town of Greenfield. Indications are that all utilities will very soon be extended to the area and the trend will then be upward. At present a poor third grade section. Unpaved streets. New water tower now being put in with WPA assistance.
Removed from factories -- adequate transportation -- schools.

A small but substantial area that stands out as better than other third grade sections of West Allis. It is fairly spotty although the majority of the houses are not old. A good third grade section. State Fair Park is on the northeast. Good rental situation. The future of West Allis looks good.

This area is in the Town of Greenfield; has seen considerable new building during the last twelve months with a distinct trend upward. Houses ranging in cost from $5,000 to $7,000 are being built here. Lower taxes are influencing the building in this section.

These are platted and very sparsely developed portions located in the Town of Greenfield. Even though these portions are platted, the development is not any greater than the areas surrounding the platted. They are occupied by a sprinkling of city workers who moved to these sections during the stress of the depression period because of cheaper living accomodations; also farmers on a small scale.  Average at from $700 to $1200 an acre.

Located in the town of Greenfield, this area is made up almost entirely of shacks built in a majority of cases by the owner with his own hands out of second hand lumber. Occupants are practically all the very low income groups who have moved to the country to avoid high taxes and obtain shelter in a section where the amenities of home ownership are entirely lacking.
Electricity, gas, good grade schools, transportation to downtown Milwaukee, and own street lighting.

This was formerly an old trading post; it is surrounded by a rich farming community -- many Milwaukee people live here. It is only one-half hour's drive by automobile away from Milwaukee with excellent roads. It is close to Whitnall Park on the south, a very fine one. Along Forest Home Avenue to the east there are fine homes with spacious grounds. This is a growing and substantial community with a population of about 1,000. Greendale, a government housing project consisting of 3,410 acres of land and costing more than $9,000,000, is about three miles to the east. D-18 to the southeast is the very old part of Hales Corners and does not adversely affect B-20. It has very few houses, all centering around the business district.
Electricity -- gas -- grade schools -- good transportation to Milwaukee -- own street lighting.

The extreme northern section of this area has some substantial homes. The east side of 108th Street is zoned for business but the west side is not. There are many old business buildings in the area, some of them 100 years old. Hales Corners was an old trading post and the land was controlled largely by the Dreyfuss family. When the State Bank was organized in 1910 they endeavored to locate in this old area, but Dreyfuss would not sell any land to them, even at $25.00 a foot. The bank helped to develop this new section and left the old business area to go to the seed.
A small county village -- houses are not modern -- A retired farmers' community -- not progressive.
Sales occurred -- almost all homes are on the market.

Population about 300. An old farmers' trading post. There are two Roman Catholic Churches. Originally settled by three families -- Gross, layer, and Jochem -- who held the place back by refusing to sell any property. A doomed community with little or no hope for the future.
This area also in the Town of Greenfield is similar in every respect to SB-6/

Located in the Town of Greenfield. This area offers promise of good development, and with such development will possibly rate a second grade classification along with B-16 to the north. Like many another subdivision, it was begun about ten years ago and development was arrested by the economic depression. The developer is the Aug. Sehrt Company, a very high grade real estate firm which assures a substantial future.
All utilities -- adjacent to Jackson Park -- schools -- transportation.

A somewhat spotted neighborhood with a very fine thoroughfare into town, considered the best section on the south side, and an up and coming district. Industry on the north does not affect the area. A rather substantial development of good homes is under way along Forest Home Avenue to Hales Corners.
Low and rolling -- sloping toward west and north.
Jackson Park on the west -- all utilities -- good schools -- fair transportation.
Industry to the northeast -- railroad to north.
Good thoroughfare via Forest Home into South Side Business District. The only paved streets are 34th (from Dakota north) and 35th. County Parkway runs through some of area; this is a WPA project.

This section located in the extreme southern part of the City of Milwaukee should develop chiefly as a result of the building of the new High School east of Twenty-seventh Street and north of Oklahoma now under construction. The area was started on the brink of the economic depression and its development, therefore, was abruptly halted. This section will undoubtedly see considerable activity during the next two or three years and it might develop into a first grade.
All utilities -- adequate schools -- adequate transportation.
Not a rent area; virtually 100% owner occupied.

This is a very picturesque small area in a wooded section developed by Harter, Chairman of the City Planning Commission, who gave special attention to the artistic features of the section. Virtually all of the financing of houses built during the last three years was through FHA Title II loans. Completion of the new Pulaski High School at the intersection of Oklahoma and 27th Milwaukee area, whereby a nearby cemetery seems to have brought no adverse influence. Jackson Park is on the north.
Level -- gradual slope toward the east from 32nd Street,
Good transportation -- shopping facilities -- schools -- churches -- and all modern utilities.
Close to industry on west and street car barns on the northwest corner of South 27th and West National.

A large spotty area where age and obsolescence are very evident. South Layton Boulevard has many large old houses; were once occupied by many prominent persons. Between West Burnham and South 31st to South 36th the land is soft and boggy; west of Layton and south of Lapham to 36th Street was once a celery field and is now swampy and boggy land. This shows up in the streets and buildings. The vicinity of Pilgrim's Rest Cemetery is poor -- would be graded "D" were it larger. Forest Home Cemetery to the southeast is another adverse influence. This area was the old National Park Section of Milwaukee.
All utilities -- good transportation -- schools, including high school.
There are a few 4-10 unit apts. located around Greenfield Ave & S. 6th St. & 14th and 15th.
3500-4000 - for Polish flats. The regular multi-family average $7,000

This is Milwaukee's heaviest Polish concentration. Throughout the area there are many so-called "Polish Flats" wherein basements have been converted into one and two and sometimes three small apartments. Around Kosciuszko Park there are some good single and two-family houses. That portion north of Lincoln Avenue between Sixth and Sixteenth is the older part of the area. Mitchell Street has the largest business section in the southern part of Milwaukee. Many of the institutions are either owned or managed by Polish or cater to Polish trade. Mexicans are encroaching in the northeast.
Level with slight grade to south.
Industry and smoke from the east and south. Beet odors from sewage plant to southeast.
Polish and mixed in southeast central

This is an old section bordering the commercial and industrial areas. Most of that portion east of 6th has been zoned for light industry. There are many Polish Flats in the area. Like D-11, it is heavily populated by Poles. The security in this area is sometimes pointed out as being older and inferior to adjoining D-11.
All utilities -- Pulaski Park on the west -- good schools -- good transportation.
North Shore Line on the east -- also industry.

A Polish section, particularly that portion surrounding Pulaski Park. The area has many "Polish Flats" (a single house wherein basement has been turned into one, two, or three family apartments). It is a desirable area for industrial workers. The northern portion is the oldest.
All utilities -- good transportation -- schools -- churches -- community center.
Proximity to industry -- St. Adelbert Cemetery to the south.
35 - 45 / Rental demand is better than in 1936

This is considered to be a good wage earners' area and likely to show an upward trend on account of its proximity to several industries. Euclid to Morgan, 12th and 11th really warrant a "B" grade -- the area is spotty. Good shopping area at 13th and Oklahoma. A new Catholic Parish at 16th and Holt will attract many people of the Catholic faith to this section.

Located in the southern extremity of South Milwaukee; another area whose growth was suddenly halted by the economic depression of a few years ago. Indications are that it will be developed and occupied by the better class of Polish. It will be a substantial section, but will not develop into a high grade area. The cemeteries to the east and inadequate transportation will tend to hold this section back. This area is known as Zalewski Subdivision.
All public utilities -- artesian well water will be in this summer, 1938 -- schools -- fair transportation
None except industry to the north and St. Adelbert's Cemetery to the west.

That portion of the area south of W. Warimont has a much better and more substantial class of homes and inhabitants. Saveland Park is in the south center of area, and a high grade class of homes and home owners are in this section. There are 14 acres of woods west of the park which makes it additionally attractive. On the north part of area there is an individual encroachment. Very spotty and difficult to grade. Among old and cheaper homes there are many new brick and stone homes on several of the streets. Continued growth will advance this to a "B" and a spotty "C".
Level and rolling to the south.
Good transportation -- all modern utilities except water which will be connected late this summer (1938) to an artesian well system 00 school.

West of Howell Ave. homes are of cheaper construction running from garage bungalows to substantial homes. The area east of Howell is much better developed and is increasing with homes of much better class. This area is directly in line of future growth south. Low taxation is a favorable influence. New water mains are being installed and will be in operation by fall and are being paid for by the Town of Lake without direct assessment against property owners. FHA mortgages here have sold recently at 103-104. The Town of Lake pays for tuition of its resident pupils to Bay View High School. A spotty area.

Has all modern conveniences -- except artesian water in that part of area in the southeast which is in Town Lake. Town of Lake artesian well water will be inaugurated late this summer. Fair transportation.
Industry to the northeast. Lack of adequate school facilities. Cemetery in the southwest portion of area.

This area is in line for future growth in the south. Low taxes in Town of Lake area a favorable feature. That part of the area on extreme eats is known as St. Francis. There is excellent transportation both to Milwaukee and to the north and south. The Lakeside Power Plant is directly east of the area on the lake front. Land values are well maintained. There is a good high school and three new grades schools. St. Francis Diocese to the east prevents growth in that direction. New construction will be FHA financed and of cheaper grade.
MILWAUKEE and TOWN OF LAKE, WIS.
All utilities -- proximity to Humboldt Park -- east on Lake Michigan and South Shore Park. Adequate transportation and schools.
Business, professional, including laborers on southwest

That northeast corner of area east of railroad tracks is the oldest. This is known as the Bay View Area. Very convenient to drive south along the lake into the country and excellent transportation into south side and central Milwaukee business district. Railroad runs through center of area. Industry is to the south. There are many old substantial homes spotted along the east side of area.
Humboldt Park, a fine park -- all public utilities -- good transportation, stores, schools, etc.
Industry and the railroad on the west.

Immediately north of Oklahoma Avenue is Gauer Circle wherein five new homes were recently constructed and more will undoubtedly be built. Included is the "New Home Show Home", a demonstration residence which attracted much favorable attention during March, 1938. The area north of Cleveland Avenue is old and much of the property is of the cheaper grade. Industry adjoins on the west. The area is favored by Bay View High School, other good schools, and Humboldt Park. New construction is in southwest portion of area.
All public utilities -- good transportation, schools, stores, etc.
Industry to the east and odors from Jones Island, Sewage Disposal Plant.

This area is older than adjoining D-13. That portion of the area east of Wentworth Avenue to Lake Michigan is a more desirable residential section than other portions of the area, being removed from industry and on the lake shore. The area around the northwest portion of Conway and South Bay was formerly identified with the bootlegging industry. There are many Italians in this section. East of Lincoln Avenue is the old and dilapidated section.
All utilities -- good transportation to downtown area, and also along the lake front to the south and out into the country. Schools. South Shore Park to east is a favorable influence.

Desirable neighborhood in which to live due to the lake front view - the Archiocese of Milwaukee is to the south and South Shore Park is along the northeast. Prevailing winds from the lake makes this area somewhat more desirable in which to live in summer. Best development along lake. Older section follows the lake. The Archdiocese of Milwuakee prevents growth to the south.
MILWAUKEE AREA FROM EAST CENTER SOUTH TO RESERVOIR
Italians coming in from the south and Polish from the north. Industry to east.

This area is inferior to adjoining D-3. There is a Polish infiltration from the north and Italians from the south; also negroes in the southwest along Garfield and Hubbard. It is occupied entirely by industrial workers largely from the riverbed factories to the east.
Adequate transportation -- adequate schools -- all utilities -- Sheridan Park to the east and City Park to the southeast.
Some unpaved streets - stench and smoke from industrial plants in part of the area, to east and west.
Wage earners, white collared clerical, clerks, some business, professional

This area embraces all of Cudahy with the exception of the adjoining "B" area. It is very spotty throughout and difficult to grade. Much of the security if grouped in any given section, would be classed as fourth grade. Property is not moving in the area. Four new houses, speculatively built in 1937, had not bee sold early in March 1938. There has been no advancement in rents during the last 18 months due to recession in industrial employment. Some doubling up became evident. Cudahy is rapidly on the down grade, especially since the Federal Tire Company sold out to the Fisk Tire Company, who dismantled the works and left town.
Lack of adequate transportation along lake road -- smoke and stench from industrial plants.

This small area, while spotty, embraces the newer and better section of Cudahy. Several new houses were constructed during 1937 west of Packard. The better and higher income groups of this industrial town reside in this area. The future of Cudahy is not encouraging. Sheridan Park is to the east.

This is the Cudahy Subdivision in the City and Cudahy. It is a very small picturesque part on the shore of Lake Michigan with less than a dozen houses of the better type of construction. The Area has seen no building since the withdrawal of industry from Cudahy some six or seven years ago which halted growth of the town and removed potential occupants of higher priced houses.

This is Silverdale located between Cudahy and South Milwaukee in the Town of Lake. It is a cheap development; has suffered from the lack of utilities particularly water. It has no restrictions, and the trend is downward.
All utilities -- homes restricted to $5,000 -- adjacent to Grant Park -- schools -- transportation.

Much of this land is held by A. J. Ricker, Joseph Saxler, and E.H. Baetke who do not care to sell. This is the best residential section of South Milwaukee. When the south extension of Memorial Dr. goes through, South Milwaukee will materially benefit and this area is particular. South Milwaukee may develop into a one industry town (Bucyrus-Erie). The future is not any too encouraging. This area was hard hit within the last twelve months by the removal of about 12 executives of the du Pont Co. who recently moved to Wilmington, Del. Under present adverse economic conditions in South Milwaukee there are no persons of like income to occupy houses vacated, and these properties are a drug on the market. The Grobschmidt Subdivision is immediately south of the Holy Sepulchre Cemetery.
Grant Park to the east -- all public utilities -- good schools -- transportation.

A part of South Milwaukee. The gradual withdrawal of the dying plant by the du Pont Company, which formerly employed nine hundred men, has hit South Milwaukee hard and has affected this area. The section is spotty and old. Oak Creek Parkway flanks it on the west and the better residential section of South Milwaukee on the east. Any future development in the area will be between Chicago and Swift Avenues. A spotty and only "fair" third grade section. There are some substantial houses between 10th and 5th, Madison and Michigan; also at Milwaukee Avenue and 6th. The eastern and southern portions are ragged. Industrial plants are located on the northeast and southwest, the largest being Bucyrus-Erie employing about 900 men. The future is not any too encouraging.
All utilities -- good schools -- churches -- transportation.

This is a ragged industrial workers' area in South Milwaukee occupied by poor, cheap houses. The portion of the area near Oak Creek is low ground. There is no development of the area and the only demand is on the part of the low income industrial workers with whom home ownership is through necessity, not choice or desirability.

East of Fifth Avenue, north by Montana; west by Ninth and south by Marion there are a substantial class of homes. Close to various industrial plants, good shopping district. The plant Bucyrus-Erie which employs about 900 men, is to the northwest. Entire eastern and southern section is very poor. Madison and Michigan between 10th and 5th is best. Milwaukee Avenue at 6th is OK.
Line Material Plant is to the east -- gaseous odors from Galvanizing Unit.
There is low land south of Marion and west of 16th. the southwest corner of area is swampy. This is a declining area, but attractive for those working in industry.
A section of scattered houses appended to the city of South Milwaukee. The section lacks utilities and conveniences. This section has no possibilities.
State Fair Park to the east.
