There is no evidence that the degree of desirability will improve.

This area is not particularly convenient to any neighborhood shopping center or to transportation.  The majority of residents find employment in the industry which is adjacent to the area, and includes a cork factory from which there are frequent obnoxious odors.  The land is rolling.  A main thoroughfare (Highway 29) is elevated, and bisects the area east to west.  The southwestern portion is low and sparsely settled.  Elsewhere the small frame houses are quite similar in type, and many were built in rows on small lots, although detached, about 15 years ago as a speculative development.  The north portion of the area has a better character than the south portion, because of a better class of people and greater pride of home ownership.  There is a good school on Chapman Street.

This gently rolling area is about 75% built up. It is in the direction of growth from Elmora Hills in Elizabeth, which is adjacent to the northeast. It is restricted and comparatively new. Construction is sound, and architecture good. Planning has been fair, although lots vary in size from 40' to 60', the majority being 50'. Homes are of individual design, and are mostly owner occupied. A new storm sewer is now being installed which will improve drainage difficulties experienced up to this time. It is about 5 minutes drive to any one of three railroad stations, but bus transportation is nearer. The main retail shopping center in Elizabeth is about 15 minutes ride, but there are nearby stores for household supplies. Schools and churches are convenient. This is a small area with not much more room in which to grow, but it is in every way a first grade area. The terrain in area C-27 to the south is down-hill from this area, and even though it is an older neighborhood, it does not adversely affect this area.

The terrain in this area is slightly rolling and scenic. It is a thoroughly restricted and well planned residential area, about 85% developed with high class homes, mostly fram, but some are built of brick or stone. There has been a generous planning of picturesque lawns, gardens, and shrubbery, and an excellent pride of home ownership and interest in the maintenance of a good neighborhood is everywhere apparent. It is close in and convenient to bus and rail transportation . Schools and churches are convenient, and there is within the area a so-called "Country Day School" for boys known as the Pingry School. This of course is a private school, and is well patronized by residents. The area is not entirely built up, and being in the direction of the city's growth, should continue to be a first class residential section for some years to come.
White-collar- Business- Jr. Executives- Some professional people

This is one of the older residential sections of the city. There are a number of fine old mansions in the area on very large lots, some of which are about 200' x 300' beautifully landscaped. One of the more modern of these, a brick colonial home, was sold in May of 1937 for $25,000. The neighborhood has inherited and still carries on, a high social value, but there is a definite trend toward apartment houses. In this respect it is restricted to high class "garden" apartments, of which several have already been built. It is close in, near all transportation and shopping. North Broad St. is a main thoroughfare, as is Newark Ave. Schools and churches are convenient. The area is practically 100% built up. While the large mansions are giving way to the gradual encroachment of apartment houses, other streets of smaller homes are not as yet threatened although their desirabiltiy as signle residence neighborhoods is lessened.

Garwood is a manufacturing community. As a whole, this area reflects the atmosphere generally found in suburban manufacturing towns. In general it is unattractive, although individual houses here and there show some pride of home ownership with small lawns and gardens and good maintenance. Many of the large houses which are older than average, have been converted into residences for two or more families, and there has been some rehabilitation of exteriors with asbetos shingles. The outer edges of the town are sparsely settled and streets are unfinished. There is a considerable amount of traffic along both North Ave., and South Ave. Neighborhood stores and small shops are located on Center Street, south of the industrial area. There is good bus transportation, and the Central railroad of N.J. runs through town, affording good commutation to Elizabethport, Newark, Kearney, Bayonne, and via ferry from Jersey City, to New York. The majority of the residents however are employed locally, or in nearby manufacturing establishments elsewhere in the County. A new school is located in the western part of this area. The terrain is flat. Of the two areas in Garwood this is the poorer, although neither is very attractive from the standpoint of residential desirability, and should not be expected to improve.

This is a typical bungalow section except at the eastern boundary near Galloping Hill Road, where some large old 1-family French-roof houses may be found. The area has all city facilities including well-paved streets, but the houses are rather closely built on small lots, and restrictions have expired. There is heavy traffic on Westfield Ave. Chestnut St. and Galloping Hill Rd. are also main thoroughfares. The bungalows are very much alike and were built in rows although, of course, detached. There appears to be an indifferent attitude toward good appearance in general on the part of most residents, which detracts from desirability and hastons obsolescence. The Lorrain and the Roselle stations of the Central R.R. are convenient, and the maximum distance from bus transportation would be about three blocks. The main shopping center in Elizabeth is not more than 10 or 15 minutes distant, although there are local neighborhoods shops for household needs within short walking distance. There is a grade school on Sherman Ave., and churches are nearby.
Clerks- Merchants- Skilled mechanics- Some laborers

This level area is the westernmost tip of Plainfield as well as of Union County. It lies between the D.L.&W. Railroad tracks and the brook which separates Plainfield (Union County) from North Plainfield (Somerset County). Myrtle Avenue between Clinton and Park Drive is the best street in the area. The poorest part of the area lies adjacent to industry and the railroad tracks along W. Front St. Here mixed types of closely built old frame structures, some with stores, may be found. There is also heavy traffic on W. Front St. Toward the southwestern extremity of the area there is a sewage filtration plant, although this is a sparsely settled section, and odors are not noticed in built-up sections. Noise and smoke from both the railroad and industry are unfavorable. Primary schools are convenient, but High Schools is 15 minutes distant. Good bus and railroad transportation are available, as well as all city facilities. Some pride of home ownership is evident, particularly on Myrtle Ave., but residential desirability is definitely declining, and the area is a poor third grade.

Flat meadow land- no trees. Subject to spring floods. Bordered by railroads on west and projected airport on north. Industry (Bendix Corp.) to north in area indicated by name on map. Celery farms near area. Most streets unpaved, few sidewalks. Majority of houses have no cellars. Poor shopping facilities. No schools or high school in area. Nearest high school one mile. Very heavy traffic along Route 2 adjacent to west. Rail service convenient- 30 minutes to downtown New York City- fare $9.10 monthly commutation rate. There have been many foreclosures here and a number of residents are on relief rolls. Estimated annual incomes would not exceed $1000 per family. Nothing whatever to recommend the area residentially. Very obviously 4th grade.
Common laborers - wage earners - clerks - some domestics, white collar workers - some executives and professional men live in apartments

This area adjoins principal business district, is from rolling to very hilly, consists of very old large houses, brick and frame, some apartment houses and some negro shacks. It has all utilities and is convenient to stores, churches and business. Many of the large old houses have been turned into cheap rooming houses. As a whole occupants are of the lazy shiftless type, willing to do just enough to eke out an existence. Upkeep of houses is extremely poor and the area has absolutely nothing to recommend it as a residential neighborhood except the fact that it is adjacent to the main business section. There are several very nice apartment houses in the area occupied by a much better type of citizen than the average in the area.
White collar - business men - Jr. Executives

Rolling, scenic country, now less than 25% built up. Residential developments are concentrated in three parts of the area. The development at the northwest corner near the State Normal School is the least active. Athenia is more active, but most of the new building construction is taking place in the Allwood section. Land values in the central portion of the area are increasing as a result of the potential residential building which will probably take place within the next ten years. This is the only area within easy commuting distance of Newark and New York where new building is likely to assume substantial proportions in Passaic County. A new extension of the highway from George Washington Bridge and the new Lincoln Tunnel is now under construction just north of the area. The area is flanked by two lines of the Erie Railroad, with stations at Allwood, and Montclair Hgts., which are about 45 minutes from New York. Local transportation by bus is convenient, and neighborhood stores are reasonably near. All city facilities are installed in built up sections, except the northwest section which has no sewers. The houses are of fair construction, attractively landscaped, and conforming in type. There is good pride of home ownership, and a good middle-class people are being attracted. A United States Quarentine Station for animals is located at Athenia, but this is not particularly detrimental because of its spaciousness, and location.

This area is low and flat, especially at the river, which often overflows its banks, and floods some of the streets in the adjacent section. There is an Erie Railroad Station in the center of the area, which take about an hour to New York. Bus transportation is available to Paterson, Passaic, and Montclair. A graded school is convenient, but the high schools are in Paterson or Montclair. A new community high school is to be built in Little Falls. Foreclosure experience has been comparatively heavy. Practically all the houses on Zeliff Street are now owned by institutions and are being currently offered at $3,000, which is about 50% of their original selling price. Construction generally is either poor, or in a poor state of repair, and very little pride of home ownership is evident. Most of the residents are employed locally, or in Little Falls proper, in the Beattie Carpet Mfg. Co., the rubber goods factory, or the Little Falls Laundry. Stores for household supplies are available. The area is a poor 3rd grade, and should not be expected to improve due to the location, lack of mortgage money, and the generally unattractive appearance of the nieghborhood. There is a volunteer fire department, but otherwise all city facilities. There are no building restrictions.
Factory and laundry workers - clerks - merchants

This is fairly low, slightly rolling country. The area is about 40% built up. The community is served by the Greenwood Branch of the Erie Railroad, and  there is good but transportation to Newark and Paterson. New York is about an hour's ride, but most of the residents are employed by local industry, which consists principally of a company manufacturing rubber specialties, a carpet manufacturing company, and a large laundry company. In recent years, however, Little Falls has become an increasingly popular residential community for people employed in Paterson and Passaic. There are now three grade schools in Little Falls, and a central high school is contemplated for Little Falls, Totowa, and West Paterson residents. At presents, high schools in Paterson and Montclair (Essex County) are used. The Beatie Carpet Manufacturing Co. owns a great deal of land in the area, and also 100 or more houses, which are rented to employees. These homes are not for sale, and are not included in the overhang above. Foreclosure experience has not been heavy. Good pride of home ownership is evident, but the majority of houses are fairly old and somewhat obsolete. There have been no new developments of speculative nature. New construction has been principally on order from prospective home owners.

A sparesly settled area about 30% built up with a mixture of old fashioned single houses, small bungalows of mediocre construction, and some shacks. Many of the yards are used for truck gardens and grape vines in a manner common to the Italian race. The land slopes upward from the river and there are some severe grades, particularly in the eastern portion. While there are some scenic advantages, the area is rocky and treeless. With the exception of main thoroughfares, streets are in very poor condition, and there are many vacant lots with an indiscriminante accumulation of rubbish. No particular neighborhood plan has been followed. All city facilites are available, but there is a volunteer fire department. The tracks of the D.L. & W. Railroad pass through the area although there is no station here. There is good transportation to Paterson by bus, and the fare is 5c. The area is 4th grade, and shows no signs of improvement through new construction, or neighborhood rehabilitation. Traffic is fairly heavy on McBride Avenue. There are two schools and several churches. The high school used is in Paterson. Neighborhood stores for household supplies are convenient.

This is the better part of West Paterson. The land is rolling, and slopes upward gradually from the river. The southern part is sparesely settled, and on the whole, the area is about 40% built up. The streets generally are in poor condition, but the main thoroughfares have good paving. Neighborhood shopping facilities, shcools and churches are convenient, except that the high school used is in Paterson. Good bus, 5c transportation is available to Paterson and Newark and the Little Falls Station of the D.L. & W. Railroad is about half a mile away, affording one-hour service to New York. Most of the residents are employed in Paterson or Passaic industrial establishments. A small local rubber specialty mfg. plant employs about 125 people. The majority of the small houses are in fair condition and a great many exhibit pride of home ownership with small lawns, gardens, and good general maitenance. All city facilities are provided except that there is a volunteer fire department. It is a 3rd grade area.

Due to the generally crowded condition of Paterson and Passaic, this is one of the suburban areas which is destined to become increasingly popular with mechanics and industrial employees with incomes up to $3,000 a year. While the houses are fairly old, they are in fair to good condition, and a pride of home ownership is apparent. The land rises gradually toward the northwest from the river. Grade schools and churches are available, but the high school used is in Paterson. A proposed new community high school in Little Falls will serve this area eventually. The main thoroughfares are well paved, but at present the paving is poor on side streets. There are bus lines on Route 6 - a State Highway and on Union Avenue. It is about an hour to New York on the D.L. & W. Railroad from the Little Falls Station within the area. Local neighborhood shopping is convenient, and the area has all city facilities except that there is a volunteer fire department. Sparsely settled toward the northwest, the area as a whole is about 40% built up. There are a few small local industrial establishments, but the section is predominantly residential in character. Many of the residents are employed by the Wright Aeroplane factory in Paterson.

The terrain in this area is rolling, being low at the river, and high toward the east. It is about 75% built up. Street surfaces are in fair condition. Schools and churches are in the area, including a parochial school, and a playground. Neighborhood stores are convenient. Bus transportation - 10 minutes to downtown Paterson - is good. The majority of the residents are employed in the silk dying industry in Paterson. McBride Avenue is a business thoroughfare. All city facilities are available. The 2-family houses are newer, and generally in better condtion than the 1 family houses. Age and obsolescence of the buildings and a mixture of types of people, make this a poor 3rd grade area.

The terrain is level, but with a gradual down slope toward the river. It is very sparsely settled northwest of Chamberlain Ave., and on the whole is about 75% built up. The houses are old and obsolete, but of fairly good appearance. They are built in rows, rather close together, but detatched. Schools, churches, and neighborhood shops are conveient. Bus transportation is good, with 5c fare to the Paterson business center, a 15 minute ride. There is no nearby railroad station. All city faciltites are afforded. The houses on Preakness Ave., opposite West Side Park are very much better than the average in the area. Otherwise age and obsolescence make this a poor third grade area.
Clerks - small business men - factory employees

A level area, sparsely settled north of Crosby Ave., and on the whole about 50% built up. Approximately 60% of the area is filled-in land and while a sub surface water condition exists, it is not serious. Street surfaces in the built up sections are in good condition. Lawns and gardens evidence good pride of appearance, and properties are maintained in good order. The neighborhood plan is simple with a regular layout of streets and rectangular blocks, representing a neat orderly appearance. Houses are well spaced and of attractive design. Neighborhood stores are conveniently near, as well as schools and churches. Union Ave. is a principal thoroughfare, although traffic is not very heavy in this area. Bus transportation is convenient and takes about 15 minutes to the Paterson business center for rail connections. Not many of the residents are commutors to New York however. Due to its comparatively remote location, flat low land, sparsely settled sections with very little new construction activity, it has been given a poor second grade. The proximity of very much poorer sections of Paterson to the northeast constitute an unfavorable factor on future improvement in the character of this area because of the possibility of infiltration of a less desirable element, and the necessity of passing through these poorer areas to reach it.

West of Broadway the area is level and high enough to be out of the flood danger zone. East of Broadway however, the land is very low from the river to N 1st St., to which point there is danger of periodical floods. From Garfeild St., (one black northwest of N. 1st St.) the land rises in a very steep grade to N 9th St (area C8) which is the crest of the hill. The slope is particularly steep along Clinton, Temple and Cliff Sts. There is a concentration of Negro families between N. & E. Main Sts. and the river, as well as on lower Temple St., and West St. Broadway and N. Main St., are the principle business streets. Union Ave., and Totown Ave., are also business streets, with some industry on the latter. This is the oldest section of Paterson. Residential building is congested, being very old fashioned row houses for the most part, although many are detatched. As a whole the area presents a drab, unattractive appearance, espcially the eastern portion toward the river. Generally speaking the portion West of Broadway and the higher portion northwest of Garfield Ave., is better. There is a new school, stadium, and playground at Totowa Ave., about opposite Jasper St. Neighborhood shopping is convenient, and bus transportation good. The bus fare is 5c and takes about 10 minutes to the main downtown shopping district of Paterson proper, across the river. Congestion, age, obsolescence, and a mixture of races make this a 4th grade area.

This area is at the highest point of a steep slope from the Passaic River. While the houses are fairly old and obsolete, they are in good condition and neat in appearance. The majority are built in rows, but detatched. Such lawns and gardens as there are show care and good maitenance. The Dutch people predominate among the various foreign races living in the area, and they are well known for their pride, neatness & cleanliness of their homes. Grade schools, 10 minutes walk, -high school, 25 minutes. Neighborhood stores are convenient, Bus transportation about 15 minutes to downtown Paterson, is good - fare, 5c. All city facilities are provided. Age and obsolescence of the buildings make this a 3rd grade area. The neighborhood is practically 100% built up.

This is the older part of Prospect Park. About 40% of the houses are built on 37 1/2 to 50 foot lots, and about 60% on 25 foor lots. Most of the houses are in rows, but detatched. There are stores and shops on N 8th St., from Haledon Ave., to Planton Ave., and there is also a shopping center on Haledon Ave. Schools and churches are convenient, although the high school used is in Paterson. The bus fare to Paterson is 5c and takes about 15 minutes. The land is rolling, and high. Age and obsolescene make this a 3rd grade area. All city facilities are afforded, except that there is a volunteer fire department.

The terrain is high and rolling. As a whole, the neighborhood presents a clean attractive appearance, with excellent streets, well kept lawns and gardens, property well maintained, and good pride of home ownership. The Dutch people are well known to be good housekeepers, and they are clean, neat, and frugal. The neighborhood is practically all built up with the exception for a small section near Struyk Ave and 12th-13th Sts. where there is a stone quarry, Because of the rolling terrain, this quarry is not detrimental to the area, and is not objectionable, even to nearby residents. Paterson proper may be reached in about 15 minutes by bus, and the fare is 5c. The grade school is in the center of the area, but the high school used is in Paterson. There are shops at the boundary line on Haledon Ave., and along N. 8th Street. Churches are convenient, Most of the Houses are built on 37 1/2 to 50 foot lots. All city facilities are provided, except that there is a volunteer fire department.

The terrain in this area is rolling. Toward the west it is high, wooded, and sparesly settled. About 40% of the entire area is built up. There is no convenient railroad station, but inhabitants travel to Paterson for rail connections. Good bus transportation is availible, and it takes about 15 minutes to Paterson. Southside Ave and Oxford Ave in this area are good two-family streets. A few very good brick modern homes are scattered throughout the area with present nominal values of from $6,000 to $8,000. Otherwise the houses are small and of frame construction, but very well maintained and indicating good pride of home ownership and civic pride among the people. The area will doubtless continue to be a desirable 2nd grade neighborhood for some years. Schools, churches, and neighborhood stores are convenient. Haledon has a volunteer fire department, but otherwise all city facilities are available.

This is the older part of Haledon. Zabriski St. in the center of the area is better than average, and the residents here exhibit good civic pride through maintenance and good appearance of lawns and houses. As a whole, the neighborhood stores are convenient, and there is good bus transportation. Paterson is about 15 mintes by bus. There is no railroad station convenient to Haledon, except that in Paterson. Because of age and obsolescence, this is a 3rd grade area. Haledon has a volunteer fire depatment, but otherwise all city facilities are available.
Farmers - clerks - silk dye work workers - mechanics

A very sparsely settled community or gently rolling, scenic terrain, with scattered groups of houses. In all, the area is about 25% built up. There is a gradual downward slope toward the central portion where there are several small lakes and the Haledon Water Works. A new grade school is located at the intersection of Squaw Brook Rd., and High Mountain Rd., but the high school used is in Hawthorne to the East (Area B3), which is reached by bus. There is a volunteer fire department, and the water and sewerage system is extended to only part of the area. There are bus lines on Belmont Ave., and on High Mountain Rd., which take about 20 mintes to Paterson for rail connections and shopping. The neighborhood stores in Haledon, adjacent to the South, are used for household supplies. There are a few two-family houses in the area with suites of from four to six rooms, currently renting for $20 to $25 a month. There are also a few houses in the $10,000 to $15,000 class, but these are exceptions to the general character of home construction. Being at present only sparsely settled, the area is worthy of a good third grade. New home construction is not active, and there is no indication of any new developments in the near future. The chief reason for this is probably the fact that North Haledon is comparatively remote from direct rail transportation.

This area is on a steep hillside which slopes precipitously downward toward the east, and more gradually toward the south. There is a good view toward the east across the Hawthorne valley, but the view southward over the city of Paterson is spoiled by smoke and gasses arising from manufacturing and silk dye plants across the river. Most of the houses are old and obsolete, and many are in poor condition. Several of the streets are unfinished, having dirt surfaces, but the main thoroughfares such as Prescott Westervelt, and Mohawk Aves have been maintained in good condition. Schools are convenient, and neighborhood shopping is done in Prospect Park, adjacent to west. It is about one mile to Hawthorne station of the Erie Railroad, from which point it is about an hour to New York. Poor location, age and obsolescence of buildings make this a poor 3rd grade area.

The principal thoroughfare through this area, Valley Road, lies at the base of a steep wooded slope which is not suitable for any future residential development. There are a few houses along the western side of the Valley Road, but most of the houses are located on the gradual downward slope east of it. The central portion of the area is now devoted to horticulture and tree nursuries. There has been no new residential construction for a number of years, and no new developments appear likely for several years at least. Existing construction is more or less scatted and houses a mixed population. Shops and neighborhood stores are located on Valley Road, and a good schoool is convenient. No great pride of home ownership is evident from the appearance of yards and houses, and there are a number of small truck gardens such as are commonly kept by Italian families. Age, obsolescence, and poor maintenance make this a poor 3rd grade area. It is about a half mile to the D.L. & W. Railroad station at So. Paterson, and there are bus lines on both Valley Road and Broad Street. All city facilties.

High rolling country adjacent to the Garret Mountain Park reservation. Valley Road is a main thoroughfare on which there are some shops and a large school. There is a bus line on Valley Road, and the S. Paterson station of the D.L. & W. Railroad is eight minutes walk to the Northeast (in Area D 4). This is a quiet neighborhood of middle class people. Houses are of sound construction, and well maintained. Paterson Area D 4 adjacent to the North is not a detrimental influence beacuse of downward slope of the terrain toward that area, the railroad tracks (bridge at Valley road over the tracks), and the sparsely settled condition of the adjacent land. There is very little room for further development in the area althought the Southern portion of the area os now sparsely settled. New construction will not proceed very far in that direction because of the steep slope ending at the railroad tracks. Thus the area has been given 2nd grade.

Hazel Ave., in the Western part of this area is high, and the land slopes gradually downward toward the east. There are several houses in about the $6,000 to $7000 class along Park Slope, which is better than the average street in the area, since it faces a Park to the South. In the Park there is a large High School and playground. It is reported that a new apartment house is to be erected back of the school. A new extension of the highway from George Washington Bridge is now being built through this park. Bus and rail transportation are fairly convenient to this area, although the majority of the residents are employed by local industry in Clifton or Paterson. The rental demand is good, but there is practically no demand for the sale of homes, many of which are obselete and in poor condition. The area has all city facilities. Schools, churches, and neighborhood shopping facilities are conventient.

This is one of the oldest sections of Paterson. The residential buldings are old, closely built, and principally in rows. There is a concentration of Negroes in the north end around Marshall St., and a mixture of Syrians and Italians elsewhere. Main St. is principally business with heavy traffic. Business and industry along the railroad tracks passing though the middle of the area. There is a D. L. & W. Railroad Station at Clay St., and bus transportation is good to Newark and other points. The land rises gradually toward the west, and is high at the city line. Schools, churches and shopping centers are convenient. Age, obsolescence, congestion, and a mixture of races make this a 4th grade area;.

Hazel St., which is also the southwestern boundary of Paterson, is the highest point in this area. From the street, the land slopes downward east and west. While these houses are old and obsolete, a good pride of home ownership exists, and most of the property is maintained in good condition. The area is practically all built up. Schools, churches, and neighborhood shopping facilities are convenient. Bus transportion is good, and the railroad station is but a few minutes walk. Age and obsolescence, and a mixture of types of residents make this a poor 3rd grade area. Main street is a principal thoroughfare, and traffic is heavy.
Middle class white collar businessmen - clerks

This is a somewhat older area but it still retains a fair degree of residential desirability, and has been given 2nd grade. A good pride of home ownership is evident. Yards, lawns, shrubbery, and houses are maintained in good condition. Many fine shade trees add to the atractiveness of the neighborhood. The land is practically level. The area is about 80% built up, being sparsely settled toward the railroad tracks at the western end. There is a large new high school and playground in the park adjacent to the north. Grade schools and churches are convenient. Neighborhood stores are near, and there is easy accessibility to both bus and rail transportation. An extention of the highway from George Washington Bridge and the new Lincoln Tunnel is now under construction through the park adjacent. It is reported that a large apartment house is to be build back of the high school, but this will not adversely affect residential desireability in this area because the apartment would be located at its northern edge.
Low income groups, clerks - laborers - mechanics

One of the oldest area in Passaic, this area has many old fashioned row-tenement houses scattered through it. Some of the flats are in better condition through rehabilitation, but the neighborhood is nevertheless congested. A gradual infiltration of the lower income groups and more or less undesirable foreign element has resulted in making this a blighted area, with practically no pride of home ownership apparent. Main avenue adjacent to the east is a principal thoroughfare and business street. There is a grade school at the edge of the area, and the high school is a half mile away. Negroes are located principally on Myrtle, Oak, Chesnut, and Monroe Sts. Busses run on Myrtle, Main Ave., and Monroe Sts., to all points, and two railroad stations are nearby in the business and industrial area. All city facilities are afforded.

This area has all city facilities. The terrain is level. Public transportation by both railroad and bus is convenient. The Clifton station of the Erie Railroad is about 40 minutes from New York. A new extension of the highway from George Washington Bridge and the new Lincoln Tunnel is now being built through the park north of this area, which will expedite automobile travel to New York City. Clifton Avenue is now a main thoroughfare on which traffice is heavy. The area has schools, churches, and convenient neighborhood shoping centers. It is practically all built up, and while there is some pride of home ownership evident, the houses are obsolete and more or less congested. Foreclosure experience has been comparatively heavy. The area is a fair 3rd grade.

This area is fairly level, but has a gradual rise toward the southwest. Grade schools, the high school, and neighborhood stores are convenient, and the area is close to the downtown shopping center in Passaic. There is an industrial area to the southwest, where a number of residents are employed. Bus transportation is good to Newark, Paterson and other points, and the D.L.& W. or the Erie Railroad stations are about 10 minutes walk, from either of which, New York may be reached in about 45 minutes. There are several apartments in the area which rent for $40 a month for three rooms, but no new apartments have been built in several years. Traffic has a detrimental influence on residential desirablity. There is a trend toward a change in use of the land for business, apartments, public and private institutions, (there are two hospitals now in the area). Some of the houses are in good condition and a fair degree of pride is evident, but the majority are obsolete. It is a poor 3rd grade. It is reported that the practice of families "doubling up" is being resumed in this area.

This is a small area joined on the west by one or two industrial establishments and the Harvey Canal. It consists of about 25 single and double cottages poorly maintained, those fronting on the main highway being occupied by white people and fairly well maintained, while those not on the highway are occupied by negroes and present a very dilapidated appearance. It is located in what is known as Harvey, an unincorporated village in Jefferson Parish. Has all utilities except public sewerage. Tax rate includes water and lighting tax and appears high, but as assessments are on a basis of about 50% of value effective tax rate is about $20.50.     

Stores are convenient on Highway 90, north boundary of area, and transportation is by bus on Highway which runs between Westwego and Algiers at frequent intervals, and provides transportation to New Orleans by way of Ferry at Algiers. Schools and churches not far distant. Proximity of industrial plants on river front provides good prospect for employment. No sales information available.

Many years ago, this was the finest residential section in Passaic. In fact, as recently as 15 years ago there were a few houses built at a cost of from $80,000 to $100,000 in the vicinity of Passaic Ave., and Boulevard. One such sold in 1938 for $15,000. Another was sold in the same year for $25,000, completely furnished. Taxes on some of these homes run as high as $125 a month. A few are rented for $150 a month. Several of the older houses have been acquired by the city for taxes, and still others are being demolished to save taxes. The area is zoned and restricted to one-family homes, although there are a few two-family houses which were built before the restrictions were imposed. There is a large hospital (St. Mary's) in the area. The location of the neighborhood is a very convenient one, having D.L.& W. Railroad Station (45 mintes to New York) on the western boundary, and the main downtown shopping district of Passaic on the eastern boundary. Passaic ave., and Main Ave., are principal thoroughfares, and traffic is hazardous. The Erie Railroad is adjacent to the southeast, although for the most part the tracks are depressed. There are two Erie stations near. Schools and churches are convient, and there is ample bus transportation to all points. There are many fine old shade trees, and there is good pride of home ownership. Age, obsolescence, and prohibitive cost of maintenance have adversely affected demand, and the area is 3rd grade. The terrain is rolling and high.

The terrain is fairly level, but with a gradual downward slope southeast to the Passaic River. There is a considerable amount of traffice along River Road, Main Ave., and other through streets. The location of the neighborhood is convienently near the Erie Railroad Station (45 minutes to New York) and to the downtown shopping district of Passaic. There are also several groups of neighborhood stores withtin the area. Bus transportation to all points is convienent. There are grade schools, but the high school is somewhat remote and students use buses. Streets are well paved, but the houses are rather closely built and obsolete, which makes this a 3rd grade area showing little or no indications of improvement.

The Southern portion of this area is low and inclined to be swampy in some places, but the terrain gradually rises toward the northwest so that it is high and dry at Passaic Ave., and Dwas Line Road. The golf course in the middle of the area has not had the usual effect of improving residential desirability in the adjacent area, which remains very sparsely settled, - especially toward the northern portion, around Ridgelawn Cemetery. Delawanna itself is fairly well built up, but it is a community of older houses in generally poor condition. Many of the inhabitants are employed in local industry which is scattered in the southeastern part of the area. Rail and bus transportation are only fair, but there are few commuters. There is a grade school in the neighborhood, and a few small stores for household needs. Sales demand is very poor, and there are no indications of improvement. This area will probably continue to be a poor 3rd grade neighnorhood for several years.

This area is level, and practically 100% built up. Many of the residents are employed by local industry adjacent to the northeast at Van Houten Avenue. Houses are closely built up, and comparatively obsolete, although there is a fair degree of pride evident in the maintenance of lawns and shrubbery. Schools, churches and neighborhoods are convenient, and there is good bus transportation to the main shopping district of Passiac, to Newark, Paterson, etc. The D.L.& W. Railroad station, a few blocks to the S.E., affords 45 minute service to New York. A favorable feature is the public park adjacent to the southeast. There is a considerable amount of heavy traffic on Van Houten Avenue, and Broadway is also a thoroughfare. The area is 3rd grade, and with little or no room for new development, shows no signs of improvement.

The terrain in this area is slightly rolling, and it rises gradually toward the west. It is sparsely settled at its south and west extremities, and on the whole is about 75% built up. There is a considerable amount of industry adjacent to the east, and small business extends along both sides of Van Houten Avenue. This is rather a poor street and traffic is heavy. The general appearance of the entire neighborhood is poor because of lack of pride and poor maintenance. Schools, churches, and neighborhood stores are convenient, and bus transportation service is good. The majority of the residents are employed by local industry. Age, obsolescence, and poor maitenance make this a poor 3rd grade area. The nearness of the industrial area where many residents find employment, maintains a good rental demand and has improved the price level of rents.

Dwas Line Road is high and the area slopes northwest and southeast from this point. It is scenic and partially wooded. New construction is taking place principally between Dwas Line Road and Bloomfield Avenue. Residential developments are unlikely to proceed toward the West because of the steep, irregular terrain, and also because of an old cemetery in that direction. There is a new cemetery between Dwas Line Rd. and Passaic Avenue at Edgewood Ave., and Ridgelawn cemetery is adjacent to the south, where the area is sparsely settled. In spite of the several cemeteries, both existing and new construction is of a very good quality. Grade schools are somewhat remote and the high school is two miles away. Neighborhood stores for household needs are conveniently located at Brook Avenue and Broadway in Area C 26, and the downtown shopping district in Passaic is about 5 minutes by automobile. All city facilities are available. There is excellent pride of ownership, and the area would deserve better than 2nd grade were it not for the adverse items mentioned.
Low income groups - laborers - factory works

Smoke, fumes, and noise from the railroads and the industrial section adjacent to this area on the east are detrimental to adjacent parts of this section from the standpoint of residential desirability. In addition, the houses are largely of the old fashioned row-tenement type both brick and frame, closely built, and unattractive. Some have been put in fair condition through rehabilitation, but an infiltration of mixed races belonging to the lower income groups has taken place. Because of low rents there is a good demand for flats of from 3 to 6 rooms. There are practically no single houses here. Many of the row tenements have stores on the street level, so that shopping facilities for the residents are ample. The terrain is level, but with a gradual down slope toward the river. Traffic is hazardous in practically all parts of the area, especially the thoroughfares running north and south, and Monroe St., running east and west. The area is practically surrounded by railroad tracks, business and industry. The best part of it is in the northeast corner. There are grade schools, but the high school is about 1 1/2 miles away. All forms of transportation are convenient. New York is about 45 minutes distant by rail from either one of the two Erie stations adjacent to the west. All city facitlites are afforded.

The terrain in this area is low and fairly level. It is practically all built up with old frame houses which are obsolete, and mostly owned by institutions. Schools, churches, and neighborhood stores are accessible. Busses are available on Lexington, Clifton, and Parker Avenues, and the Erie Railroad station is nearby. New York is about 40 minutes by rail, and the new highway through Area C-21 to the north will make New York City easily accessible by automobile via the George Washington Bridge and the Lincoln Tunnel. The population is mixed, and very little pride of home ownership is evident. The majority of the residents are employed in local industry, which is adjacent to the area. Traffic is hazardous along main streets. All city facilities are available.
Clerks - mechanics - small business men - laborers

Being somewhat older and more congested this area is somewhat poorer than Area C-20 to the north of it. It has more character, however, and is a better neighborhood thatnArea C-22 to the south. From the east to west across the northern part of the area, a new extension of the highway from George Washington Bridge and the new Lincoln Tunnel is now being constructed. It will be about 15 miles on this direct route by automobile to New York. The Erie Railroad to New York is convenient, and takes about 40 minutes. Excellent bus transportation is accessible. There is a considerable amount of traffic on Lakeview Ave., and also on Lexington Ave., through the center of the area. Neighborhood stores, schools and churches are convenient. The houses are closely built in rows, but detatched, and a fair degree of pride of home ownership is evident. All city facilities are available.

This area is about 50% built up with small frame houses of fair construction, and the residents exhibit pride of ownership in most cases through good maintenance and neat appearance of lawns and buildings. The land rises gradually toward the southwest. Trenton Ave. and Lakeview Ave. are main thoroughfares, and traffic is hazardous. There is also a considerable amount of traffic on all four boundries of the area. Neighborhood stores and small business establishments are located on Crooks Avenue, and on Lakeview Ave. Grade schools are convenient, and the high school is located across the railroad tracks in the park to the Southwest. The lakeview station of the Erie Railroad is near, and there is ample bus transportation. The area has all city facilities but because of age and obsolescence it has been given a good 3rd grade. Sufficient space not available for any important new residential construction since existing buildings are more or less scattered, and the type and character of the neighborhood is already established.

The terrain is fairly level, with a gradual downward slope toward the river. Market St. is a main thoroughfare to New York, and traffic is heavy. Sections adjacent to the railroad tracks are less desirable because of industry and business along the tracks, and noise and dirt from the trains. Bus and rail transportation are convenient, and there are a number of neighborhood stores for household supplies. The main downtown business center in Paterson is about 5 minutes ride. All city facilities are provided. There is a hospital  at Madison and Market St. The houses are old style, 2 1/2 story type with front porches. They are closely built in rows, but detatched. A fair degree of the pride of home ownership is evident, but they are is 3rd grade because of age and obsolescence.

Lakeview Avenue is the highest point in this area, and the terrain slopes gradually downward toward Trenton Avenue. The cemeteries to the east are located on the down slope between Lakeview Avenue and the River, thus lessening the adverse affect which they might otherise have on this area. In addition, Lakeview is a very broad thoroughfare. There is a large new grade school and playground in this area, but the high school is 2 miles distant, and students usually travel by bus. Bus transportation to all points is convenient. There are practically no stores in the neighborhood, but a good shopping center is within half a mile. This is a comparatively new area. The streets are regular in their layout and have good paving. The houses are small, but neat, well maintained, and of attractive design. The area has a good appeal for skilled mechanics and white collar workers in the Wright Airplane Co. and other nearby industries, and the rental demand is reported to be the best in paterson. Small lawns and shrubbery are well kept, and evidence pride of home ownership. As a whole, the area is about 60% built up. Better than average houses may be found along Lakeview Ave.
Clerks - small business men - factory workers

Very sparsely settled, particularly west of Trenton Avenue, which is a thoroughfare. There are a number of two-family houses on Trenton Avenue which are in good condition because of recent rehabilitation. Toward the southern end of the area there are a number of large old fashioned houses in poor repair. In the northwestern corner of the area on Iowa Avenue, there is the Holland House for the aged. There is a new school and playground on Michigan Ave and Trenton Ave. The terrain is fairly level, with a gradual down slope westward. There is a 20-family apartment house on Illinois Ave. Elsewhere types of homes vary from small bungalows to the 2 1/2 story type. It is not likely that the sparely settled section will be developed for residence because the land is flat and uninteresting and the outlook unattractive toward the railroad and the industrial section. Both bus and rail transportation are convenient, although a majority of the residents are employed by local industry.

The terrain in this area slopes gradually downward east and west from 29th St. Twenty-five year years ago this was a high class residential section and some of the fine old houses remain, a few of which are occupied by the original owners. Apartment houses have replaced others. Park Ave., Broadway, and 14th Ave. are better than average streets. Schools, churches and a synagogue are convenient, as well as neighborhood shopping facilities for household supplies. The main downtown shopping center in Paterson is but a few minutes ride. Bus transportation is good. All city facilities are provided. It is a good 3rd grade area because pride of home ownership is still evident, although age and obsolescene have lessened demand and adversely affected residential desirability. Broadway is a principal thoroughfare to New York, and traffic is heavy.

This is the best residential section in Paterson. The terrain slopes upward from the river, and is generally rolling and high, north to south. East side park is a favorable influence, and is located on high rolling land in the center of the area. North of the park, some of the streets are winding and attractively landscaped. Houses generally have well kept spacious lawns, and excellent pride of home ownership is evident. Jewish families predominiate in this section, and there is a large Synagogue on Broadway and 33rd St. The high tax rate has jumped maintenence costs, and sales demand is poor. Vacant houses are comparatively large in number, and many others are for sale. Many former residents have moved to Ridgewood, Hawthorne, and other suburban communities. There is a grade school at the south end of the area, and a high school 1 1/2 miles away. Bus transportation is convenient to all points, and Broadway is a main thoroughfare to New York. Traffic is also heavy along the river road. Neighborhood shops are fairly convenient on 33rd street, and on Vreeland Avenue. The Erie railroad station is about a mile to the east, and takes about 50 minutes to New York. Despite the desirability of the area in general, it has very little room for further development, and is now about 85% built up. For this and other reasons cited above, it has been given a good 2nd grade.

This is a fairly level area in the main, but there is a gradual upward slope toward the north. A considerable amount of business and small industry is scattered throughout the area. Bus transportation to all points is excellent, and rail transportation to New York is coneviently near. The area is practically 100% built up, being one of the older sections of Paterson. Generally speaking, houses are closely built, old, and obsolete. There are a few Negro families on Hamilton, 22nd, and 23rd Sts. Restrictions have expired, and almost any type of building may now be erected. Several apartment houses are in the area, the Paterson General Hospital, and there are ample churches, schools, and playgrounds. There are several groups of neighborhood stores, and the main downtown shopping center of Paterson is a few minutes ride by bus. All city facilities are afforded. Age obsolescence, a transition toward business and industry, and a mixture of types of people, make this a poor 3rd grade neighborhood.

The terrain is high at 5th Ave., with a downward slope from that point north and southeast. The area includes the "Nordyke" Section, bounded by 7th Ave., 9th Ave., 25th St., and 28th St., which is better than the rest of the area. Here the houses are newer and in better conditon. Small yards are well kept with lawns and shrubbery giving evidence of good pride. Elsewhere the houses are very much older and generally in rows closely built, though detatched. There are a few apartment houses on 10th avenue renting for $11 a room per month. Grade schools are within nominal walking distance, but the high school is 2 1/2 miles. Neighborhood stores are convenient. Ample bus transportation is afforded. The main downtown shopping district and the railroad station are about 8 minutes by bus. All city facilities are available. As a whole, the area is about 80% built up. It has been given 3rd grade because of general obsolescence of buildings, and a mixture of types of people.

This is one of the oldest sections of Paterson, Residential building is congested, being mostly in rows, but with many detatched. Business and industry is scattered throughout, but it is prinicipally concentrated near the railroad tracks which pass through the middle of the area. The land is rolling, treeless, and somewhat higher to the north. Many of the streets are narrow, although the paving generally is good. The decline in residential desirability has been going on for 25 years or more, and it is now generally occupied by a mixture of foreign races in the lower income groups. There is a park between Lawrence and Montgomery Sts., at Mercer St. and houses facing this park have a very much better appearance. There is a large orphan asylum on Market St., at E. 18th St. There are several schools in the area and some have sizable playgrounds in connection. There are a number of churches. Neighborhood shopping centers are scattered throughout, and the area is close in to the downtown district for shopping and rail connections. Large dye works are adjacent to the north and west at the river, from which smoke and gasses are a detrimental influence to that portion of the area. Age, obsolescence, congestion, scattered industry and business, the adjacent manufacturing area, and a mixture of races, make this a 4th grade neighborhood.

The terrain in this area slopes gradually downward from Lincoln Avenue westward, but in the main it is fair level. The Erie railroad passes diagnoally through the section, and only Wagaraw Road crosses the tracks. Wagaraw Road and Lincoln Avenue are the best streets in the area. Here the house are in better condition and there is more pride of home ownership. These are also main thoroughfares having a considerable amount of traffic - particularly Lincoln Avenue. Busses take about 15 minutes to Paterson. It is about an hour to New York from the Hawthone Station of the Erie Railroad near the Northern boundary of this area. School, churches, and shopping centers are convenient. Many of the street surfaces in the area are dirt, or neglected paving full of holes and ruts. Generally poor maintenance of property indicates a lack of pride, and most of the houses are old and obsolete. There has been little or no planning in the location of houses, and there is no appeal from the standpoint of residential desireability. Most of the residents work in Paterson factories. Just south of the intersection of Wagaraw Road and the railroad tracks there is a sewage filtration plant, although odors from this operation are not noticable in this area, but the plant and its surroundings are unsightly and therefore a detrimental influence. This is a 4th grade area.

This is a very sparsely settled area, especially toward the North. As a whole it is about 35% built up with small homes in fair condition, but mediocre construction, and worthy of only a poor 3rd grade. The land rises toward the east, and Lincoln Ave is high. The Hawthorne Station of the Erie Railroad is about 15 minutes to Paterson. The central shopping point is at Diamond Bridge Avenue and Lafayette Avenue. Schools and churches are convenient. There is some industry and a coal yard along the railroad tracks. Surfaces of main thoroughfares only are in good condition, others being dirt surface, or neglected paving now full of holes and ruts. Foreclosure experience has been heavy and there has been some institutional dumping, especially around Central Avenue. The acceptance of shares for properties by B & L Associations has also tended to keep the market prices low, and demand has been poor for sales. A new highway now under cosntruction through the northern part of this area will facilitate automobile travel to New York via the George Washington Bridge and the Lincoln Tunnel.

There is a good grade school and playground on Washington St. in the area. The area is practically level, and there are a number of good shade trees. While there are two or three 2-family house in the area in which the suites rent from $35 to $45 a month, the majority of the houses are small singles, new within 8 years. These are attractive and well maintained, showing good pride of home ownership. The land is about 95% built up. The high school is about 10 minutes walk, being located in Area B 3 to the east. Lincoln Ave and Diamond Bridge Ave are principal thoroughfares. There is a bus line on the former, taking 20 minutes to Paterson. It is one hour to New York via the Erie Railroad from the Hawthorn station adjacent to the east. The principle shopping center in Hawthorne is near the railroad station. A large Catholic Church and parochial school  are located in the neighborhood. The northwest corner of the neighborhood is wooded and the streets here are not cut through. This is considered an advantage because it lessens traffic and noise from the railroad to the east. Diamond Bridge Ave and Warburton Ave are through streets running east and west. The railroad tracks adjacent to the southeast corner are below street level and are not a serious adverse influence on this neighborhood.

This is a homogenous neighborhood of substantially built attractive homes occupied by middle class poeple who family income ranges from $3500 to $6000 a year. Lawns and gardens are well maintained and evidence a good pride of home ownership. The terrain is a high plateau overlooking Bergen County to the east and the hills of Wayne Township to the west. The area is about 60% built up. Adjacent to the south and east on the down slope, the land is sparesly settled, or unsightly and vacant. Due to the comparative remoteness of the area there has been little new construction and it is unlikely that adjacent land will be developed in the near future. A new highway now in process of construction cuts across southern extremity of the neighorhood which will facilitate automobile travel to and from New York via the Lincoln Tunnel or the George Washington Bridge. Railroad transportation by the Erie R. R. is available from the Glen Rock Station about a mile east. This takes about one hour to New York. Bus trasportation (20 minutes to Paterson) is available on Lincoln Avenue, which is a main thoroughfare, with some traffice hazard. Grade schools and shopping centers are about 10 minutes distant, and the high school is a mile away. Van Winkle Ave. was the first street to be built up and the houses are about 25 years old.

Off the southwest corner of this area there is a stone quarry located in the side of a high cliff. The cliff is heavily wooded and steep immediately to the west of this area, which is located on its lower slopes. East of Goffle Road the land slopes gradually toward the Erie Railroad which runs through the valley. It is approximately 1 1/2 miles to the Hawthorne Station from which point it is about an hour from New York. There are a few small shops adjacent to the southeast but the main shopping center is at the Railroad station. The only direct steet cut through from this area to the center of Hawthorne is Rea Avenue. Schools are about 1/2 mile distant. The area is about 70% built up. New construction is principally on Watchung Drive, a new streeet being cut through. Further development westward is precluded by the cliff. Pride is evident in the good maintenance of homes and lawns. Goffle Road is a main thoroughfare on which there is a bus line.

There is a fine new high school within this area, well landscaped, and with a large playground adjacent to it. The terrain is flat, and about 95% built up with small modern homes of good construction and neat appearance. Between Brookside Ave and Goffle Road there is an attractive park development which is favorable to the rest of the area. There are only a few houses on Goffle Road, which is very much higher than the rest of the area, and immediately west of that there is a high cliff in which a stone quarry is located. This does not adversely affect the major portion of the area. On Diamond Bridge Road there are four modern frame 2-family houses in which 4 rooms and bath rent for $50 per month. Except for Diamond Bridge Road and Warburton Ave which are thoroughfares, the streets are very poorly paved. Although streets were paved some time ago, maitenance is bad and they are now full of holes and ruts. Bus lines on Lafayette Ave and Diamond Bridge Ave afford 20 minute service to Paterson, and the Hawthorne station of the Erie Railroad adjacent to the east, is one hour from New York. The principal shopping center of Hawthorne is located at Diamond Bridge Ave cor. Lafayette Ave. The grade school is about 10 minutes walk. Most of the houses are set back from the street, and lawns and gardens show good pride of home ownership.
White collar business men - clerks - mechanics

This is one of the older sections of Hawthorne. The land is fairly level but there is a gradual down slope toward the west, where a park development is a favorable feature. Lafayette Avenue running north and southh is a main thoroughfare, but traffic is not particularly heavy. The main shopping center is at Diamond Bridge Avenue and Lafayette Avenue, near which there is also the Hawthorne station of the Erie Railroad, about an hour from New York. There is some industry and a coal yard along the railroad tracks. Good bus transportation is available to Paterson, which is about 15 minutes distant. Schools, churches, and neighborhood shopping centers are convenient. Some pride of home ownership is evident, and in some parts of the area shade trees add to the attractiveness of the neighborhood. Many of the streets have had poor maintenance however, and are full of ruts and holes. Most of the houses are small, somewhat obsolete, and in very poor demand. Foreclosure experience has been comparatively heavy, and there has been some dumping by institutions. It is a good third grade area

The entire village has been placed within one grade because of sparse development, being only about 25 per cent built up. Nearly all structures are 5-room, frame cottages. The terrain is slightly rolling in parts, but principally low, flat with few trees. Shopping facilities are reasonably convenient. Churches and schools are convenient. Many employees of the Electromotive plant, which is 6 miles distant, reside here and this has brought rents up. There is no transportation to this plant except by private automobile. Special assessments were largely in default here but were recently "re-spread". Cass Avenue is the principal throughfare within the village. The C.B. & Q RR bisects the area from east to west, with attendant train noise. Development thins out considerably toward the west end of the town. This is a good working-man's town and may see some improvement, but will likely remain the lowest grade village between Lyons and Downers Grove. Sparse development, class of population, type and condition of houses have been considered in grading this "C".

Developed by a speculative builder of small, jerry-built houses. Terrain level with some large old trees. Bounded on the west by a village owned tract via tax foreclosures. The northern boundary is Ogden Ave. (U.S. Route 34). High-speed traffic along this thorofare. North of Ogden avenue is forest preserve. There have been some rent increases in this section due to a shortage of rental units throughout the town. Machinists and other workers recently employed by the Electromotive Plant near La Grange have created this demand. The plant was erected about three years ago and has seen a rapid increase in employment, thereby absorbing lower rental properties. Schools, shops, and transportation are not particularly convenient. Bus line along Ogden avenue. Railroad station half a mile from the center of area. Much of this area was sold on contract to a poor grade of buyers and has reverted back to the builder. Third grade due to cheap constructio n and lack of convenience.

The terrain is level and generally characterized by large old trees along the streets and in the yards. Homes are well kept up, but architecture is somewhat out of date and in a declining market. The plots in this area are large in size and houses amply set back. Schools, churches and neighborhood shops are conveniently situated in as much as this area is bounded on the north by the business section of Western Springs. Some evidence of reconditioning old homes is apparent throughout the area and it is reported that houses thus rehabilitated can be sold here with very little difficulty. There are a scattering of old houses. Residents of this area are principally Chicago commuters and the proximity of the C.B&Q. Railroad Station to the area is a favorable influence, although train noise is bjectionable along the northern extermity of the territory. The neighborhood is still fairly well regarded and because of good demand and convenience to shops, transportation, can be given a good third grade.

The area is generally level with scattered trees. This was a sub-division of promotional character. The owners erected about ten new homes, and from these as samples sold a class of buyers, some of whom were unable to carry the property. As a result, quite a number were foreclosed, but have been resold. The present residents,of the area have an association, the purpose of which is to foster good upkeep and community spirit. All improvements are paid for. Building restrictions are $7500 for the structure. Schools, shops, churches are conveniently located. There is no bus transportation available. The C.B.& Q. Railroad Stations is about 10 minutes walk from the center of the area. Residents are about 95% Chicago Loop commuters. The area is adjacent to a much older area at the north, but is seperated from it by a principal thorofare which practically eliminates any effect of the older properties. To the west, south and east it is bounded by sparsely built-up territory. Homes are of good construction and homogenous size and architexture. Ample opportunity for additional development here which will very probably be along similar lines. Vant lots here offered at $45-65 a front foot.

This area is generally level and open, with very few trees. Most of the streets have been paved during the last ten years. Considerable improvement is noted here in that appreciable numbers of the foreign element which originally built up the territory have moved out and in their places have come a somewhat better class. Nevertheless there are still about 25 per cent laboring class - Polish and Germans - residing here. Many properties have been improved and in time this area will probably surpass the section bordering it on the west because of having more room for future development and larger building lots. Schools and churches are convenient and a shopping area is adjacent on the north. Railroad influence is felt somewhat along the northern border, but the convenience of transportation has a tendency to off-set this objection. Many building lots have been sold here during the past ten years, and are at present hold  by individuals some of whom are expected to build in the area. At the south and east lies sparsely developed acreage.

Best of the second grade areas in the village. Level and newly planted with trees. Some of the streets running east and west have not yet been paved, and at the north extremity of the area just south of Ogden Avenue which is the village limits, sparse development is apparent. This is probably due to expectation of gasoline stations, and taverns along Ogden Avenue. One of the most popular sections of Western Springs, because of moderate price levels. About 50 per cent of the houses not more than 2 years old. Many of these are built of contract for owners. The area is filling rapidly with middle clas residents via FHA financing. Shops convenient at the south extremity. A grammar school near the center of the area. C.B.& Q. Railroad to Chicago required 25 minutes by Express. The area is generally very active as to sales and rents. Graded "B+" because of active development and somewhat exceptional demand. A little too old for first grade.

This is an older section of Western Springs, but still in favor with original residents. The area is fairly level with many large old trees. Schools, churches and shopping facilities are reasonably convenient. Rents here are somewhat higher than in the adjacent "B+" area to the east due to the fact that larger size properties prevail here. Most of the rented units are owned by individuals who have left town and are renting until such houses can be sold. Considerable number of building lots are available for new construction. The area is bounded on the north by Ogden Avenue (U.S. Route 34); high speed traffic along this thorofare. Nort of Ogden Avenue lies an undeveloped tract of forest preserve. Within the area adjacent to Ogden Ave. is sparse development. This is probably due to the anticipation that Ogden Avenue will largely develop along business lines. The section is graded "B" because of age and mixture of architectural types.
Good for smaller houses up to $7000

This is the old section of Western Springs and was the location of the residences of the prosperous element of town prior to development of outlying subdivisions. The terrain is flat with a scattering of trees. Lots are somewhat irregular in size. Houses reflect fairly good maintenence and it is noted that reconditioned houses in this section can be sold readily. Shopping, schools, and churches are convenient and the shopping center of the village lying adjacent to the area at the south. It is a section favored by old residents of Western Springs. It is somewhat handicapped by proximity of the C.B.&Q. Railroad main line to the southern extremity of the area. The area is surrounded on the north, east, and west by better neighborhoods, but because of age and mixture of architectural typies is graded "C".

The area is slightly rolling but not wooded, and about 75% built up. It is of small extent and lies between the Chicago and North Western Railroad and St. Charles Road, which is a principal highway in the south extremity. There is a grammar school in the area, but pupils of high school age attend the Elmhurst High School. Smal Grocery and provision stores along St. Charles Road. The C. & N.W. station is 1/2 mile distant from the area. There area many unpaved streets in here and about 300 building lots available, which however are not likely to be improved in the near future. North American life had a considerable number of foreclosed properties in the area, but is understood to have moved out most of them. Some idividual mortgages still hold properties which were taken back. Mortgage loans at present are very difficult, and in general, made only on a case basis where the property is in good or excellent condition with no outstanding taxes or assessments and where the individual is carefully investigated. Most of the village's relief burden occurs in this area. Very little future predicted here, as the area is adjacent to even less desirable property in the neighboring towns at the west. Poor uniformity, low grade of population, cheap construction, and railroad influence indicate fourth grade.

This is the newest portion of Villa Park and lies at the south extremity of the village, surrounded on the east, south and west by undeveloped tracts. Nearly all the houses in this area were built from 1928 to 1930 and most of them are on 50 x 187' lots. Since these houses were built at the peak of construction cost, they are now selling for considerably less than depreciated reproduction figures, probably as much as 25 per cent below their original value. The area is still very thinly developed, probably not more than 20 per cent built up. Construction, however, is uniform and of good quality, and if there is to be any speculative building at all in Villa Park, it may very well go in here. This area while very good in appearance is somewhat penalized due to distance from transportation, shoppping facilities, schools and churches. Chicago, Aurora and Elgin (electric) railroad station is about 3/4 mile from the area. Chicago & North Western R.R. is over a mile fro the area. Train service to Chicago loop district requires about 43 minutes. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.05. The electric line is preferred due to the more frequent service. This is a favorable circumstance inasmuch as it is far more conveniently situated, in respect to the area under discussion, than is the steam road. In some respects the area has the appearance of first grade, but is penalized because of lack of activitiy and sparse development.

The terrain is level but not wooded, and about 35 per cent built up in the eastern portion. It is somewhat more fully developed west of Ardmore Ave. St. Charles Road is the southern boundary and along this therefore are small shops, gas stations, and miscellaneous commercial structures. The area lies between two railroads passing east and west and is somewhat penalized thereby. Ardmore Ave. the east-west dividing line of the village, is to be extended to meet North Ave., a main trunk highway running east and west, which will probably result in much heavier flow of north-south traffic along this highway (Ardmore ave.) At present Villa Ave., the eastern boundary of the area, is the principal north-south connecting highway between North Ave. and St. Charles Road, and consequently it is rather heavily traveled/ There are many building lots available and indeed entire blocks within this area are undeveloped. However, Villa Park is not a very popular community with the commuting class and not much development is expected here. Transportation to the Chicago loop district is via the Chicago and North Western Railroad (steam) and Chicago, Aurora & Elgin (electric). About 43 minutes is required. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.05. Mixture of architectural types, appearance and railroad influence justifies third grade for this area.

This is an area of mixed single and double cottages and predominantly occupied by colored people. It is separated from the Mississippi River by the levee. The U.S. Industrial Alcohol Company plant is located at the south end of the area and provides employment for some of the occupants of the area, while others employed as domestics work in areas to the north.     

All utilities are available and transportation is adequate. Schools, churches and stores convenient.     

Conveyance records for 1937 show 6 sales of improved properties, one for 2 double cottages at $1500 and 2 for 2 single cottages, price in each conveyance shown as $1150, also 2 for single cottages at $2800 and $4000 respectively and 1 for a single and a double cottage $1600; for 1938, 2 double cottages, 1 for $1250 and 1 for $2000; and 2 single cottages, 1 for $2750 and 1 for $3000.

This area includes the greater portion of the village lying south of the north-south divding line (St. Charles Road). The terrain is nearly level and not wooded; about 55-75 per cent built up, except at the southeast corner which is sparsely developed. Most of the foreclosures in Villa Park, of which there are plenty, occurred west of Villa Ave. Villa Park was a very fast growing town in the '20's, and many small speculators brought lots and permitted assessments and taxes to accumulate. As a result, many building lots at present undeveloped, have assessments on them in the amount of twice what the lot will sell for. This fat has been a serious detriment to residential development throughout the village. In general, there has been a little better activity and a better demand in that portion of the area south of Chicago, Aurora & Elgin railroad tracks. About 43 minutes is required by rail to the Chicago loop district. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.05. Shops, schools, and churches are all convenient to this area. At the eastern extremity along the Chicago, Aurora & Elgin railroad is a large brick fatory engaged in the production of a beverage known as "Ovaltine". This affords employment for around 200 wage earners. Rather mixed type of construction, thin development in portions and railroad influence indicate third grade.

This area is nearly level, with some planting of fairly good trees along the streets. It is about 80% built up and best values are east of Harvard St. The area is rather mixed as to age and is the location of some new and some quite old property. Washington Street, bisecting it from east to west, is a through street but not very heavily traveled. There is ample opportunity for further construction in here and building lots are generally priced from $900 to $1500 for 50 x 187' lots. There has been no specualtive development, but the fea houses which have ben built in the past year were built to order for owners, and this type of growth is likely to continue. Investors with $5000 or more, desiring to reside in Villa Park, almost inevitably seek the south side, of which this is one of the best locations. Churches and schools are moderately convenient. Two small shopping centers are located within two blocks of the north extremity of the area. The principal shopping center of the Villa Park lies 1/2 mile north along St. Charles Road. Transportation is via the Chicago, and Northwester R.R. and the Chicago, Aurora and Elgin. About 43 minutes is required. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.05. The electic road is preferred because of the more frequent train service. This area is considerably nearer the electric road than it is to the steam road. Grade "B" because of quality of construction, stability of inhabitants, and faily good demand.

Steger (pop.est. 3400 in 1940) was founded in the early 90's by a man of that name who estabished a piano factory there. That factory virtually sustained the small community until 1925 when it discontinued business. The town has two small factories located two miles south of Chicago heights, where Steger residents are employed. The town as platted is built up 35% to 40%. Houses are mostly cheap frames. There is very little evidence of pride of ownership. Streets are unpaved, lots unsightly. Demand for property is very slow with only the lower income groups moving in. The best homes in the city are along Halsted, Green Emerald, and Stella Bouleard. South of 34th Street is Wil County; north of 34 St. is Cook County. There is nothing to presage a change for better or worse, as far as real estate is concerned.

This section is about 20 per cent built with modest houses, the older units being of somewhat mixed character, altho the area as a whole is now improving with desirable 6 rom houses.
