The character of the district seems fairly well established., and its continued development is expected with improvements similar to those recently built. Schools are convenient, but the local shopping center and transportation are somewhat distant. Ground is gently rolling, and there are fair sized trees along all streets. In spite of its improving character, the section in its present development does not warrant a first class rating at the present time, and it is doubtful that it will ever be better than a second grade neighborhood.
These two streets have no better than third class improvements of mixed character.

This si the old, central part of Mt. Prospect/ It is now about 80 per cent built up, but little further development is anticipated. The general appearance of the area is rather mediocre, but demand is good because of convenience to schools, shopping centers, and transportation. Ground is flat and has fairly good trees. Because of its age, the district is slowly declining in desirability and the area is therefore graded third class.

This was a 1928 subdivision, now about 15 per cent built. The street layout is attractive and most houses are of pleasing architecture. The area is rather barren because the trees are still small.. When originally subdivided, property owners were given a share in the gold course adjoining on the south. The golf course was heavily mortgaged and the mortgage was subsequently foreclosed and property owners therefore lost their privileges. Te gold course has since been turned into a daily fee course, and the present owner has extended courtesy privileges to persons residing in this district, with the thought of encouraging further development. Schools, shopping centers, and commuter transportation are quite distant. In its present development this section should be considered static in desirability; but the builder who promoted the "Scarsdale" section in Arlington Heights is planning on sponsoring additiona building in this area; and there is reason to believe that this neighborhood will show noticeable improivement when this happens. The neighborhood is graded second class because of its sparse development and age of present structures, but given a plus rating bcause of the influences noted above.

This section is about 10 per cent built. The ground is slightly rolling, but somewhat barren in appearance because of lack of trees. Housing is fairly uniform altho there are a few scattered bungalows on Elmhurst Ave. and on Pine St. Schools, transportation, and the local shopping center are convenient, except at the soutwest corner. Because of the limited amount of new construction coming into this district at the present time, trend of desirability is considered static, but it is felt that the future of this section may show some improvement. Loft sizes are quite generally 50'; all streets are paved and utilities available. The section is graded second class because of its sparse devlopment and the characer of present improvements.

This is a remote section lying south of the village with access on Finley Road or Main St. It is slightly rolling and treeless. It is very difficult to get mortgage loans in this area, same being handled only on a case basis and where no special assessments are past due. H.O.L.C was stuck rather badly out here. Sewer assessments in this area just about "broke the back" of the section, and neighborhood B.&L.'s also took a loss here. However, some foreclosed houses have been sold into stronger hands, which has not generally improved the neighborhood's position. This area is about 30 per cent built up and still has all hard surface roads with no paving. Small grocery and butcher shops in the area. Transportation, schools and churches are somewhat remote. Isolation, poor uniformity, low grade population, and poor demand are considered in grading this "D plus".
Possibly up - has gone as far down as possible

The most attracive situation in the village of Lombard. High and slightly rolling with shade trees planted along streets. The area is about 1/2 mile distance from shops, schools and transportation. The principal thorofare is Main St., which is the east-west dividing line of the village. There is some traffic along this highway. West of Main St. values taper off rapidly; the land slopes downward to grassy meadows, which are as yet underdeveloped. East of the area is a tract with streets laid out, high, slightly rolling, and offering good possibilities for future development if and when special assessments are cleared up. Along Garfield St. there is not a single building. All lots are subject to unpaid assessments, general and special amounts running as high as $1,000 per lot. There are 2 or 3 large, very old houses in this area situated on very desirable plots which may eventually be demolished in favor of new construction. At the north end of the area is a sparsely developed territory west of Main St. and on the east side of Main St. is farm land. This area is occupied by Chicago loop commuters of a good class. Fail transportation via either of two railroads requires about 45 minutes to Chicago loop district. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.30. Graded "B" because of quality of improvements, type of population, and future prospects.
Postal clerks, salesmen, "white-collar" small business men, few laborers

This is an old section of the village somewhat sparsely built up in portions. Better values occur in the western extremity, which is newer probably averaging about 10 years old, and more uniform than the balance of the area. Washington Blvd. passing thru the area from east t west is an arterial thorofare, and Myers Road north and south is also a main thorofare. However, traffic is not very heavy along either highway. This section has been rather hard hit by higher sewer assessments and is still feeling the effects of same. Many available building lots have an accumulation of assessments which is likely to retard development for some time to come. There is a school in the area and at the north end is a small shopping center and the station of the Chicago, Aurora & Elgin Electric R.R. About 45 minutes to the Chicago loop district. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.30. To the east, west and south of this area lies undeveloped tracts, rather flat and unlikely to see any activity for some time to come. This development, rather poor mixture of architectural types, age and poor prospects determine a poor third grade area.

This is the northeast portion of the village of Lombard, and is characterized by railroad influence and a very poor and mixed conglomeration of properties north of St. Charles Road. There is a junk yard along the railroad near this point. The south and east portions are considerably better with best values occurring along Second and Third Ave. A combination under and overpass is to be constructed on St. Charles near the intersection of the two railroads, which may have some favorable effect on the area. Highland Ave. is zoned for apartment buildings, but it is very doubtful if any of these will be constructed. There is a project on foot to extend Maple St. as a gas tax road through the undeveloped area at the west. This may result in further development to westward, but it is highly doubtful if such development would be along very desirable lines. Transportation to Chicago loop via either of two railroads is about 45 minutes. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.30. This area falls just short of being a slum and for that reason is graded "D plus".
Possibly up - has gone as far down as possible

This is the northeast portion of the village of Lombard, and is characterized by railroad influence and a very poor and mixed conglomeration of properties north of St. Charles Road. There is a junk yard along the railroad near this point. The south and east portions are considerably better with best values occurring along Second and Third Ave. A combination under and overpass is to be constructed on St. Charles near the intersection of the two railroads, which may have some favorable effect on the area. Highland Ave. is zoned for apartment buildings, but it is very doubtful if any of these will be constructed. There is a project on foot to extend Maple St. as a gas tax road through the undeveloped area at the west. This may result in further development to westward, but it is highly doubtful if such development would be along very desirable lines. Transportation to Chicago loop via either of two railroads is about 45 minutes. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.30. This area falls just short of being a slum and for that reason is graded "D plus".
White collar commuters, few executives, accountants, etc
Firm - may be up in Better portions.

This area includes the older portion of the village surrounding railroad stations and principal shopping center. It is traversed by three railroads, with 2 stations lying within the area. Main St. is the principal thorofare. This runs north and south and is the east-west dividing line of the village. There is some traffic also along Maple St. east and west. There are two small spots within this area which are somewhat more attractive and with better values than the balance of the area. These are Charlotte and Martha Sts. within one bloack of Maple St., also Grove St. between West Road and Elizabeth St. This last mentioned locality is unusual, in that it is heavily wooded as compared to the rest of the area. Poorer values and poorer appearance is characteristic of the portion north of the Chicago& Great Western R.R., also south of Hickory Road. There are no sewers west of West road, altho city water has been piped to that area. As a whole the area is somewhat mixed, with a few 40-50 year old houses along Maple, Main, Stewart and Craig Sts. There is ample opportunity for development in all portions of this area, but the only appearance of concentration thereof is in the vicinity of Martha and Maple Sts. Transportation, shops and churches are convenient. Age, and mixture of types, and railroad influence relegate this area to third grade.

Largely developed by the Joern Company, which has made a conspicuous success of its opeations here, 95% of the speculative houses having been sold prior to completion. The terrain is level with no trees, but good layout. No special assessments in here. Eleven new homes now in construction for spring sale. Price ranges for old houses showed a sharp rise, due to new development about 1936 and 1937. The outstanding area of La Grange Village and La Grande Park. Schools, shops and churches are readily accessible. Shopping district of La Grange about six city blocks from center of the area. A considerable number of building lots available, but only in connection with new construction by Joern. The area was formerly a golf course, later opened up as a sub-division and highly developed. It has received national publicity in real estate and architectural journals. Station about ten minutes walk from center of the area. Newness, sound construction and charm make this first grade.
Firm - very litle to rent here

Somewhat mixed type of construction. Terrain east of Fifth Avenue is a little lower and less desirable. Generally level throughout, bordered on the north by the forest preserve and, on the east and west, by undeveloped land. Schools, churches and shops not particularly convenient. Shopping center of La Grange ten minutes walk from center of area. This area contains practically the only available timbered lands in La Grange of La Grange Park. Ample opportunity for development. north of Jackson Avenue is the most desirable portion of the area. South of Jackson and east to La Grange Road is a little lower priced but in popular demand. The area is well regarded by older residents, many of whom still reside here as original purchasers. East is rather new, somewhat low, and overbuilt. Principal thoroughfare has moderately heavy traffic. A little too old and mixed to rank better than second grade, though some smallportions might justify an "A" rating.

The oldest section of La Grange Park. Terrain is level, with some planting of good trees along streets. There are a number of large. old houses here which find a ready sale after reconditioning. Schools and churches are convenient and the shopping center of La Grange is within four city blocks of the center of the area. Lots throughout this neighborhood are generally 50 feet in width and houses have the average setback. The area has been benefited by a very desirable sub-division adjacent to the most (Edgewood Park). Although old, this neighborhood cannot be said to be declining and real estate authorities expect a gradual remodeling to take place here, as has been the trend in the last few years. A few small shops are at the intersection of Catherine Street and Woodlawn. The principal thoroughfare is La Grange Road; moderately heavy traffic. Bounded on the east by low undeveloped land. Graded "C plus" because of age and mixture of architectural types. Twenty-one minutes to Chicago via C. B. & Q. R. R.

The area is level, treeless and somewhat lower than the rest of the town, having been built up on a flat meadow. Railroad traverses this neighborhood from north to south and shopping center of La Grange is the northern boundary. Somewhat sparsely developed, this area reflects poor maintenence throughout and the houses are in a state of dilapidation. Values are further depressed by concentration of negro population throughout the area. Two negro churches are in the area and colored population are principally servants and chauffeurs who may be said to constitute a good grade of this race. Bounded at the south by sparsely settled territory, racial concentration and poor quality of a mixed architectural type make this fourth grade.

This area is level, with few trees. It is bounded on the north by Ogden Avenue (U.S. Route 34) along which passes heavy and high-speed traffic. This is a new section and is increasing in popularity among LaGrange residents. It is reacting favorably to the influence of the adjacent area to the north in La Grange Park (Edgewood Park). Schools, churches, and shops are reasonably convenient. By far the majority of residents here are Chicago Loop commuters. There is plenty of room for new development and the new construction that is going in is of good quality throughout. Best values are along 41st street, which is about the center of the area. It is graded "A" because of newness, stability and popularity with the better class of La Grange residents. Sales demand very good. Not quite so desirable or well established in trend as the other two "A" areas in La Grange, due to isolation, the influence of three boarding schools on the north side of Ogden Avenue, and railroad influence near south end.

Terrain is generally level and treeless and the area is sparsely built up at present, particularly along the eastern portion. Building lots here are heavily encumbered by special assessments for all improvements and, for this reason, are not readily salable. As a result, development has been and is likely to continue, very slow. Churches and shops are about ten minutes walk, but a school lies in the center of the area. When these lots can be sold at a reasonable price, it is expected that this section will see rapid development, since people are showing a preference for the suburbs which was not evident five or six years ago. Further influence here lies in the proximity of this section to the Electromotive plant at the south. This plant affords an opportunity of employment for high-grade mechanics and technicians. A few, small neighborhood shops are found along 47th Street and Fifth Avenue at the northwest corner of the area. Territory adjacent at the west is of considerable better value and likely to exert some influence when developed further. Lack of present development is a principal reason for labeling this third-grade.

This area, while classes as "A" throughout, comprises two distinctly different sections. The eastern extremity (Blackstone Ave. and Sunset Ave.) represents the concentration of the highest priced property in La Grange. The remaining portion is very good but considerably lower in price. Area, as a whole, is level with a good planting of young trees. It is a closely knit and neighborhood socially and, while values differ materially, all price levels here are highly desirable. There is more room for development at the west end and smaller hoomes are going in here. A new school is to be built in the neighborhood. Another advantage consists in proximity to transportation facilities and to the business center, this area being nearer to the center of the village than any new development in town. Bordered on the west and south principally by undeveloped territory lying without the village limits. It is about 75% built up and the eastern portion of this section is known as a "deluxe" area, while the west half is know as Leitchworth. Distinctly first grade and the most highly regarded section of the village, principally because of excellent quality of homes and population.

The terrain is generally level, with large old elm trees lining the streets. Conveniently situated with respect to the business district of La Grange, which borders it on the north; also conveniently near schools and churches. There is a scattering of large, old-style houses in this area, and while an excellent rent demand exists here, buyers are somewhat hesitant because of age and a declining trend. Residents are largely commuters; railroad station is about five minutes walk from center of the area. The eastern portion of the area is somewhat less desirable, due to proximity of colored population and to an orphanage which is just beyond the borders of the area at the east. Age and declining trend indicate this to be a third-grade area.

The terrain is level, with all improvements in and not paid for, very few trees and plenty of room for expansion. This is a section of new homes, developed principally in the last ten years. A good demand exists for property in this area and restrictions are of three classes: first, $5000 minimum is the southeast portion; second and third, the remainder of the area divided from $7500 to $10,000. Shopping center of La Grange is about a half-mile from the area and railroad station some distance. Many commuters live in this area. This area is separated from adjacent third-grade area on the east by the principal thoroughfare. Best values are west of Kensington Avenue. At the west and south of the area lies undeveloped territory outside of the village of La Grange. Distinctly first grade; trend being upward and good development expected here

An old section of the village of La Grange, this area is level and is completely deveoped. Fine old elm trees are planted along many of the streets and the area is built up with many large, old houses, a considerable number of which are still occupied by the original owners. Offerings in here are generally somewhat above the market price. Inasmuch as distress sales are practically unknown in this section, any house offered at market price is readily salable. The area is still very popular with the older residents and pride of ownership, good maintenence are quite apparent. It is conveniently situated with respect to schools, churches, and the shopping center of La Grange is no more than five minutes walk from the center of the area. The west portion is somewhat more desirable, due to the influence of well-kept, expensive homes in the adjacent green area. Because of uniformity and good quality of construction, the area is graded "B". It is somewhat too old to be considered first grade.

This area was built up about 15 years ago and, in the last few years, has seen very little new construction. It is a good section of moderately priced houses, occupied by American-born residents. The terrain is level with a fair scattering of old trees. All improvements are in and paid for. The section was developed during the building boom of the 20's and there are very few lots still available, these being held at high prices. It has been very popular during the last decade, due to proximity to schools, to shops and transportation. Inhabitants are principally all loop communters. As stated above, the area is very well built up but still uniformly desirable, with a good class of population and well-constructed homes; hence, second grade. Real estate men find this on easy section to sell.

This area is adjacent to high-class residential sections of La Grange on the north and south but, however, is somewhat blighted, due to the influence of main line C.B.&Q. railroad passing through it. The area is level and treeless; conveniently near transportation via the C.B.&Q. to Chicago, also convenient to churches and shops. The majority of residents are commuters. It is zoned for two-family but no construction of this kind has gone in here within the past ten years. South of the railroad tracks are a fwe high-class two-family flats, also a high school athletic field which is at the eastern extremity of the area. Two-family dwellings rent with heat furnished. Generally speaking, north of the tracks are one-family structures and south of the tracks are two-family dwellings. The area is adjacent to the shopping section of La Grange at the east and is graded "B" because of the railroad influence and because there are a few apartments in the neighborhood.

The oldest section of La Grange, immediately adjacent to and surrounding the business area. Terrain level. Streets lined with fine, old elm trees. A scattering of two-family structures and apartments is found near the business section. Trend is toward this type of housing and a number of old single dwellings converted recently into two-family units. Declining properties here are being picked up for conversion, and there is a fair demand for such structures. No new apartment construction is anticipated until apartment rentals are increased. A small portion of the area may go into business usage in the future. Schools, churches and shops are very convenient in this area; the railroad section is but a few minutes walk from the most distant portion. Age of structures and multifamily trend, proximity of business and railroad, make this a third grade area.

The oldest section of La Grange, immediately adjacent to and surrounding the business area. Terrain level. Streets lined with fine, old elm trees. A scattering of two-family structures and apartments is found near the business section. Trend is toward this type of housing and a number of old single dwellings converted recently into two-family units. Declining properties here are being picked up for conversion, and there is a fair demand for such structures. No new apartment construction is anticipated until apartment rentals are increased. A small portion of the area may go into business usage in the future. Schools, churches and shops are very convenient in this area; the railroad section is but a few minutes walk from the most distant portion. Age of structures and multifamily trend, proximity of business and railroad, make this a third grade area.

The oldest section of La Grange, immediately adjacent to and surrounding the business area. Terrain level. Streets lined with fine, old elm trees. A scattering of two-family structures and apartments is found near the business section. Trend is toward this type of housing and a number of old single dwellings converted recently into two-family units.
