This area has all utilities, good trasnportation, close to schools, is spotted with new construction, lots are 50 x 150 and priced from $1000 to $1500. The trend of growth is to the east. There is a good class of inhabitants living throughout the town. The type of construction north of Ridge Road is somewhat better than the south, and on Reigle Road, on the south end of the area, is some good development. The area is well treed and surrounded with vacant and farm land to the east and south, with some industrial development at the north. Taxes high.

This is a newer area of smaller lots than the "A" area. The lots here are 50 x 130, ranging in price from $1500 to $1800. All utilities are in. This district is on the upward trend. There is a scarcity of lots. It is close to the shopping district, also to school and churches. There is not so much landscaping here as in the "A" area. It is not a rent area, and while it is newer than the "A" area and the trend up, homes are not so elaborate and not so well situated, and smaller in size. This area, however, is a very desirable section of Homewood.
Good up to $10,000 - none for sale

This area with an average age of 12 to 15 years, is a high class one, the best in the city, where all improvements are in, lots are large, 60 x 140 and upward, and priced from $2000 up. It is close in, very well landscaped, paved streets, and protected on the west by the Homewood Golf Club. It is well treed with oak and maple, and there are a number of high-class hoomes. It is restricted to single residences. There are a few high-class Jewish families, but they are leaving and going to Highland Park. It is not a rental area and is quite distinctive from the rest of the city as to its general appearance, and the care taken of properties. North of Maple and west of the Dixie Highway to California, is a new sub-division with all improvements and restricted to $8000 homes which should develop in line with A-1. At this time there are about 12 to 15 singles under construction and priced at $8000 to $20,000. These are homes of noe to two story with six to eight rooms of brick colonial construction.

This area is the oldest section of Homewood, with predominantly German ownership. As in many small towns, while it is graded as a D, yet the homes are quite substantial, and well looked after by this element. The transportation is good, all utilities are in, and a very good shopping center exists. The business center to the north is developing with a recent new theatre ad post office and also $135,000 municipal center. The area is spotted, well treed, and yards well kept. There have been comparatively few losses of homes through foreclosure. The land to the south and east is very sparsely settled but all improvements are in and the trend of development south of the area, should be up. To the west across the Illinois Central Railroad is the Homewood Golf Course.

Terrain is low, flat and treeless and largely populated by a group of Seven-Day Adventists who work at the Hinsdale sanitorium and hospital adjacent to this area. The south boundary is the main line of the C.B.&Q. railroad, with resultant train noise. It is doubtful if any of these inhabitants are commuters, however. No streets within the area are paved and only about 30 per cent improvement is noted. There is an Adventist school and church within the area and a railroad station at the southern extremity. Shopping section is about half a mile distant. The village operates a free bus service for public school children. Poor appearance, poor future and low-income groups make this fourth grade.

This is a very hilly area, rolling and treeless, with a general upward slope to the south. Nearly all of the territory is undeveloped but many lots have been sold and are owned by individuals who may build here at some time in the future. Heavy assessments have been levied for recent improvements. Thirty new houses are to be built at the extreme southeast portion of the area. Construction is now going ahead on some of these and the prices are around $9500. The area, at present, is only about %5 built up and ordinarily would be shown as undeveloped except in this case the impending development has been considered in determining its boundaries. A Catholic church and school are adjacent on the north. Shops are about half a mile distant. Active impending development with uniform type of construction by responsible contractors justify a good third grade.

This area is somewhat rolling and partly wooded. Though not particularly convenient to schools, the village operates a free bus service for school children of residents. Shops and churches are about three-quarters of a mile distant and the principal shoppng section is south of the C.B.&Q. railroad. This section has been developing steadily during the last 15 years and a large percentage of the homes in here are comparatively new. It is favored by residents with modest incomes because of good layout and charm, although slightly less desirable than the "B" area south of the railroad. The land is somewhat lower at the east and not quite so well developed here. The area as a whole is only about 35 per cent improved. A drawback consists in the fact that it is completely surrounded by less desirable property. Good appearance, good construction, good type of inhabitants and a good demand justify second grade.

Area is flat with very few trees. Lowest point in the area is in the vicinity of Sixth and Vine Street where a peat bog occurs over an area of about two city blocks. There are a grammar school and two parochial schools in the area - and the new high school site is adjacent to the south. Best values in demand are in the eastern portion, as this is more attractive and better developed. It is probable that the entire area will be developed eventually with a cheaper grade of homes. At present, it is about 45 per cent improved and U.S. Highway 54 borders the area on the west. Heavy traffic passess along this thoroughfare. The area generally has seen little or no improvement in value on demand during the past five years, and this goes for rents as well as sales. A mixture of architectural tyes prevail here, special assessments are due on many building lots, and it is a location of heavy tax delinquency. Shopping center is adjacent on the northeastern extremity and the C.B.&Q. mainline railroad passes from east to west through the area. Age, mixture and stagnation indicate this third grade.

This area is slightly rolling and wooded with elm, oak and maple trees. There is a scattering of large old houses, many of which are being modernized by private owners who buy up such properties for the purpose of remodeling. Schools, churches and shops are about a half-mile distant from the center of the area. Inhabitants are principally Chicago commuters. The area is about 60 per cent built up, with most of the vacant land in the southern portion. Property is somewhat older at the northern extremity and not quite so desirable although, generally speaking, a good demand exists throughout. Bordering the area at the south is undeveloped territory. Good demand in spite of age, good maintenence and attractive layout have been considered in grading this "B".

This area is known as Woodlands. The terain is high, rolling and heavily wooded toward the east with oaks, elms and maples. Plotted lots here are about 25 percent improved and restrictions contemplate 100 feet minimum average, together with a minimum cost of structure equal to $12,500. Schools are not convenient, but a free bus service is operated by the village of Hinsdale and churches are about one mile distant. All the residents of this area are Chicago commuters and the distance from the area to the railway station is about one mile. This is probably the finest residential neighborhood along the C.B.&Q. railroad west of Chicago. Great charm, excellence of structures, uniformity and high grade of population, with a very good demand, justify an "A" rating.

This area is somewhat rolling but not very wooded. At the northwest extremity a new development is going on. This section is the location of best values and best demand within the area. A junior high school and grade school are about in the center of the area and this is a good inducement to buyers, inasmuch as children do not find it necessary to cross railroad tracks on their way to and from school. Shopping facilities are about a quarter of a mile distant. The village center and village library are located within the area. Some reconditioning of scattered, large old houses is going on here. A small portion of the area lies south of the C.B.&Q. railway (Main Line). Good condition and good demand, with conveniences, have been considered in grading this "C plus".

This is known as Hinsdale Highlands. It is bordered on the north by Ogden Ave. (U.S. Route 34) along which thorofare passes a constant stream of high-speed traffic. Here are found tea rooms, antique shops, trailer camps, gas stations riding stables, and at the eastern extremity, a very high grade tea room. The area is generally flat, with the exception of a portion lying north of Ogden Avenue, which is moderately wooded, hilly and at present undeveloped. It is expected that this section will be built up along somewhat better lines and with somewhat better quality construction than occurs throughout the remaining portion of the area. South of Ogden Avenue the land was originally sub-divided to afford large gardens for prospetive owners. It is burdened by heavy assessments and the development there has stagnated. There have been more foreclosures here than in any other portion of Hinsdale. It is generally remote from shopping facilities, except for a small group of neighborhood stores along Ogden Avenue. Land within the area is only about 15 per cent built up and for this reason, and because of rather poor appearance and high assessments, it is graded "C minus".

This area is occupied by a lower class of foreign and colored laborers with an infiltration of Polish and Negro. About 40 per cent of the inhabitants are Polish and 40 per cent negro. About 40 per cent of the inhabitants are Polish and 40 per cent Negro. There are no sewers, or paved streets, except east of Seeley. From Seeley Street west, it is sparsely settled, with a low-grade of home. East of Seeley and west of Wood, between 145th and 151st is well settled, predominantly with Polish people, and has a sewer and also school facilities. Transportation, however, is poor. Industry lies to the northeast. Land is level. The area is one where it is hoped that the various negro settlements in Harvey will ultimately migrate. There is little to be said about it.

This area is very popular for industrial workers who work in the industries immediately at the north, and a very stable rent situation always exists. South of 160th, there are no sewers, gravel streets exist, and it is sparsely settled. The majority of this southern section has neither electricity nor gas. In this sparsely settled section there are approximately 15 good hoomes costing between $7000 and $10,000 built from seven to ten years ago. This section was once called Michigan and was originally settled by Germans. The best class of foreigners are living here. Immediately east, outside the city limits, is Phoenix, which is predominantly Polish with many negroes. The area is sometimes called the East Side area, and also the Phoenix area, neither being complimentary. There are few multiple units scattered throughout, and the area is spotted.

Known as the North Harvey area. The west end, (From Turlington Ave. and Lexington) is sparsely settled. The section north of 147th, and west of Loomis, has no streets or sewers. Area borders on the manufacturing district to the west, and extreme noise and dirt from these industries is detrimental. North of the area is a County Forest Preserve. The north central section, older and originally settled in 1890, is not heavily occupied. Buildings throughout the area are, however, well maintained. Fifty per cent of the streets that are in are paved. The south central section, south of 147th, east of Turlington and west of Halsted, surrounds the high-school buildings and Central park; a desirable section. Multiple unit construction is mostly east of Halsted. Area is very convenient to the IC depot for quick transportation to the loop. A good shopping district and an excellent grade school. No colored attendants. Several old buildings, well maintained, are at the far northeast corner. The whole area, however, is quite spotted.
Business, professional, low income tax bracket of wage earners
Mixed nationalities, hill-billies from the south
Frame, many converted from large old homes for income purposes

West of Loomis are some multiple units; majority however, are east of Loomis. Age of majority of the are west of Loomis averages 16-17 yrs; east is 30 to 35 years. Homes west of Loomis (where there is a small community of negroes) run from $2000-6500, while in the other portion of the city, $3500-4000. Area is well built up, except around the aforementioned nego homes. Located around the center of Vine and 152nd, these homes are inhabited by the better class negro, who bought and built here many years ago, the city's expansion having built around them. This community is not considered detrimental by those who live in the vicinity, although outsiders consider it so. Radiating from this negro group are many homes, particularly on the west, with large income. Trend is toward elimination of those negroes, as no new ones are coming in. East of Loomis (which is the oldest section of Harvey) hillbillies are coming in from the South; with better class gradually leaving. Sales taking place are of the better homes and are sold only because of proximity to the busines center. Lots are, in the main, 25 feet wide, with a few 24 feet; house are extremely close to one another. Most of the streets are brick. Very few foreigners. Close to depot and shopping district. Non-resident owners are milking (?) the business properties and making no improvements. Area is rapidly declining in the center and the east to a low-class rooming district.

An inferior fourth grade area with mixed foreign population of which 10 per cent are negroes, entirely occupied by the low-class laboring element. The south central portion between Ashland and Myrtle, and between 158th and 160th is predominantly negro, said, however, to be a good class property owner, who bought or built their homes many years ago and have since been surrounded by the growth of the town. This fact, however, has retarded progress south in the area. There are no such sewers south of 159th. There are many cinder streets. There is a convenient school at 157th and Loomis. The western section of the area west of Wood is restricted to whites, and is somewhat newer. This section has water and electricity, but no sewers or gas, and is sparsely settled. In this area the future trend of growth is believed to be fair especially between 155th and 159th. There are no multiple units, and the area is spotted, with transportation only fair.

This area is central and close to the main business district of the city, which has all modern conveniences. It is a desirable area due to the fact that wage earners, business and professional men residing here are of the better income group, and there are many old time German residents. There are very few vacant lots. Between Ashland and Center, on 155th, are many fine old homes, amongst the best in the city. There is a good grade school on both the north and the south of the area. It is very well treed, and the central portion east has brick streets. It is, however, quite spotted. There are no negroes reported living here. South of 155th there are many homes built on 25 foot lots. About 20 per cent of the area has multiple units. New construction last year amounted to six homes built for owners, of five to six rooms, priced at $5000 to $6200.

This is the best residential district in the city. It was given a "C+" rating so as to specify where the better class buildings are. The two only restricted sections in the city are located in this area, viz, from 149th to 151st, and Myrtle to Ashland in the north, as to price (where the most expensive homes are located). In the southeast from 157th to 149th, Ashland to Paulina has restrictions as to white people and brick construction. Along 155th street boulevard from Center to Ashland, lies what is probably the best old section of Harvey which retains much of a former elegance though spotted. The average age of this particular section is between 20 and 25 years. The area has all conveniences, well timbered, and 155th Boulevard is wide with grounds well kept. There are approximately a dozen negro families of the better type who live around Vine and 152nd. These people built or bought their homes many years ago and the city expanded and built around them. People living north and west attach no particular significance to this situation, and accept it philosophically. Outsiders, however, consider it detrimental.

This small area, lying between Ashland and Wood Boulevard south of 147th to 151st, is predominantly Polish, and is known as the area on the west side where the better Polish class live. An objectionable feature is that the area is in School District No. 147. This school is located at 147th and Winchester, and has approximately 40 per cent negro and 40 per cent low-class Polish attendants. All utilities and improvements are in and the area has a small shopping center of its own on the south. Multiple units are scattered throughout, but represent only 5 per cent of the total. Between Paulina and Page, on 149th, is located the city of Harvey's stand-pipe, an emegency water supply building, which is unsightly. Industry is located at the north and east of the area, and the Grand Trunk Railway runs diagonally across the northeast corner. The trend of this area is definitely static.

This area has all improvements - not quite so old as "C" directly north. It has the best grade school in District 147. The average rate of pay to wage-earners living here is between $120 and $150 per month. The future trend of development is believed to be into this area. There are no multiple units. South of 155th is sparsely settled, and immediately south of 157th is vacant. There is a good hospital located on Page Avenue and 155th, and foreign born families are only 20 per cent. The area is spotted with new and old buildings and there is a small business, shopping district to 15rth at Ashland. The Harvey Gold Course is immediately to the west. While there are no negroes reported in the area; yet these peopleseem to crop up all over the city, and it is somewhat difficult to peg just where they are as the city is so diversified with all class of inhabitants.

This is the most eastern tip of Glen Ellyn and is nearly surrounded by sparsely developed territory. The terrain is wooded and somewhat low and marshy toward the eastern extremity. It is particularly convenient to schools, shops, and churches and about one mile from rail transportation. Nearly all highways are unpaved and there are few sidewalks. St. Charles Road at the northern extremity, is the principal thorofare. A small cemetary is situated just east of the area. This section is no more than 25 per cent built up, and mortgage loans are difficult to obtain and in general available only on a case basis. This section is adjacent to a very much better territory at the south, which however, does not influence it greatly as there is a rather sharp break between these two sections. Sparse and haphazard development, rather poor appearance, and adverse influences, determine a poor third grade.

Area is high and slightly rolling with few trees. Construction is more uniform than in any other portion of Glen Ellyn, and at present the area is about 25 per cent built up and of rather open appearance. Good maintenence is very apparent, and there has been better activity here than in any other portion of town, altho development is not what could be called brisk. Schools and churches are reasonably convenient, but shops and transportation are about one mile distant. About 47 minutes to Chicago loop district by either of two railroads. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.80. Building lots are generally 70-80' wide and of a good depth. Prices would generally run from $30-40 a front foot with an absolute minimum of $25.00 a front foot. The land falls off rather sharply to the east into a sparsely developed third grade area. To the south is undeveloped farm land. Values have increased slightly with continuing development here and this condition is expected to hold for some time to come. Not quite active enough for straight first grade

Slightly rolling with some good shade trees along sidewalks. This area is about 60 per cent built up at present, and contains some of the most expensive homes in town, these running from $25,000 to $40,000 in value, along Park Blvd. between Phillips & Turner Aves. Land values are generally about $25.00 a front froot, but there are too many 50' lots in the area, whereas prospective home builders able to buy in this section prefer larger plots. Lot sales in the past year have been picking up for building purposes, and there is an impending development on the six acre tract between Turner Ave. and Lakeview Terrace where a small lake was drained and filled. These houses will cost not less than $12,000. Properties are somewhat older and less desirable north of Turner Ave. Schools, churches, and transportation are convenient. 47 minutes is required to the Chicago loop district via the Chicago & North Western R.R. (electric) or Chicago, Aurora and Elgin (steam). A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.80 Quality of improvements, good class population, and convenience of location, indicate a second grade area.
At least firm because of possible change in usage

The terrain is low and lnearly level. The area lies along the railroad in the western portion of Glen Ellen. It surrounds a small industrial section about the center and is adjacent to a retail shopping district in the eastern portion. Schools, churches, shops, and transportation are convenient. Sparse development south of the railroad and in the western portion of the area. Poorest values along Duane. North of the railroad is somewhat better in appearance and desirability. It is difficult to obtain mortgage funds in this section, which is easily the least desirable part of Glen Ellyn. Transportation to the Chicago loop district requires about 47 minutes via the Chicago and North Western (steam) or Chciago, Aurora & Elgin (electric) railroads. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $8.80. Lack of activity, poor appearance, railroad and industrial influence indicate a poor third grade.
Clerks, draftsmen, "white collar" artisans, laborers, majority commuters.

This is the southwestern porrtion of Glen Ellyn, south of the railroad and bordered on the south by undeveloped territory. The terrain is rolling but not wooded. Lay-out and planning are rather haphazard and irregular. The area is convenient to shopping centers, schools, and transportation. There is some negro concentration just west of this area in the adjacent community of Wheaton. Values are poorer and development sparse in the western portion of the area. Best values occur along Hill Ave. in the vicinity of Brandon Ave. The area is very thinly built up in the south portion, and as a whole is not more than 45 per cent developed. In common with other sections of Glen Ellyn, mortgage funds are generally ample loans being made up to 80 per cent on new construction with FHA insurance. There are a few large, expensive old homes near the center, at the eastern portion of this area, Graded "C" because of sparse development, mixture of quality and types, and adverse influence at the west.
Mixed - "white collar" tradesmen, engineers, commuters, school teachers

This is the southeastern portion of Glen Ellyn, lying south of the railroad and extending to undeveloped tract east of Spring Ave. The terrain is slightly rolling with good trees along the streets in the northern end, and somewhat low in the eastern portion along Whittier and Longfellow Ave. Shopping center is at the western extremity of the area or about 1/2 mile from the center of the area. Schools and churches are convenient. Railroad station is about 1/2 mile from the center of the area. There are two negroes owning property at the north eastern portion of the area, north of Duane St. However, no infiltration is threatened. The area is somewhat affected by railroad influence along the northern boundary. As a whole it is about 60 per cent built up. North and south streets in the eastern extremity north of Orchard St. are very sparsely developed. The northeast corner is somewhat less desirable. There are many vacant lots available for home building throughout the area, and the new construction without exception, has been built to order. There are some large, old single frame dwellings scattered throughout the northern and western portion of this area. Mortgage loans are readily available up to 75% of the appraisal on existing construction. This is the best third grade area in Glen Ellyn, and is surrounded by better neighborhoods, and due to this fact and because of fairly good appearance and construction, it is graded "C plus".

This is the northwestern portion of Glen Ellyn, lying north of the railroad. The terrain is generally high and level, except at the southeast corner, which is low and somewhat marshy in the vicinity of Ellyn Ave. near the southern tip of the lake. Schools, churches, and shops are convenient, the shopping center of the village being at the south extremity of the area. A small shopping center is also located at the northeast extremity on Geneva Road. The principal thorofares are Geneva Road and Main St. running north and south, which connects with North Ave., an important east-west highway out of Chicago. There is some negro influence apparent near the northeastern boundary of this area, and a possibility of some slight infiltration in this neighborhood. Development is sparse at the north and west extremities of the area, and in general, it would be no more than 40 per cent built up. There is a small park near the northeastern portion. Marion and Oak Sts., west of Newton, have seen some new construction built to order for owners. Best values in this area are near the southeast end due to conveniene of transportation and shopping facilities, also because of the influence of the adjacent desirable second grade area. A small court continuing about 6 or 8 attractive hoes is located just off of Ellyn Ave., a little north of Crescent. The terrain at this point, however, is somewhat low and marshy, and the property is penalized on that account. It is not difficult to obtain mortgages up to 80% of the value on existing brick structures for a term within 15 years. Mortgages with longer terms are unusually written with FHA insurance. Some what sparse development, age, and lack of uniformity, indicate third grade.

The area has exceptional topographical advantages. It is nearly all heavily wooded and portions are rolling and hilly, the general slope being toward a small lake in the center. Between Ellyn Ave. and Crescent Blvd. lies a narrow ridge from which the land slopes downward sharply northwest and southeast. Land values average $35.00 a front foot and go as high as $50.00. There are 3 very large, old single houses on the west side of Crescent along the ridge, all situated on acreage plots. A very fine high school is located in the south portion of the area. Shopping facilities, schools, transportation are all conveniently situated. The eastern extremity along Woodlawn Drive, Edgewood Drive and Hickory Street is somewhat more sparse than the balance of the area, but has a good possibility of future development due to excellent appearance and lay out. Values diminish somewhat west of Forest Ave. Most of the new activity is south of Crescent o Riford and Englewood. The RFC owns a tract of land on the west side of Riford for which they are asking $35.00 a front foot. The area in general is somewhat mixed as to type and size of property, with a few running as high as $40,000. A park borders the lake and a small club house is the center of winter sports activity, affording wonderful recreational facilities for young and old. There were some distress sales in this area up until 1937. Convenience and great charm indicate a good second grade.

This area is nearly level and rather open. It is separated from the main portion of the city by Salt Creek and new highway #54 running north and south. A railroad passes along the northern boundary and another skirts the northeastern corner, in addition to which two roads pas near the southern boundary of the area. The area is remote to schools and transportation. To the east is an undeveloped tract which has an uncertain future and may go into cheap housing. There are some commercial possibilities along the new highway, just eastwad of the area. Best values are along Monterey Ave. and it is notable that the south portion is better than the northern end. There are homes priced as low as $2000-3000 and 2 or 3 which would appraise $12,000 or thereabouts. At the extreme north end are 3-4 room "cigarbox" type of houses, probably worth no more than $1500 in today's market. The area is characterized by kellastone stucco construction on plaster base, which does not stand temperature variations. St. Charles Road, the southern boundary, is a boulevard and along here are a few small neighborhood shops and gas stations. The area is more influenced by and proximate to Villa Park, than it is to the city of which it is a part. Mixed, rather poor construction and uncertain future indicate a poor third grade.

This area is the location of some of the best activity in Elmhurst. It is level but not wooded, and of very good appearance. About 40-50 per cent built up. A portion is restricted by deed to $12,500 minimum amount for building construction. Another portion in the northwest corner is restricted by deed to $6500 minimum. The average building lot in here is marketed around $1500. A new highway has been cut through about 1/4 mile west of the area and is expected to have some influence on future development to the westward, although such future development may very propably not be of as good a pattern as existing structures in this area. It is pertinent to note that the area is more or less surrounded by adverse influences: cheap property at the north and proximity of railroads at the north and southwest corner. Moreover, it is not very far removed from quarry operations at the north of the railroad, which constituees a very serious objection. About one mile to shopping centers and nearly a mile to grammar schools and churches. High school is adjacent to the area. Construction is of mixed type, the majority being comparatively new, but some are as old as 12 years. Graded "A-" because of adverse external influences, altho appearance justifies first grade.

This area is level and not wooded, and probably not more than 40 per cent built up. Special assessments are high inasmuch as many lots were bought by speculators who allowed taxes and assessments to accumulate. Very few building lots are now available as low as $1500 and this fact has retarded development. There are a few cheaply constructed houses, but also a number of high priced as $15,000. The area is somewhat distant from high school and junior high school, which is one drawback. Another disadvantage is as mentioned, the large number of vacant lots with taxes and assessments outstanding. The tract directly east of the area is considered by local real estate men to be the best possible location for logical future development. Negotiations are at present under way to reduce the tax and assessment load, and therby stimulate construction. The area is undeveloped at the south extremity, due to railroad influence as well as to the assessment situation. The pattern of construction is very good and the lay out reflects charm and desirability. Very probably good future development will go in here. Graded "B plus" because of appearance, future possibilities, and opportunity for expansion.

This area is level and comparatively treeless, except for small saplings planted along streets. Convenient to schools, churches, and local shops. Transportation is adequate, the area being situated about half-way betwee two railroads: electric and steam. It is bordered on the east by an undeveloped tract of land owned by the same developer, which will probably be built up along the same lines and commensurate with existing construction. At present the area is about 30 per cent built up with very good and uniform grade of houses. There are no outstanding special assessments and all utilities are in. Institutions will lend to 80 per cent of the appraised value with FHA insurance. Insurance companies will lend readily in this area up to 60 per cent of the appraised value. Interest rates vary from 5 to 5 1/2 per cent and with no commission. Minimum land values for new construction in this area generally run about $2000 a lot, with a minimum building restriction by deed. Buildings in here are very uniform in archiecture and size; the area is well situated and in line of future development it is likely to remain very stable for a number of years.

This is a rather poor, remote and sparsely settled development about 10 per cent built up. No paved streets, most all highways being dirt roads, and some sidewalks are not in. This area is outside of the city limits and is characterized by low priced housing. Schools, churches, and transportation are remote and inconvenient. The only hope for future improvement lies in the possibility of a new highway out of Chicago skirting or cutting the area. This appears a very remote possibility. Inconvenience, poor location, and cheap construction indicate a poor third grade.

The terrain is level and appearance is generally uniform and somewhat better than in the surrounding areas. This section is about 80 per cent built up and is the most desirable location north of the railway. Shops, schools, and transportation are quite convenient, and there is a fair sales demand up to $8000. There is no reason to expect much future development in here due to the fact that the area is entirely surrounded by somewhat lower class neighborhoods. North Ave. is the main thorofare with heavy and high speed traffic. Best values occur along Walnut St. at the west extremity, and Addison Street, the eastern extremity of the area. While the properties in this area are somewhat mixed in type and value, nevertheless the area as a whole is generally better than the surrounding neighborhoods and for that reason has been taken out of the third class. Transportation to the Chicago loop district requires about 42 minutes by either of two railroads: The Chicago and North Western (steam) and the Chicago, Aurora & Elgin (Electric). A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $7.85.

The terrain is nearly level and heavily wooded. The area is bisected east to west by a high speed arterial highway, State Route #64. The north one-half is very sparsely developed. The south portion is about 35 per cent built up with a conglomeration of small cheap houses, some of them comparatively new. The area has one redeeming feature; the accessibility to the new tri-state highway U.S. Route #54, which lies a short distance to the west and also its proximity to State Route #64 (North Ave.) This highway is zoned comercial on both sides to the city limits. However, the area under discussion is just outside the corporate limits of Elmhurst. A community association is strictly opposed to annexation by the city of Elmhurst. There are generally no building restrictions, but land values have risen sharply in the last two years, as tax rates are lower than in the city of Elmhurst and also because of the demand for wooded building lots. Gas and electricity are in, but no sidewalks, no paved streets, no water, sewers, or street lights. The area will qualify for Title #2 also Title #1 class 3 on a case basis. Transportation is about 1 1/2 miles distant, schools 1/2 mile, high school one mile. Bus lines available at city limits. Quarry operations at the southeast corner are a blight. Poor third grade because of mixed cheap construction and adverse influence.
To build ow new ones Mod-weak

Situated about in the center of town and surrounded entirely by a good class of property. The terrain is level and somewhat wooded. About 70% built up. There are about 6 large older houses on acreage tracts in the south half of the area. It is likely that these estates will break down into normal size building lots, in fact this change is at present under way. Land values are quite high, being $4500 for 50' lots and in some cases listed as high as $200 a front foot along Cottage Hill Ave. Nearly all mortgage lending operations have been through FHA and 75-80 per cent loans are quite common in this area. Local institutions have had a minor part, the majority of loans being made by Chicago banks and B&L's. Schools, churches, shops and recreation centers are very convenient to this area. It is of interest to note that one large, old home was condemned by the city as unoccupied and hazardous, but despite the condemnation a value of $200 a front foot was set upon the land.

The area is level but not wooded. It is bounded on the east by an undeveloped subdivision. Adverse railroad influence is felt at the north and south extremities of the area. Pride of ownership is evident, and a good community association with 100 per cent membership of property owners contributes to upkeep and stability. Community spirit is outstanding in this area, which is about 60 per cent built up. Schools, churches, shopping centers and transportation are reasonably convenient. Land values are about $35.00 a front foot. There is a public utility booster station and a grain warehouse a little way out of the area at the west. Best property values are in the eastern extremity near the undeveloped tract at the east. Incidentally, this tract was subdivided, streets laid out and paved, after which the developers went broke. Many lots had been sold to speculators, who let the special assessments ride so that it is unlikely that this tract will see much development in the near future. Proximity of railroad influence and rather poor location preclude a better grade than B.

The area is generally level but not wooded. About 50 per cent built up and subject to somewhat adverse influences, consisting of low grade mixed section at the west, quarry operations at the southwest, railroad and small business-industrial section in the south, as well as the principal business center of Elmhurst at the east. It is, however, convenient to schools, churches, transportation and shops. North Ave. (State Route #64) passes through the area from east to west constituting a traffic hazard. There are a very old homes in the south end near the railroad. These might well be 60-70 years old. There has been some scattered new construction in this area in the past year and due to convenience of the central location, probably more will follow. The south end, south of Second st. is somewhat poorer and older than the balance of the area. Best values are generally north of North Ave., which is somewhat newer. There are some "Dutch Colonial" houses on Addison, which were built about 1925. Transportation to Chicago loop district requires about 42 minutes, and a 54 ride monthly ticket costs $7.85. Mixed and somewhat poor surroundings indicate third grade.
Detached singles; 5-6 rooms Few brick bungalows on Geneva Ave., blt.1928,sold$8500-9000, sell today at $5000

This is the northeast and north extremities of the city and is adjacent to a large cemetary and park at the east. The main thorofares are North Ave 9State Route #64) York St. (the north-south dividing line) and Lake St. There are two or three multiples in this area, two-family and four-family. On Berteau St. is a small development of $3500 homes. A new grammar school is located within the area. High schools and churches are reasonably convenient. Railroad transportation is available in the southern extremity of the area. 42 minutes is required to the Chicago loop district. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $7.85. This is not a new portion of town, and institutions foreclosed a number of properties here and still own about 30. In 1928 about 20 brick bungalows were built along Geneva Ave. and sold at that time for between $8500-9000. These are selling in today's market for about $5000, which is about the "tops" in demand for the area. Construction is proceeding at the present time, on the new park just east of the area, which will afford 20 acres of recreational facilities including a swimming pool. This factor may, and probably will, stimulate development in the eastern portion. The northern extremity, north of Fremont Ave. is somewhat less desirable. Appearance, age, and quality of construction, indicate third grade.

This area is part of the older part of Algiers, occupied by some very substantial citizens including one city commissioner, some bldg. and loan executives, etc. Streets are all paved and majority of properties fairly well maintained. Area has all utilities, schools, churches and stores.     

Transportation by gasoline bus to Algiers center, but almost entire area is within easy walking distance of this center. Ferry across river to New Orleans proper docks almost adjoining the northwest corner of the area - with a 10 minute schedule for 24 hours daily. On the north and west of the area are commercial establishments and industrial plants along river.     

Conveyance records for 1937 show 21 sales of houses, double cottages predominating and largely between $2000 and $4000; for 1938, 9 sales of houses, double cottages predominating and in about the same price range as for 1937.

This area is nearly level but not wooded, and would probably not be more than 40 per cent built up. The area is traversed by 3 railroads and bordered on the south by a large, undeveloped subdivision. This area has probably had more foreclosures than any other spot in Elmhurst and the overhang is still moderately heavy. There are two small shopping centers in the area, but schools and churches are somewhat distant. There has been some activity in the vicinity of Mitchell and Bryants Sts. in the south portion and between Seminole and Eggleston at Prospect. Land values probably do not exceed $25-20.00 a front foot and nearly all lending operations at present are via FHA. Principal thorofares are York St. north and south, and St. Charles Road, which touches the area at the northwest extremity. Existing construction is of fair quality but somewhat mixed, and surprisingly enough, there appears to be an active demand for houses up t $7000. The area may develop slowly. Railroad influence and lack of planning indicate third grade.

This area is the best and most centrally located of the second class neighborhoods of Elmhurst. It is the older section of town but because of conveniences and good maintenance it is still strongly in demand. It is about 75 per cent built up and there is opportunity for further development which will probably consist of scattered single houses throughout the area built to order for owners. Land values in here range from $50-75.00 a front foot, but there is a somewhat better demand in the south portion. There has been a lot of new construction recently in the southwest extremity where there is activity and good demand. Highest values in the area are about in the center where 100' lots are the rule. On Kenilworth and Arlington Sts. north of St. Charles Ave. are large houses and larger lots. The area is convenient to a small college, junior high school, library and park. It lies between 2 railroads, electric and steam, which afford transportation to the Chicago loop in about 42 minutes. A 54 ride monthly ticket costs $7.85. In spite of the mixture in age, this area is graded "B" because of convenience of local activity, good demand and good construction.
Very difficult except FHA on new cons.

Low in the center, somewhat higher and wooded along the northeast and southern extremities. A small creek runs through the center of the area. East, south and west of this area lie undeveloped tracts, or forest preserve. Poor development throughout. Mixed architectural types include some shacks. The C.B.&Q. R.R. borders the north end. Small neighborhood shops at the northwestern extremity but the main shopping district is a mile distant. Land values here are low; streets are unpaved; and there are no sewers. A cemetary is located near the southeastern extremity of the area. No schools or churches are convenient. Village disposal plant about the center of area. The western portion of this area lies outside the village of Downers Grove, but has been included since it is a part of the Downers Grove map. mixture of types, poor construction, sparse development, lack of conveniences make this a poor third grade. Better development likely at south end.

This section is known as Denburn. It is slightly rolling, rather low in the northern portion and heavily wooded in the northern part. The northern boundary is a small stream which cuts the area from east to west. There is one bery good private school located in this section. Plotted lots are only about 20 per cent improved, heavier development being at the south end. Shops, schools and churches are reasonably convenient. The most desirable portion of this area is toward the north, around Turvey Road and Jacquel Drive. Nearly all inhabitants of this territory are Chicago Loop commuters. The area is bounded on the west by undeveloped forest preserve and, at the southern extremity, by open tracts. This is easily the best section of Downers Grove and contains some fine homes. Only sparse and haphazard development prevents this from being a B+ neighborhood, or even better.
Business men of moderate incomes (average incomes $3500)

This area is somewhat rolling and heavily wooded with oak, elm and maple trees The terrain is a little higher at the northern extremity. Houses are built on lots varying in size from 60 to 120 feet. Best values are near the northwest extremity where a small amount of new construction is going on. The area is bounded on the north and west by undeveloped territory within the village and the main line of the C.B.&Q. railroad cuts it from east to west at the south. Most of the inhabitants are Chicago loop commuters. Shopping facilities, schools and churches are reasonably convenient and all improvements are in. Sparse development and railroad influence have been considered in grading this "C plus". However, it is expected that this area will in time improve.

This area is fairly level and treeless. There are some unpaved streets in the eastern portion. A Polish Catholic Church and school are located in the area and inhabitants, particularly in the southern part, are principally Bohemian and Polish. The area is bounded at the south by the retail district and stores, churches and schools are conveniently located. At the north Ogden Avenue (U.S. Route 34) bounds the section and along here are found gasoline stations and a few taverns; also heavy traffic. To the east is a vacant tract of land and the area itself is only about 20 per cent improved over all. The C.B.&Q. railroad (Main line) passes near the south of the area with attendant train noise. Thin development, some foreign population, business district and railroad at the south and poor activity indicate this a poor third grade area. Less desirable than adjacent "C" area on the west.
Small business men - office workers - trainmen
8 O.B.2 spec. Nearly all built to owner

This area is nearly all level and somewhat wooded. There are many old homes scattered throughout but maintenance in general is fairly good. It is very convenient to schools, shops and to the railroad station - in fact, it borders the shopping area on nearly all sides. It is the oldest section of town and north of the railroad is built up about 95%, where slightly higher values occur than in the balance of the area. The southern end is rather sparsely settled and is bounded by undeveloped land. There are three grade schools in this area, one parochial and a high school north of the railroad tracks. There are eight churches within the area. Three modern brick apartments are located just south of the business area, all are rented at prices from $37.50 to $70.00. There is some business encroachment north and south of the business area along Main Street. The main line of the C.B.& Q R. R. passes through the center of the area. Due to age, mixture, encroachment in parts, railroad influence and proximity of business, the area has been graded "C".

This desirable neighborhood was a development of the late '20's, and has a concentration of good class one family brick homes. The ground is now about 15% built up and altho development is arrested, the section appears to have good possibilities, as the character of the neighborhood is well established. Schools and shopping centers are distant, but there is a commuter train stop on Wolf Road. The time to the Chicago loop is 32 minutes. The neighborhood is graded second class because the trend of desirability at the present time is static, and with any volume of additional building, this section could show considerable improvement.

This is a new area which has been rather rapidly developed in the past two years. The ground is now about 15% built, and is quite barren in appearance. Houses are small 5-6 room frame units of only fair construction. Schools and shopping centers are very distant, but there is a commuter train stop of Wolf Road, and a local bus operates also along Wolf Road, but the service on this is very poor. The area has no sewers. The section is graded third class because of its isolation, and lack of conveniences, but given a plus rating because of the newness of all houses. This has been a promotional subdivision and its future is none too well assured.

This section is about 80 per cent built up with modest houses, most of which are on small lots. The center of the area is about 1/2 mile from shops, transportation, and schools. The general appearance of the area is just fair, and even when new this section was hardly better than a second class district. There are a few old houses scattered through the territory and it might be said that the section is holding its own at the present time. The neighborhood is penalized because of its general appearance, and therefore rated third-class.

A small section of comparatively new houses, now about 50 per cent built up shopping centers and transportation are inconvenient. This is a fairly good section and because of its comparative newness, it is given a plus rating, although it is graded third class because of its general appearance.

This area is attractively laid-out with winding streets and fairly uniform houses. The ground is about 90% built and most houses are on 50 foot lots. Schools, shopping centers, and transportation are most convenient, and the neighborhood is generally considered to be the most wanted section of Des Plaines. The neighborhood houses a very stable population and has a number of retired wealthy farmers. The section is graded second class because of age and given a minus rating because of somewhat mixed types of architecture. It still continues as a desirable residential section.

This is a very mixed area of good and poor houses with the bulk of the units more or less centered in the north and near the business district. The ground is about 75 per cent improved, is flat, and has small trees along all streets. The appearance of the district is very heterogenous as no attempt has been made at uniformity of design or setback of properties from the street. Two story residences and bungalows are interspersed throughout the district, many built on small lots, some fronting on the sidewalks. In the sparsely settled portion at the south end, there are a number of shack type properties. The future of this district is very doubtful and trend of desirability is downward. Schools, transportation and shopping centers are convenient in the northern end, but the souther portion of this district is at leas 3/4 mile to all conveniences. The neighborhood is graded third-class because of its mixed character and doubtful future.
Lower middle class - few lower class

This is a very mediocre neighborhood bordering on the commercial district in Des Plaines. The section is about 75% built, but little further development is anticipated. The neighborhood is steadily declining in desirability, primarily because of obsolescence and poor maintenence. Many of the persons living in this section work locally in the Benjamin Electric Co. The ground is quite generally flat. Most streets have fair size trees, and all lots are 50 foot; but the primary appeal of the section is its suburban location. Schools, shopping centers, and transportation are all very convenient. Pride of ownership is woefully lacking and practically every house in the district is in need of paint. The neighborhood is graded third class because of its general appearance and declining trend of desirability as a residential neighborhood.

Known as Country Club, the best section of Chicago Heights, and industrial city 33 miles south of the Chicago Loop. It has slowly built up during the last 18 years with a substantial type brick houses. Houses along Country Club Row are restricted to a minimum of $10,000, and on Irving Place $8,000. The area has other restrictions, all utilities. The higher income busines and professional men of Chicago Heights occupy the area. Only two homes each costing $20,000 have been built during the last four years.

This is considered the best part of Chicago Heights as far as demand for property is concerned, being an area of bungalows within the price range of the "average" or moderate income wage earners. Its popular-priced-houses makes it the best and most active sales area in the city. A dozen new houses built during the last twelve months are moving slowly because the demand runs to the substantially built, older houses which offer greater values due to the high cost of new construction. The neighborhood is reasonably close-in, has all utilities, adequate schools and transportation.

An old and poor section abutting the principal industrial district. Occupied almost entirely by Italians. There are a large number of flats for which there is a good demand. it is the poorest section of Chicago Heights as far as sales are concerned.

The oldest portion of Chicago Heights, surrounded entirely by a belt line railroad and industrial plants. Negroes are scattered throughout the area with a concentration on Wentworth. A mixed foreign population with Italian and Polish predominating. All are workers in nearby factories. The business district along 14th was once the principal trade section of Chicago Heights, but has rapidly declined in recent years with the building up of the principal business district to the west. Property sales are very slow in the area, but typical of the entire city, there is a good rental demand.

A small area about 60 per cent built up of small one-story frame houses. The factory of the Railway Steel Springs Company adjoins at the west. The factory at the west. The factory now employs only 60 people. In 1931 the company moved its principal operations to a plant in Pennsylvania. This adversely affected the area which housed workers from the near-by factory. The area has all utilities and adequate schools. It is unslightly in appearance, definitely a moderate income wage earners section, destined to be very slow in developing.

A small area near the business district and industrial section of Chicago Heights, where about 40 percent of the occupants are Italians who evidence a pride of home ownership. The area has all utilities, adequate transportation and schools. Being close in is another advantage. The area is considered slightly better than the "C" area adjoining on the west but hardly as good as the "C" area across Thorn Creek.
Mixed - business - professional - small business - wage

This large area in the heart of Chicago Heights, an enterprising community with diversified industry, located 33 miles south of the Chicago Loop, has a wide variety of houses; 2 story frames predominate. It is a typical close-in area which has been declining for years and due to decline further. Demand for the larger houses has been slow. It is an excellent rent area with virtually no units available. The area is considered inferior to "C" Area at the west. The area has all utilities, good schools, and adequate transportation. Chicago Road, a transcontinental highway, which intersects the city in its central part, is a semi-business street.

This desirable section is now about 15 per cent built and slowly improving in general character. The ground is slightly rolling, and there are small trees along all streets. Improvements are comparatively uniform, altho there are a few scattered frame units of poor appearance. Distance to shopping centers and transportation is objectionable, and the section is rated minus because of this isolation, but given a second class rating because of its improving character and the comparative newness of improvements. Its suburban location in Arlington Heights is generally considered favorable.

This is the old central part of Arlington Heights and as such has a number of buildings of substantial age and obsolete architecture. Altho shopping centers, schools, and transportation are most convenient, trend of desirability continues downward; but demand for all houses is good, and there is some indication that an upward adjustment in rentals may be effected during 1940. The area is graded third class because of the obsolescence factor and the mediocre appearance and age of many of the houses. The better part of the district is east of State Road.

This area is now about 20 per cent built and developing fairly well with houses of a better class than those which were originally built in the district. The section is favorably affected by the activity in the first grade section adjoining on the east, and its future seems to be one of improving character, altho it is doubtful that it will ever improve beyond a good second class neighborhood. Except for the northeast corner, transportation and shopping centers are rather inconvenient. The section is graded second class because of its scattered development and general appearance.

This is known as the "Scarsdale" district in Arlington Heights. The bulk of the houses have been built in the last three years. Improvements are uniform and good class, but the district is rather barren in appearance, because the trees are still relatively small. The ground is about 20% built and the street layout is fairly attractive. Virtually, all of the houses in the area have been built by one builder. Some of these have been speculative and the promotional character of the whole subdivision is in part responsible for the minus rating which is given to an otherwise first class neighborhood. As long as development continues on the present basis the neighborhood may be said to be improving, but it is felt that new construction coming into this district is somewhat better than the neighborhood warrants. The section is graded first class because of its newness, uniformity, and improving character, but given a minus rating because of influences noted above.

This section compares with the third class area directly north of the railroad tracks. It also has a number of old, obsolete structures. The ground is about 75 per cent built, the sparse development being at the west end. Further development is rather doubtful. Schools, shopping center, and transportation are all convenient. Trend of desirability is down and general appearance of most properties is mediocre. Section is graded third class because of poor future, age of structures, and poor upkeep.

This is an attractively laid-out subdivision now about 15 per cent built, but development has been arrested, and there is some doubt that any volume of additional building will come into the territory. Three States Road which runs through the center of the section, is to become a State highway, and the heavy flow of traffic which will naturally follow will adversely affect trend of desirability of the neighborhood. Schools, shopping centers, and transportation are quite distant. More favorably located houses in this section would probably sell up to $15,000 and in many respects they are as desirable as those in the "Scarsdale" section of Arlington Heights, which is graded first class. Houses are very uniform and of attractive architecture, but adversely affected by the lack of new building. The neighborhood is graded second class because of its static condition.

This is the best residential section of Passaic. The land is high and dry. It is comparatively quiet, and there is a fine public park adjacent to the northeast. Passaic Avenue is a main thoroughfare, and while traffice is fairly heavy, it is primarily passenger car traffic, and not noisy. Bus transportation is convenient, and the railroad station is across the park. The D.L. & W. Railroad takes about 45 minutes to New York. Schools are convenient, and neighborhood shops are only a few blocks away. All homes are well maintained and show good pride of home ownership. The area is practically 100% built up, however, and there is very little likelihood of its growing southeast toward the railroad. The Passaic city line is its southwest boundary, beyond which lies one of the better sections of Clifton. It is therefore a 2nd grade area, and probably will remain so for several years to come, despite the fact that mortgage money is now available from local institutions only, and somewhat limited to newer properties. All city facilities are provided.

Almost wholly a low-lying section occupied principally by French mill workers. Cellars are usually damp and sometimes flooded. Single and double houses predominate 25 to 30 years old in poor to fair condition. Values are down 50% at $1,000 to $4,000 and rentals have declined about the same amount to $10 or $15 a month. The new Simonds Saw plant in this area is completed but not yet in operation.
Fairly level, slightly higher than adjacent areas. Highest part along Wolcott Ave. now wooded and undeveloped.
Good school - good bus transportation - well kept property
No zoning, no restrictions. Trap rock quarry on Everett & Belknap Sts to be fenced in by city. It is now abandoned and filled with water
Native born skilled mechanics, business people & clerical workers
A desirable, convenient,  residential section for middle class people, not entirely built up
Marshall Ryder, Manager, Mortgage Information Bureau
Tower Hill. Steep grades. General high elevation. Highest at corner of W. Lowell and Lowell Sts and near Yale St. Slopes sharply down from Lowell St to River.
Scenic. Good bus transportation, schools, amenities close in. West end of city. Prevailing winds all from West, thus eliminating possibilities of smoke and odors from manufacturing.
No zoning. No restrictions. Irregular streets because of steep grades in some places.
This is generally considered to be one of the best residential sections in Lawrence.
Marshall Ryder, Manager, Mortgage Information Bureau
Clover Hill. High and dry. Sightly
Good transportation. Berkeley St. bus line and Lawrence St. School. Home for the Aged large and well kept property.
Native born business executives and professional people
Marshall A. Ryder, Manager, Mortgage Information Bureau
Prospect Hill. High and dry. Level in center portion; slopes rapidly down from Ferry St on the east and High St. on the west.
Good bus transportation. Sightly. Schools and churches. Well kept gardens & lawns.
Executives, business and professional people, native born

Greatest building activity in last 5 or 6 years in this area, particularly near Kendall St., High St., and Ridge Road. Generally considered to be the second best residential section in the city. and Ridge Road. Generally considered to be the second best residential section in the city.
Marshall Ryder, Manager, Mortgage Information Bureau
Low, inclined to be swampy from Florence Ave. westward
Near churches and schools. Higher and more desirable part is east of Congress Street.
Inadequate drainage. No zoning. No restrictions. Low lying. Insecure foundations.
From Florence St. westward to city line low, inclined to be swampy, making foundations insecure. Higher and more desirable part from Congress Street eastward.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Generally high, sloping toward the river at the South and the railroad tracks at the East. Highest at Crescent St., lowest at Water St.
Proximity to business district. Good bus transportation
No zoning. No restrictions. Sandy soil. Sand pit east of Mulloney Park
Originally a high sand bank, much of which has been excavated. Area east of Mulloney Park now being excavated. Best of area around Forest & Crescent Sts.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Proximity to business district. Haverhill St. one of the main through routes (State #110 from Worcester to the ocean)
No zoning. No restrictions. Old large residences. Rooming house section
Impossible to determine because of wide variety of types, age, and use of structures
Some large old singles now used for clubs and high type rooming houses. Many clubs, fraternities and churches grouped around the Common. Lawrence grew up around this area over the past 75 years.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Level in the main, sloping from North to South toward the Spicket River
Proximity to Arlington Mill. High and dry
No zoning or restrictions. Closely built congested area of old type houses
An old section of Irish who have been replaced by a mixed foreign population comprised of Armenians, Polish and Russian principally.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau

Last portion know as Prospect Hill. It is high and dry from High Street East. From High St. to Prospect St. a gradual slope and from Prospect St to Spicket River a precipitous drop. Storrow Park is high & Pleasant St. declines sharply around it.
High and dry. Bus transportation. Good school.
No zoning or restrictions. southeast section subject to smoke from mills carried by prevailing West winds.

Impossible to particularize because of the wide variety in types of structures. Rental values will vary in some cases from $3 to $6 a week in similar buildings depending on location and type of occupants. Generally speaking, val. declined to 75% of 1929 and have recovered to 85%. Rents in 29 were about $1.25 a room on the average. This declined to 51 in 1932 and now the average is about $1.10 a room.
Section bounded by Kendrick, Albion and Wilmot Streets at the Spicket River occupied by native born clerks, business men and mill foremen. This is the best part of the area. It is close in.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Southern part high sloping gradually toward the Merrimack River.
High and dry. Good bus transportation
No zoning. No restrictions. No sewers in the southerly portion. No school. Unimproved streets
Rental activity is now nil because there are no available units.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Inforra tion Bureau
Good bus transportation. Close in. Good school Park and municipal swimming pool
No zoning. No restrictions. Cellars flooded in Spring of 1936

Houses along Sanborn St. about 10 years old frame 2-family in Fair condition. Houses along Salem & Kingston Streets about 40 to 50 years old 2-family frame, fair condition. The southern portion of this area was formerly a shallow pond. It has been drained and filled.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Mt. Vernon St. is high. The slope is gradual north and south.
Good bus transportation. New French Catholic Church at So. Broadway and Groton Sts.
No zoning. No restrictions. Closely built 2-family frame houses, adapted to French tastes.

The portion north of Mt Vernon St is the most desirable. While mortgage funds are ample, ratio of loan to value would be under 50% unless substantial amortization agreement is made. These French people are frugal and industrious. Adjacent undeveloped area to the West recently sold by the Essex Company to Louis C. Cyr,  a French contractor.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Generally level - gradual slope to Shawsheen River
No zoning. No restrictions. City dump east of Shawsheen Road. Smoky and unsightly. Northern section around Market and Greenfield Sts flooded in Spring of 1936
2 or 3 on Osgood St and Grafton St

Southerly side of Market St and both sides of Greenfield St as well as easterly end of Salem St have a group of about 60 small single cottages originally constructed by American Woolen Co. & recently sold to private individuals at an average of $3,000 a piece. This is a desirable neighborhood occupied by skilled mechanics, mill foremen, and middle class business people. The area is very sparsely settled south of Exeter St.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Flat, but out of danger zone.
Good bus transportation. Close in to mills and business section. Good schools and churches
No zoning and no restrictions. Borders B & M PR freight yards.
About 25 families, principally around Springfield, Salem & Bailey Streets.
One of the older residential sections of the city. Proximity to railroad yards and tracks as detrimental influence partly offset by demand from railroad workers to live in adjacent properties.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Close in. Good bus transportation. Adjacent to Broadway which is the main cross-town throughfare. Close to mills.
No zoning, no restrictions. Coal pocket off Wendell St at railroad. Small area with 7 short dead end streets.\n\nNoise and dirt from railroad.
No zoning or restrictions. Congested multi-family tenement rows with stores in many of the lower floors. County jail north of Auburn St.

Very difficult to determine because of the wide variety of cheap tenements from 2 to 20 families. No one size predominates. One 3-family tenement on Tremont St_probably worth $5500 in 1929 declined to $4200 in 1934 or 25% and would now be worth $4800 or 85% of 1929. A 4-room tenement in this building rented for $3 in 1935 and now rents for $3.75 and $4.00, an increase of 30%
Local savings banks own 25 buildings in this area ranging from single cottages to a 20 family tenement block - not readily salable.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Flat. Gradual upward slope to the north
No zoning. No restrictions. Badly congested rows of old frame tenements

In many of these buildings the lower floor is given over to stores and shops for which there is no present demand and therefore many are vacant. A number of bank owed properties here have been razed. 60 properties were owned by savings banks of which 2 have been razed. Some razing was done to admit light and air to other buildings on the same lot. Six-family predominate. Slum clearance project under consideration.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Gradual down slope to the north toward the Spicket River.
Close in. Good transportation by bus. Good churches and schools.
Many of these properties have small shops in the lower floor

mill type brick rows 3 family frame tenements

Low between Marston St. and the Merrimack River. From Marston St. west, the ground is gradually rising.

No zoning. No restrictions. Near gas works to the south. City dump to the north - obnoxious odors Badly flooded in 1936 from Marston St east. Inadequate transportation. Marston St., the main thorofare,  is in bad repair. Several short dead end streets.
Altho small single cottages predominate, there is no character to the neighborhood. There are many types, sizes and shapes to structures, fom shacks to multi-family tenements.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau
Low and flat. Somewhat higher along Hancock St.

Large wholesale junk yard on Medford St adjoining this area. No zoning. No restrictions. Six narrow, dead end unimproved streets of Water St. Congested old buildings. Water St., main thorofare into Lawrence from the West, has narrow, rough granite block paving. Considerable trucking & traffic.Sand pit west of Hancock St.
yes, on Oxford and Melvin Sts

Very old section of the city

No zoning, no restrictions. Borders the railroad Portland St. unimproved. Conglomerate mass of old frame buildings of all types, shacks, singles, two family, 3-family. Truck gardens, chickens

About 12 of the 25 buildings in this area are small shacks. One 3-story flat roof house unimproved now rents for $3 a week per unit. Sales value would be about $2250. These values would be approximately 75% of 1929.
This has been a poor area for many years, and values have steadily declined.
Marshall Ryder, Manager Mortgage Information Bureau

The majority of the residents of this area are Swedish industrial workers of the poorer class. Three-deckers and small single houses in poor to fair state of repair. The American Steel and Wire Company has a rolling mill located in the area, and the Sewage Purifying Works have a detrimental influence, although little obnoxious odor escapes from the plant.

This area is occupied by middle class American business and professional people and some skilled craftsmen. Single houses predominate with some two and three-family in good condition. Buildings are from 10 to 60 years old. The undeveloped section is heavily wooded and contains no improved roads, but it appears to have possibilities for future development, especially near the Lynn-Salem line around Spring Pond. Values, generally, are down about 33%. There is a negro settlement on Eutaw Avenue in Section 10 just east of Memorial Park which may in time extend to the adjacent parts of this Section 5. The green areas near Flax Pond contain newer homes, some of which were built within the last 10 years in about $10,000 class. Much of this section 5 is adjacent to Lynn Woods Reservation which is a natural and beautiful park of 1400 acres. It contains a newly constructed public golf course and a modern fully equipped club house.

Occupied by middle class business and professional people native born. Single and two family houses predominate, from 15 to 50 years old in good condition. Some of the older structures have been modernized throughout. Values have declined 35% to 40%.

Single and two family houses predominate, some of which are about 40 years old but maintained in good condition. Occupants are middle class merchants and business people principally native born. A considerable part of the area is high ground with circuitous streets and a number of steep grades.

Occupied by native born middle class business people and skilled craftsmen. Apartments of about 6 units, two, and three family houses. Age, from 15 to 60 years, in good condition. Values down about 30% from 1929.

Built within the last 10 or 15 years, this is the newest section of the city, this is the newest section of the city. A considerable part of the area is as yet undeveloped but if building activity is resumed it is likely to take place here. Four new homes are now under construction just beyond the city line in Lynnfield. The section close to the Lynn-Peabody line is the low-lying and therefore not so desirable as the high sections in the southwest portion of the area. Single homes predominate in the $5,000 to $10,000 class, some of which are brick construction. Values are off about 25% from 1929 levels. Occupied by middle class business people.

This area has been considered for many years to be the best residential neighborhood. Occupied by business executives and professional people, some of whom are Jews of the better class. Large single homes predominate which are from 15 to 60 years years old and are in good condition. There is practically no demand for this type of house today and values are off 50% to 75% from 1929 levels. There are a few 12 to 16 unit apartment houses and some two-family houses of the duplex type. Convenience to the ocean and Lynn Shore Drive as well as to the down-own business section are favorable factors.

The built-up section of this area is on higher ground than the undeveloped portions. Small singles of the bungalow type predominate in fair to good condition. Occupied by lower middle class native born. The section is not readily accessible except through Fays Avenue on the east. Values are off about 35%.

The northern part of this section is on a steep grade and largely undeveloped. Occupied by poorer class industrial workers of mixed races. Small single houses closely built 15 to 50 years old in poor to fair condition. Values have declined about 33% since 1929.

Occupied by poorer class mixed native and foreign population. Negro settlements may be found around Autaw Avenue near Memorial Park and also around Groveland Street near the railroad tracks. Two family houses predominate, with some three-family and multi-family tenements, many of which are closely built. Buildings are 15 to 50 years old more, generally in poor condition. The Western part is considered the best neighborhood although it is built on the rocky and irregular sides of a steep hill, on the summit of which stands High Rock park and an observatory tower. Values are off about 40% from 1929.

Western Avenue is one of the principal thoroughfares for traffic to Salem and points north. There are a number of small business establishments on this street and many old closely built frame treatments, in poor to fair condition. Other structures in the area are various types- cottages, singles and two-family. Occupied by small merchants and mill workers native born and mixed foreign races. Values are down 35% to 40%. Flax Playground, near the pond, and the Lynn Stadium are rather detrimental influences.

Occupied by a mixture of natives and foreigners of the poorer class. Some professional people have their offices in buildings along the Common. Two and three decker houses predominate, many of which are 50 years old and more, generally in poor condition. There are a number of small shops and stores along Summer Street. Values have declined about 40% since 1929.

Largely occupied by Italian and Armenian mill workers and poorer classes. There is a colony of French Canadian skilled craftsmen in the southeastern part of this section near Western Avenue. Small single cottage type houses predominate with some two-family. Closely built and in poor condition. A considerable portion of the area is undeveloped, and contains a number of clay pits. The Isolation Hospital for contagious diseases is located in the area north of the city farm. Many of the structures are 50 years old and in poor condition. Values have declined about 35% to 40% from 1929. The section near Breed’s Pond is the best part of the area, and the most likely to improve. It is high ground and overlooks the extensive Lynn Woods Reservation.
