A great deal of this area contains dilapidated obsolete tenements although there are some poorly maintained singles and two-family houses, closely built. Occupied by lower class Americans, Italians and Jewish mill workers and laborers, many of whom are on relief. There are also a number of Armenians and Greeks. Structures are 50 years old in poor condition. Values generally are off 30% to 35%. Proximity to the industrial sections might be considered a potential beneficial influence for rents and occupancy, but there are great many vacancies at this time throughout the area

Occupied by poorer classes of Jewish industrial workers and laborers. Mear the manufacturing district. A proposed continuation of the Market Street extension to the shore drive may have a beneficial effect on this area. At present there is a mixture of shacks, small single homes, small stores, and some frame tenements in poor condition. Age, 50 years or more. Values down 35% to 40%.

Occupied by a mixture of the undesirable and foreign element chiefly Italians and some negroes. Poorer class industrial workers and laborers. Small single houses, two- family and some frame three deckers 50 years old or more and in poor condition. Values are off about 35% to 40%.

High class residential section. Many of the more well-to-do live in the Hancock section (M-12) in homes costing from $40,000 to $75,000. Within the last year or two several new dwellings have been built north of Hancock Hill in the $20,000 class and up. There is a trend of this development toward the north and west. Other homes of brick and frame construction in this area in the $15,000 to $20,000 class are occupied by professional men and business executives. Some houses in the southern portion of the area are 20–25 years old, but many of the residences are are less than 10 years old. There are no detrimental influences except that the nearest fire station is about one mile from Hancock Hill, but a station is to be built within the area in the near future.

A concentration of French industrial workers on both sides of the B. & A. Railroad in the neighborhood of Canterbury Street (I-23) and a Polish settlement north of Compton Park as far as Lamartine Street (M-22), and southeastward to Ward Street (N-23). Lithuanians occupy the area down as far as Maxwell Street (M-25). The majority are industrial workers and laborers of the poorer class. Three deckers from 40 to 75 years old predominate. They are in poor condition and mostly without central heating plants. Many other modern conveniences are lacking. A number of similar structures have been razed in this area because of obsolescence. There is a gas production plant and a railroad yard near the center of the area.
Inhabited by the poorer class. Industrial workers. Cheap tenements in poor condition. Contains a wire mill, Atlantic Refinery storage yards and a foundry.

This probably would be classed as the second best residential area. It is occupied by business and professional men. Mostly single houses in about the $10,000 class and a few of the better type two family houses. Some new single houses were built in 1935 south of the State Normal School. There is still a demand for houses costing $6,000 to $7,500 in the neighborhood as well as the area eastward around Morningside (J-15) and Amherst Road (K-14). In the western portion there are some two and three family homes. All are maintained in a good state of repair. No detrimental influences are apparent. Some of the better class Jewish people are concentrated in the portion around S. Lenox Street (I-15), and pride of home ownership maintains the section in good condition.
Not greatly built up, but mostly single homes in good condition. In the path of possible future extension of #1 area now to the south of it.

A Swedish concentration in the Greendale area (T-8) extending eastward to Burncoat Street (V-9) and southward to Wildey ave. (S-10). The large Norton Company, manufacturers of grinding machinery and abrasives, is located on New Bond Street (R-8), and although many of these people are employed here, they are skilled artisans and office workers for the most part. Many of the unskilled laborers live in #11 and #13 areas. There are homes here of the one, two, and three family type in fair to good condition. Many dwellings are 20 years old or more, there has been some new home construction in the last 10 years. In 1935, about 10 new single houses were built in the Barnard Road section (S-13), and 2 or 3 in each of the sections around Burncoat Park (T-13) and Clark Street (W-9). These were in the $4,000 to $5,000 class. The Boston and Maine Railroad runs through this area, but it does not have a detrimental influence on property values except for the locations immediately adjacent to the tracks.

One of the older sections of the city, containing many fine old residences 50 years old or more, but well kept up and still occupied by descendants of the original owners. Some of the better class two family houses are located here, renting from $65 to $80 a floor. Elm Park in the west end is an asset, and the area is convenient to the downtown business section.

Residents mostly business men and office workers, and around Clark University (I-21) college professors. One and two family houses predominate, and there are some three-deckers. Improvements are from 20 to 50 years old in the main, and fair to good condition. Several new single and two family homes have been built within the last two years near Columbus Park (G-19), and east of the University near Norwood Street (J-21).

There is a concentration of Irish in the western section and of Jewish in the southeastern section of this area. Most occupants of the area belong to the middle class. The newer type of two and three family houses predominates, now renting for $30 to $35 a unit, but formerly these were rented for about $60. The majority of these structures are less than 10 years old, and are in a good state of repair. Vernon Hill playground, about 15 acres in extent, is located on high ground in the center of the area.

A small sparsely settled section housing some of the poorer class. Cottages and small homes not in good repair. Although beyond the limit of Worcester Street car lines, transportation service by motor coach is available on the Worcester Oakdale line.

Many industrial workers live in this area as well as a few negroes. The three-decker type of house predominates; and there are some two family houses. Many of the structures are from 50 to 75 years old. Some houses are in a good state of repair, but the majority are in poor condition. There is very little tendency for the area to spread beyond its present limits.

There is a concentration of Swedish industrial workers north and east of the intersection of Belmont Street and Eastern ave. (R-18). Negroes live in a small section around Clayton Street (P-19) and Liberty Street (Q-18). The section along Shrewsbury Street (Q-20) eastward from Mulberry Street (P-20) and including Bloomingdale (U-20) is inhabited by Italian industrial workers and the laboring class. Toward the business district there is a scattering of Syrians and Armenians. There are many three deckers and two family houses in the area from 40 to 50 years in a poor to fair state of repair. Summer cottages and other small single houses predominate along the lake front and in the Lake View section (W-22). Some of these are in the $3,500 to $5,000 class and in fair condition. The railroad yards are located just north and west of Oak Hill (R-22), and it is thought the yards now located in #15 area will be consolidated here.

The Union hill section (P-23) is principally inhabited by Jewish people of the poorer class. South of Oak Hill (R-22) between Dartmouth and Grafton Streets is the French section. Much of this section, especially toward the east in the neighborhood of Bedford Avenue and Revere Street (S-24) is low lying land even swampy in some places. The area is mostly composed of the poorer class. There are many old three-deckers built from 30 to 50 years ago, a number of which have no central heating system, and lack other modern conveniences. Small single houses are scattered through the area, many in need of repair.

There is a small concentration of negroes southeast of Beaver Brook playground (J-19) although it is not spreading to adjacent streets. The area contains many of the poorer classes. In the eastern section three-decker houses predominate, many of which are 40 years old or more, and in a poor to fair state of repair. The western and southern sections are mostly built up with one and two family houses. The area is fairly well served by street car and motor coach lines.
Ground rising from the Lincoln Highway.
Cheapness of construction and character of neighborhood.
Rolling and wooded land adjoining a country club.
Pleasant surroundings and outlook. Marked pride of ownership. Zoned for single family houses costing not less than $15,000.
None save lack of utilities, schools, churches and stores.
This section of small estates is actually no part of the Perth Amboy - Woodbridge area. Residents are commuters to New York and even shop at other points
Rolling and wooded land with pleasant outlook.
Pleasant surroundings and marked pride of ownership. Zoned for single family houses.
Lack of utilities, schools, churches and stores.
A sparsely settled area which, in portions, is rolling and in other portions is flat.
Lack of utilities, schools, churches and stores.
Somewhat rolling ground adjacent to the town of Woodbridge and also to an industrial area.
Age of structures and general environment.
A main highway prevents the undesirable spread to the section in the north.
Level ground adjacent to an industrial area and just beyond the city limits of Carteret.
Poor location, cheapness of construction and lack of utilities.
Level ground sparsely improved in the north.
Meadow land. Obnoxious odors from the creek and from both the oil and metal refineries. Lack of utilities, schools and churches.
An area of cheap construction subject to rapid deterioration.
Ground rising from the water and becoming level. The northern portion overlooks the swamp land.
Lack of utilities, schools, churches and stores. Occasional obnoxious odors from metal refining plant to the west

This is an old section originally designed as a suburban area for Perth Amboy. Changing conditions and the explanation of industry have altered intrinsic values. A number of older and better class families still reside here and will probably continue to do so. At the moment security grading warrants a “B” but the future trend is downward. There is a fair mixture of dwellings.
Slightly rolling land near the town of Fords.
Poor transportation, lack of utilities and stores and nature of neighborhood.
Poor transportation facilities and inferior stores.
Level ground near the center of the town of Ford and on two main traffic arteries.
Cheap construction and character of neighborhood
Level ground rising from the water front.
Pleasant outlook. Convenient to industry and center of city.
Nearness of industry and encroachment of business.
The average contains some dwellings which are above the average.
Rolling and high ground surrounded by an area partially industrial and partially unimproved.
Level ground comprising an old section of the city.
Convenient to places of work and to the center of the city.
Age of dwellings and general character of the neighborhood. Encroachment of business.
Factory help and white collar class
Rolling land well and conveniently located.
Nearness to places of work and center of the city.
Factory help and small business men
The central portion is somewhat more desirable than the balance.
Ground rising from Staten Island Sound and rolling.
Convenience to both industry and business.
Noise and dirt from factories and railroads. Age of structures and character of neighborhood.
Ground rising slightly from the water.
Good outlook and convenient. Fair pride ownership.
Somewhat flat with wide streets and shade trees. Good pride of ownership.
Some homes in this section are considerably above the average - others below. A main high-way prevents the spread of the D" area in the south. "
Ground in portions is level - in others, slightly rolling.
Suburban atmosphere - good transportation. Clean section of model homes.
Transportation will be improved by new boulevard through the section.
Level - to hilly in southern part
Obsolescence - smoke and noise from mills
New boulevard into section will tend to improve values. New road is direct route to Wilmerding. This is a fair working- man's section located close to employment.
Obsolescence - smoke and dirt from mills blows into this section.
Smoke and dirt from mills along river is blown into this section.
Fairly new desirable section - good schools, churches and transportation.
Smoke and dirt from mills - view of mills.

Rated second grade because of its poor location. Brockton Street is somewhat older and prices have not improved about 60% of 1929 prices. Section would never have developed had other ground been available.

A very sparsely settled section which has a few houses concentrated on Washington Street of fairly good character. Development of the section will be somewhat retarded because of topography and dirt from mills, along the river. There are a few houses on Sarah Avenue east of Ander Avenue which are very mediocre. This influence is not considered strong enough to prevent development of the section with good second grade properties.
Desirable residential section of fairly good character. Well removed from dirt and smoke from mills.
Section is similar in character to B-3, but somewhat newer. Sales demand is not as good in B-3 because of the distance to employment and center of the city.
Free from industrial dirt and noise.
Much of the vacant ground is not suitable for development because of topography.
Hilly - somewhat isolated from transportation. Mediocre housing.
Outlying ground is not conductive to development because of topography.
Fairly new homogeneous section of good character. Good elevation. Good transportation. The only new high grade development in the city.
Houses were very well held throughout the depression with literally none offered for sale. The only high class section in the city, with room for additional building.
Desirable residential section - good schools - transportation - good elevation.
Best selling section of city- first section in the city to start to move in market. Considerable modernizing is taking place. Protected against area D-2 by steep hill below Jenny Lind Street.
Convenient to town - High class populace.

This is the highest class section of McKeesport in point of residents. Section is very desirable and building sites are held at very high figures. Properties are substantially built but of old style architecture. A first grade section in point of desirability, but second grade in point of housing.
Near employment - good transportation Good park in the area.

Served by 3-cent car-fare. A very modest section of fair character. A fairly stable demand exists for this section. Similar in character to section C-2 although this area is strictly residential except for normal commercial corners.
Well located - 3-cent carfare - strong Polish Catholic church influence.
Obsolescence - crowded section - small lots - cheap housing - some houses without conveniences.
Considerable dirt and smoke from mills is blown into this section
Near employment - good schools and transportation.
5th Avenue properties are better than other units, but they are principally apartment units above small stores. Buyers for this class of real estate are still unable ti meet purchase requirements.
Crowded - Obsolescence - smoke and dirt from mills. Railroad tracks.
Properties fronting on 5th Avenue are generally desirable for business purposes. Similar in general character to section D-1. Many apartment units over stores on 5ht Avenue.
Near employment. Walking distance to town.

Many fine old families still living in this section. Area slowly going into rooming houses section. A very stable demand exists for units close in to the center of city. Business expansion into this section is questionable because of topography of the ground.
Level to hilly in southern end.
Near employment - cheap rents - central location.
Obsolescence - subject to flood in part. Concentration of low-class populace. Smoke and dirt from mills.
A typical steel laborers section. Houses are built very close together and in poor condition. Good rental demand because of housing shortage for low rent families.
Unsanitary conditions - low-class people Housing in poor condition. In flood area.

Demolition in northern end. Properties are held for income purposes principally, but rents were not collectable during depression. Many alley properties in section. This is the poorest neighborhood in McKeesport. There has been some talk of slum clearance and replacement with a government housing project in the section."
A fair demand exists for properties in this area - local labor primarily. Reliance Steel Co. is building a plant below this section and will employ about 4000 men.
Desirable residential section of fairly good character. Close to employment. No smoke.
Transportation lacking at present but will be remedied.
New bus line into section over new bridge will furnish transportation. Eastern end of the section is the best with white collar class concentration.

A new $80,000,000 strip mill being erected across the river from this section will draw heavily on local labor. Section is also very accessible to new location of Reliance Steel Co. which will employ about 4000 men when their plant is completed.
A small plot of ground now vacant which when developed will probably be similar in character to section B-4. The area is subject to smoke and dirt from the mills at the foot of the hill.
High but somewhat flat ground. This is the best residential section for moderately priced homes. Development is more recent and still continuers. Area adjoins both a golf course and park.
Good location and transportation as well as proximity to Hartford. Good landscaping and marked pride of Ownership.
A later development consisting the most expensive homes in the city. Plots are of fair size and well landscaped.
Restricted to individual homes costing not less than $7
There have been comparatively few sales in the high brackets. Even institutional holders are not inclined to dispose of properties until the demand increases. As a consequence
High rolling land. A somewhat older section of moderately priced singles
Small business men and White collar class
High rolling ground. An older development of bungalows and cottages occupied by shop foremen.
Location with pleesent outlook and pride of ownership.
Distance from city and lack of schools.
This section rates a low Blue" or a very high "Yellow"."
Rolling land. An area of fair age which remains the most desirable section of two family homes in the city.
Good transportation and convenience of location.
Singles in the north / Doubles predominant in the south
Static in south - up in north
Good transportation and fair pride of ownership.
New construction by speculators still continues and sales of same are active. Despite newness of development
Room for expansion and highness of ground.
Land slopes from high ground in the north to low in the south. An older section n ow given over to Polish workingmen's homes. Multi-family of from three to six units predominate.
Age of structure and in the south encroachment of industry.

High land sloping to the south. An area almost entirely given over to Poles and Italians. Houses are almost entirely given over to Poles and Italians. Houses are almost entirely one and two family and of moderate age.
Proximity to places of work and good transportation.
Cheapness of construction and character of inhabitant.
Low land rising in the south. A section containing the homes of office workers. Structures range from singles to multi-families built quite closely together.
Proximity to center of city. Excellent schools and parks. Good transportation.
Encroachment of business on two main arteries.

Ridge land sloping to the east and west. An area out of reach of the railroads and factories yet most desirable to the better laboring class and particularly to the large number of Swedish inhabitants. Sections to the north and south are only sparsely developed.
Good transportation and sufficiently near places of employment.
This section rates a C" owing to the better class of its inhabitants."
Slightly rolling land. An old section of the city closely built up with multi-family homes and combination stores and dwellings and given over to small shop keepers and laborers.
Sales values do not include dwellings in excess of four family of which there are a number.
High ridgeland sloping off in the north.
None, save distance from center of city.

A newer development of moderately sized homes of varied but pleasing architecture. Plots are not large but are well landscaped. Pride of ownership is quite marked. This is an area which is extremely desirable from the lenders point of view.
Distance from center of city, schools, churches, stores, etc.

A small, attractive area containing three large, modern homes of varied but pleasing architecture. Grounds are extensive and well landscaped. Pride of ownership is most evident. Two of these homes are owner occupied; the third is the property of the H.O.L.C. and vacant at the moment. Vacant and sparsely improved land is all that separates this from the less desirable area to the south.
Attractiveness of development and convenience of location.

A newer development of high class, well built, small, single family houses. Architecture is varied through pleasing. Plots are small but nicely landscaped and taken care of. Lenders consider this to be one of the best areas in the city.
Intermingling of old and modern homes.
A section of better and more modern homes and which are sandwiched in with old houses. Most of these old dwellings are quite sizeable. Plots are not large but are well cared for.
Land rises to the north and becomes rolling.
Convenience of location save in the extreme north.

An area containing one and two family detached homes of moderate size, situated on small plots. Desirability of dwellings varies as does pride of ownership and for this reason, section rates a low Blue"."
In southern portion, distance from center of city.

An area of somewhat newer, detached, single family dwellings which evidence a high degree of pride of ownership. Section to the west and south of this area is still only sparsely developed. Both homes and plots are of moderate size. Pride of ownership throughout is generally noticeable.

A slightly older section containing modestly sized, detached, single family homes located on small plots. The southern portion of the area is only sparsely improved. Pride of ownership is generally in evidence but section rates a low Blue"."
Land rises to the south, becoming high and rolling.
A pleasant location and convenient to places of employment.
Distance from shopping center and schools.

This is a somewhat newer but still only sparsely improved area containing modest dwellings of not overly attractive architecture. Lots are not large and pride of ownership is somewhat spotty. Rating is a low Blue"."
Attractiveness of location; adjacence to park.
Only distance from center of city.

An area in which the newer homes are to the south and which, in the east and south, is still only sparsely improved. Dwellings are of modest size, detached and situation on fair sized plots. Pride of ownership is evident and section rates a high Blue"."
Intermingling of the old and the new.

An area displaying a decided mixture of old and new, one and two family detached dwellings located on small plots. Those north of 15th Street are slightly newer and more desirable. Many older structures need both paint and repairs.
Age and obsolescence of average structure.

An old, unrestricted area where are found a mixture of one and two family, detached homes situated on small plots. North of 15th Street, homes are somewhat newer. The extreme northern tip remains only partially improved. Many dwellings are sadly in need of paint and repairs. Section rates a low Yellow". Lenders exercise particular care in the section of loans."
Hillside land rising from the south.
Type and condition of residential properties.

This area contains a mixture of very large and small dwellings in every conceivable state of condition. Many of the large house have been converted into apartments, rooming houses, clubs and professional centers. Land values should increase but values of improvements should decline. Lenders are wary of this section.
Hillside land rising to the north.
Convenient to center of city and places of work.
Age and condition of structures as well as encroachment of business.

A section of old, one and two finally homes built fairly closely together. Dwellings are rapidly depreciating since low salaried occupants cannot afford necessary repairs. Area rates a low Yellow". Lenders steer clear of this section."

A foreign section of one and two family homes of non-descript architecture intermingled with occasional factories and stores. Plots are small save in the sparsely portion in the northeast. Lenders are inclined to pass this area over.
Hillside land rising to the southwest.
Convenient to business area and places of employment.

This is a slightly older section containing modest sized, detached single family residences; a number of which are in need of paint and repairs. Plots are small and homes are built fairly closely together. The northwestern portion is only partially settled.

A section of small singles and doubles, detached but built quite closely together. This area has had an especial appeal to the better class of Italians who are moving from even less desirable sections. Singles and units are frequently occupied by more than one family.
Land rises to the south and becomes rolling.
Intermingling of old and fairly new structures.

An area of one and two family dwellings built fairly closely together. A number of larger singles have been converted into doubles. Also another case of the intermingling of old homes with those somewhat newer and more desirable.
Poor avenue of approach to center of city.

An area of detached, small sized singles erected not too closely together. Cleanliness and pride of ownership are generally in evidence. Portions to the north and south are similarly but only sparsely developed.

This is an area of rather delapidated singles and doubles intermingled with some stores and a few factories. This is Jamestown's nearest approach to a slum area. Rather than foreclose, institutions are inclined to abandon mortgages. Some of those previously obtained are being demolished or dumped at the best available figure.
Small singles, shacks and some multi-fam.

A lowland area, a large portion of which is only partially developed. Dwellings range from shacks to multi-family. Many foundations are unsubstantial with the result that houses are out of plumb. Practically all are sadly in need of major repairs. Many institutions are inclined to abandon mortgages and the city has done some work of demolition.

Some new single homes built within 5 years valued $6,000 to $7,500, occupied by middle class business people native born. Decline in values and rentals nil. No vacancies, good salability. Undeveloped area to the North now a golf course and good area for future development.

Single homes predominate about 10 years old in good condition. Decline in values and rentals nil; no vacancies. Adjacent area most likely spot for new development. Occupied by native born merchants and business men. Parts of the undeveloped adjacent area are low, but drainage would be no great problem.

Single homes predominate, occupied by native born business and professional people. Homes range in value from $6,000 to $25,000. No vacancies, good salability. The majority of dwellings are under 20 years old.

High ground. Single cottage type and two family houses 50 to 80 years old in good repair. Values have declined about 20%. Practically no decline in rental values. No vacancy. Occupied by Irish-American skilled leather workers.

One and two family houses predominate, many of which were built within 25 years. Some of the older homes built about 75 years ago are modernized. All are in good repair, occupied by middle class business people, office workers, city employees and some skilled mechanics. Values have declined about 10%. Practically no vacancies; slability good. Financing readily available on a fair percentage of value.

Single homes predominate; some two family houses. A few new homes built within 5 years, but the majority are 15 to 40 years old in good condition. Occupied by middle class native born skilled mechanics, postmen, firemen and policemen. No vacancies. Decline in rental values nil; salability good and mortgages readily obtainable.

One of the best residential sections of old Salem. Dwellings 75 to 150 years old, modernized and maintained in good condition. A few have been built within 25 years. Old colonial frame single homes predominate, occupied by native born business and professional people, many of who are descendants of old families. The area is near the business center. No vacancies are reported. Values off 15% since 1929.

A good section of old Salem. One and two family brick and frame colonial dwellings from 50 to 150 years old, modernized and maintained in good condition. Occupied by business and professional people principally native born. Area is close to the down town business section.

Single cottage type houses predominate many of which have been built within the last 10 years. High ground near the modern brick factory building now under construction by the Hygrade Lamp Company. Decline in values and rentals nil. No vacancies are reported. Salability good.

Some very high class single homes along Fairfield Street, Lafayette Place and Saltonstall Parkway, many of which were built within the last 10 years. Practically all of the area north of Roslyn Street new since the 1914 fire. Other homes 50 to 100 years old modernized and in good repair, many of the old colonial type. Rentals $35 to $60 a month are off 15% to 20% since 1929. Values have declined about 30% and homes now range from $6,000 to $25,000. No vacancies are reported.

Forest River Park a beneficial influence for the southern part of this area, occupied by better class of French merchants and business people. Two family and multi family houses predominate and there are some single homes. In the main, the area is closely built up. Values off about 30%; few vacancies.

“Salem Willows” Willows park is an area frequently used as a picnic ground. There are several restaurants specializing in shore dinners. Stores and places of amusement are to be found along Fort Avenue, but this does not depreciate real estate values in the built up section. Single homes predominate about 20 years old in good condition, occupied by native born business people. Values are off 10% to 15%. Salability good and financing readily available. The Cove and ocean front here are beneficial influences.

Single cottage type and two family houses 50 to 150 years old in poor to fair condition. Some parts of the area closely built, multi-family houses, occupied by Irish-American lather mill workers. Rents $10 to $15 a month on the average.

Occupied by Jewish people in the junk business, and poorer classes of Armenian industrial workers. One and two family homes predominate approximately 70 years old in poor condition. Some tenements 50 to 100 years old, many of which have little or no sales value. Values off 25% to 30%.

Occupied by poorer classes of mixed races. Small single homes predominate, some of which are of brick construction in poor to fair condition. Detrimental influences here are due to the North River being muddy and unsightly at low tide and proximity of the area to the mouth of the canal. Values are off 30% and rentals down 20%.

"Castle Hill". Occupied by poorer classes of French mill workers. One and two family homes and some three deckers 40 to 60 years old in poor to fair condition. Undeveloped area not desirable and right between the Marblehead branch and the main line of the Boston & Maine Railroad. Values off about 30% and rentals down 20%.

Single family cottage type houses in poor condition along the Canal Street extension and vicinity. The northern part of the area around Dow and Palmer Streets is composed of brick tenements 6 to 12 families, and some 2 family homes built mostly since the fire in 1914 particularly for French mill workers employed in the Naumkeag Steam Cotton Mill at the foot of Harbor Street/. Houses would probably be unsuitable for other tenants and stable rental values depend upon mill activity. Tenements now are well rented and in fair to good condition. Values have decline about 30%. Sales and financing difficult.

Large single and two family homes 60 to 70 years old in poor to fair condition. Some modernization. Occupied principally by Polish foreign born machinists and mill workers. Values off 10% to 20%. Rentals off 15%. The Boston & Maine Railroad runs through the area and the North River at this point is a detrimental influence, being muddy and unsightly, especially at low water.

One of the oldest sections of Salem. Houses built from 50 to 150 years ago. Cottages, small stores and tenements closely built and in poor condition. Occupied by poorer classes of Polish mill workers.
Largely undeveloped. Low swampy area bordered by the city stone crusher on the west and railroad yards and an industrial section on the east. Small single cottages in poor condition.

Single homes, some of the cottage type and some of the old colonial type in poor condition. Also many multi-family frame tenements 60 to 150 years old. Some modernization. Occupied by poorer classes of mixed nationalities, principally Polish foreign born. Factory workers and unskilled laborers. Values off 50% and rentals down 25% although there are few vacancies reported. Sales and financing difficult. The North River is muddy and unsightly at low water and there is a gas production plant on the Collins Cove side of the area.
Undeveloped- This large undeveloped area is composed of high rocky ledge which makes it difficult and closely to develop. Probably no new construction will take place here for some time to come.

"Prospect Hill". Steep scent up Frospeat Street at the top of which are e number of estates and large mansions occupied by wealthy manufacturers. Lower down the hill are a few smaller single homes. Practically no vacant land except within private estates. Houses about 80 years old valued from 410,000 to 6100,000. Frame construction predominates. Smaller homes in the $5,000 to $7,000 class. Values declined 25% but have recovered about 5%. About 75% owner occupied. All structures in good condition.

Precipitous incline of undeveloped area north of Blossom Street affording fine view, Large single homes atop this hill of $20,000 to $80,000 value. Elsewhere in the 74,000 to 610,000 class, all in good condition. Occupied by the more well-to-do families. Values were off about 30% but no properties have been offered to indicate extent of recovery. Practically 100% owner occupied.

Single homes predominate. Frame and brick construction. Shade trees and well kept lawns and gardens. Comparatively level and close to downtown section. Values from $10,000 to $25,000 are off about 40% from the high. Practically 100% owner occupied.

Known as the "South Side" section; this la a high plateau and about the only level high ares in Fitchburg. Approaching streets rapidly ascend from the river away from confusion and noise of traffic, yet it is convenient to the downtown business section. About 25% of the land Is undeveloped, and a dozen houses have been built within the last 5 years. Values range from $5,000 to $15,000 which in some cases represent a 50% decline. Rentals of from $30 to $50 a month were off 60%, but have recovered 75% of the decline. Singles predominate, with some two-family homes. All are in good condition. No vacancies are reported and about 50% are owner occupied. Inhabitants are native white business and professional people.

West Fitchburg section. Singles predominate with some two family duplex and double decker type. The mills own a number of these houses which are from 15 to 30 years old, but generally in good condition. Occupied by English and Irish middle class skilled workmen. Near mills, churches and schools. Values $3,000 to $6,000 were off 30% but have recovered 85% of the decline. Mill rentals to employees at $20 to $30 a month are about $5 a month under normal. About 50% of the homes are owner occupied. Approximately 10% of desirable wits vacant.

Westminster Hill road a steep grade, overlooking the city. A hilly area largely undeveloped and used for farming. Occupied by Irish and Finish mill workers and farmers. Streets are unimproved, dirt surface but maintained in good condition. Mostly single frame homes 20 years old in fair to good condition. Some new within 5 years. Values $3,000 to $6,000. Few offerings or sales. About 75% owner occupied.

Lower third of Prospect Hill. A steep grade north and south but fairly level east and west. Close in. Occupied by native born middle class business people. Single homes predominate 20 to 30 years old of frame and brick construction in good condition. Values from $5,000 to $7,000 were off 25% but have recovered about 20% of the decline. The fluctuation in rental values is about the same and now ranges from $35 to $45 a month. Approximately 75% are owner occupied.

About 25% of this section la undeveloped, heavily wooded and hilly. This is principally in the northern part of the area. The State Normal School is in the middle of the section between North Street and Highland Ave. and It has rather a beneficial influence on the surrounding neighborhood. Singles end two family homes predominate; frame construction, about 30 to 60 years old, In good condition. Values range from $3,000 to $7,500 and financing is readily available. 50% to 60% are owner occupied. Valuation shrinkage from the high is about 30%. Rentals are from $25 to $40.

Single and two family homes from 20 to 50 years old in good condition, occupied by middle class native born business end professional people in the higher sections around Milk and Pine Streets, The southeastern portion is lower ground and occupied by skilled mill employees some of whom are Italian. Values range from $3,000 to $10,000 representing a decline in some cases of 40%.

Much of this area is adjacent to the business section, and the homes have been transformed into rooming houses. Bungalows, two and three family homes in the upper section, with some closely built tenements along West Street. Structures are 25 to 75 years old in fair condition. Values ranging from $3,000 to $8,000 are off about 40%, and rentals are down about the same amount at $15 to $25 for the single units. Occupied principally by Finnish skilled and unskilled mechanics and mill workers.

About half of the northern portion of this area is unimproved and used for farming and track gardens by the nearby residents. Single and two family houses predominate in the southern portion, in poor to fair condition, built 30 or 40 years ago. An abandoned fair ground, part of which is now used as a swimming pool has a detrimental influence. The area is occupied principally by Jewish people of the poorer class. Values have declined 40% to 60% and have recovered but little, Houses are offered at from $1,000 to $7,000 but there is a poor demand. Rental values are from $10 to $25 a month, representing a decline of 20% to 30%.

Single and multi-family houses on steep grades. The section where Florence Street is shown Is nothing but a steep rocky impassable cliff, stop which is Crown Street forming the border of a good residential section (#4). Houses are about 30 years old in poor condition. Values are off 50% or more and rentals are down about 25%. There is no demand for homes in the section and arrangements for financing would be difficult.

Small single houses 15 to 20 years old in poor to fair condition. Occupied by French and Italian mill workers. Many streets are unimproved. Values of $500 to $3,000 are 50% down from the peak and there has been practically no recovery. Rental values are $10 to $15. There 1s no demand for houses or lots in this section.

French, Greek and Irish predominate in this section. The types of houses consist of single, multi family and row tenements. Most of these buildings are in poor condition needing extensive alterations. A great many industrial workers reside here.

There is a 35% shrinkage from 1929 on single and multi family houses; 70% shrinkage from 1929 on row tenements. A large number of these buildings owned by the banks by foreclosure should be torn down. 

The textile mills in this section employed upwards of 40,000 in 1918 with a payroll of $38,000,000 and in 1932 the workers employed dropped to 12,000 with a payroll of $9,000,000.

The Cleghorn section is principally a high plateau of cheap tenements with some single and two-family homes valued from $1,000 to $8,000 in poor to fair condition 30 to 50 years old. Occupied principally by French and German mill workers and un-skilled laborers. About 1/4th of the area is undeveloped. Property demand fell off badly as large mills closed down, but there has been a gradual improvement as small industries are established in the old mill properties. There has been no new construction in several years. Values were off 25% to 50%, but have partially recovered in some cases. Many of the streets are improved. Favorable factors are its nearness to the mills, churches and schools, and It has a playground and swimming pool. Unfavorable factors in addition to the steep, uneven approach are the lack of zoning ordinances, unsightly character of the neighborhood and dust from the stone quarry on Rollstone Hill. Rentals are reported from $6 to $25 a month, and occupancy about 70%. Some increase in rentals have been made. The Appleton Circle section was built about 12 years ago. Single homes of cheap construction which have sold as low as $800. Occupied by French, Irish and English mill workers. The section is hilly and barren.

Adjacent to the railroad and gas production plant. Principally occupied by Italian laborers of the poorer class in single and multi-family poorly kept houses, some in a dilapidated condition. There is no demand for this property. Values and rentals ere down 40% to 50%

Bordering the railroad and manufacturing section, this is an area of steep irregular streets. Closely built multiple family houses predominate in poor condition. Occupied by poorer classes of French factory workers and unskilled laborers. Values from $500 to $2,000 are off 40% to 50% with no recovery. Rentals are off 50% at $5 to $15 a month. About 1/3rd of the units are vacant.

This section is occupied by American families of moderate circumstances. Single homes predominate. Average value $4,000. About 90% of these homes have been built within the last 12 years. Principally store workers live here.

It is considered a good medium grade location.

This section is principally occupied by French and English, mostly industrial and store workers. Single homes predominate. A majority of the homes are 35 to 60 years old. 

Values have shrunk 50% of 1929 levels.

There are a number of one to two family homes here, also a number of six to twelve family row tenements in this section. The one to two family homes have shrunk on average 25% to 35% while some of the tenements in the lower part of this section have shrunk 50%d from 1929 values. (These tenements need repair) Industrial and store workers reside here. 

Values have shrunk here from 25% to 50% since 1929.

This section is commonly known as “Swedish Village”, occupied principally by Swedish people. Small cottage types of homes fill this area, averaging in value from $900 to $1,200. This is now an oversupply of these homes in this section. In 1923-4 these same cottages sold for around $2,500. Industrial workers occupy this area.

Values have shrunk here 50% from 1929 values.

Irish predominate in this section. The one and two family homes are the most popular. These homes are valued from $2,000 to $4,500. They are the older types of 35 to 40 years ago. Industrial and store workers live in this area.

Values have shrunk here from 25% to 50% since 1929.

This is the second best section of Lowell. One part of this area, known as Middlesex Village, is principally occupied with tenements, row houses and single homes. Some of these buildings need repair. Irish predominate. The Middlesex Village section has shrunk 50% from the values existing in 1929. Industrial workers occupy this area.

The balance of section #3 is built up mostly with one family homes occupied by better type Irish Americans. This area has shrunk 25% to 35% of 1929 values

French Canadians (the better type) predominate in this section, and there are some Irish and English. Industrial and store workers occupy this area almost exclusively. This is one of the oldest sections, built up principally with one family cottages having a market value today of from $900 to $1,200. These same cottages sold in 1923 for sound $2,500.

Valuations have shrunk 30% to 50% from 1929 to 1936.

Irish predominate in this area. This is a very old section. The northern part has mixed types of buildings, some row tenements, commercial business, some single and multi tenements. The slum section of Lowell is in this area on Winter and Summer Streets (Armenians and French extraction) This area shrunk 50% from 1929 values. 

The Central and southern part of this area is largely occupied with one to four family homes and some row tenements. The shrinkage here is 35% of 1929 values. This ar3a inhabited by industrial and store workers.

Greeks predominate in this section. Most homes are single family with market gardens. Poor class of industrial workers. Homes have a market value of $1,200 to $1,500.

Values have shrunk 50% to 70% from 1929.

The northeast part of this section consists of large old homes now occupied by Irish Americans, but Greeks and French are slowly moving into this section. The shrinkage here from 1929 values is about 30% to 50%.

In the northwest part of this section, one to four family houses predominate. Irish Americans reside here.

The southern part of this section contains a number of tenements, housing twelve and more families. 

Houses in all three parts of this section are 40 to 60 years of age.

The shrinkage is about 35% to 40% in the last two parts of this section from 1929 values.

French, Polish, English and Irish occupy this area. 

The northeastern part has fairly good one and two family homes; also some row tenements 35 to 60 years old. Mostly industrial workers live in this section.

Average shrinkage 35% from 1929 values. The textile mills closing down in this section affected values.

Polish section. One, multi family and row tenements.

Bridge Street is the community shopping area. The Lake View Avenue section good for slum clearance. 

Single homes are valued at $1,500 to $2,500. Row tenements rent for $2.50 to $3.50 weekly.

This section has had shrinkage of 50% from 1929.

This area is called “Little Canada” on account of the great number of French-Canadians of the proper class who reside here. Industrial workers predominate.

Single, multi family and row tenements are scattered throughout this section. Average of properties is about 40 years.
Values have shrunk more than 40% since 1929.

Mostly Armenians in the northern part of this area. Irish predominate in the southern part. There is a mixed population throughout- single, multi family and row tenements. Some of the oldest buildings in town are in this section, averaging 40 to 75 years of age.

Property has shrunk about 40% in this area since 1929.

This section is made up of mixed nationalities- Greeks, Poles, Armenians and numerous others races, mostly foreign born. Largely row tenements.

The large mills formerly located in that area attracted these industrial workers. A number of these plants now are closed down. Formerly employed 18,000 workers where today the employed are 6,000.

Low grade business section along Mood Street. Merrimack Street, which divides this area, is considered the best business section in the city.

Shrinkage has been 40% to 60% in the residential part of this area.

Polish and Irish-American live here. Mostly industrial workers. 

Single, multi-family and row tenements of the poorer type. Very old buildings - a hazardous area.

Part of this section is commercial and used for light manufacturing.

Shrinkage 50% from 1929 values.

This development is in slightly rolling country. Wide streets, large lots, and shows good planning. Inhabited by American born whites, executive and professional people. Well served by transportation. A very small proportion of the land is vacant. Ten or twelve new houses have been built within the last 12 months, but no previous new construction for five years. One family houses entirely, with an average age about 30 years. The newer sections are  on the outer edges of this area. Frame construction predominates. Condition excellent. Property values range from $6,000 to $15,000 with a very few falling within the $20,000 to $30,000 bracket. Values have declined about 75% and have recovered approximately 25% of this loss. Demand is reported to be slow to fair. A few lots have been sold recently in the Kenilworth Brunswick St. section. Rentals are now about $35 to $75 a month. Rental values shrank about 75% but have recovered about 20% of the decline. Demand for rentals is reported good.

This is a newer development of attractive, moderately sized homes located on proportionate plots. Landscaping is excellent and pride of ownship is most evident. Mortgage lenders look with favor upon this section.

This is the Spadina Parkway section. Spadina Parkway itself is 100% built up, but the balance of the area is undeveloped. People are native born of the more wealthy class, professional and business executives. High ground. The section is comparatively new. Houses are about 5 to 15 years of age in an excellent state of repair. At the low point, values had declined 55% but have since recovered 20% of the loss. Principal demand has been for houses in the $5,000 to $7,000 class. Rental values are now about 80% of 1929 levels which represents a recovery of about 20% from the low. There are practically no vacancies in the area and the rental demand at from $30 to $60 a month is good.

The character of the land in this South-center section is rolling. Inhabitants are 90% Native born and include the better classes of skilled mechanics as well as some of the more wealthy business executives and professional people. It is close to the down-town business section. As well be observed, about half the area remains undeveloped, although only about 15% of the land is vacant where streets are shown on the map. No new construction within the past three years. One family houses predominate with some two family, and a few of the better grade multi-family. Generally 30 to 50 years old, most of the structures are in good condition. The predominant type of home in the area would sell now for from $5,000 to $7,000 which represents about 80% of their 1929 value. There are in the area a few estates which were formerly valued at from $40,000 to $150,000. These are not no vacancies in this area in desirable units, and the demand for rentals is good up to $40 a month. Present rental offerings are from $25 to $80 a month as compared with $30 to $125 a month prior to 1929.

This section is largely undeveloped beyond Backman Ave., with the         exception of 10 or 15 new single homes now being built along West St. near Onota Lake. At this point the ground is high, and commands one of the best views of the surrounding country. The sewerage system does not now extend beyond Backman Ave. is occupied by average factory employes, principally native born. Most of these houses are 20 to 30 years old, but a few have been built within the past ten years. All are in good condition. Single houses predominate, with a few two family on Marion and on Euclid Streets. As in other good sections of the city, the average small home now sellings for about $4,000 has declined in value only about 20% from 1929 levels. The larger houses formerly selling for about $40,000, however, are being offered currently at 50% of that figure, or less. One of these is now renting for $100 a month, but others rent in the area are from $25 to $60 a month, indicating a decline of about 20% from the 1929 rental value.

This section is fairly level ground having only a gradual slope toward Elm Street. Inhabitants are mostly middle class merchants and business people, and a few families of the better paid factory employes. Frame single houses predominate, and there are also quite a number of two family houses. All are in fair to good condition. This is one of the older neighborhoods, and reported as less likely to improve. Majority of the people are native born, but there has been some infiltration of foreigners. Five new homes are 25 to 50 years old. Present values range from $4,500 to $10,000 which is approximately 80% of 1929 levels. Rental values now range from $25 to $50 a month. There are very few vacancies and the demand is reported good.

inhabitants in this section are principally average factory workers about 50% of whom are native born of foreign parents. Other occupants of the area are middle class business people. In the northern end of the area small single houses and cottages predominate, from 15 to 30 years old, and in good condition. About 50% of this northern section is undeveloped, and no new building is reported. Older single and two family houses predominate along First and Second Streets, some of which were built about 50 years ago. These are now in fair to good condition, and a considerable amount of rehabilitation seems to have been completed recently. This is also true of the Seymore Street neighborhood. Favorable factors are: proximity to the downtown business section and to the General Electric mills and other manufacturing establishments. There is a fair to good demand for rental space in desirable units at prices averaging 15% under 1929. Values are reported to be from $4,000 to $10,000 which are about 80% of 1929 levels.

This section is developed on fairly high ground and is close to the General Electric Mills. A number of new small singles have been built along Dalton Avenue, which is now being resurfaced to make a broad highway. The section is known as Morningside, or the Allen Tract. In the Dartmouth St. neighborhood are some two and three decker tenements in good condition. Elsewhere in the area are small single cottage type homes, single and two family houses, and some multi-family dwellings. Structures are from 5 to 35 years old in fair to good condition. Values of from $3,500 to $6,500 are 85% of 1929 prices. There is an estimated vacancy in desirable units of 6%, but a good demand. Rentals are from $22 to $40 a month which are 75% of 1929. Inhabitants are mostly skilled and unskilled mill workers, 25% of whom are of foreign extraction.

Occupied by a mixture of Irish-American and Italian mill workers. The area is called the Victory Mill section, and is along the principal highway to Albany, New York. Single frame homes predominate with a few multiple family dwellings 15 to 45 years old, generally in fair condition. Some of the small single homes are comparatively new, but appear to be very cheap construction. There are some abandoned railroad tracks in the area, and a tannery is located between the two small ponds. Values of $2,700 to $4,500 are reported to be 85% of 1929 levels. Rental values of from $15 to $30 a month are only slightly off from pre-depression prices, and the demand is reported to be fair.
Wooded land rising slightly from the water. Zoned for single family homes.

Polish and Roumanian mill workers of the poorer classes in habit this section and there a few negro families. Some Italian families have concentrated near John and Linden Streets, and Jewish people of the poorer class live in the Robbins Ave., and Daniels Ave. neighborhood. On Onota Street there are several frame three decker houses 25 to 40 years old in poor condition. A mixture of types may be found elsewhere in the area from small singles and cottages to multi family dwellings. Houses are mostly of cheap construction old and generally in poor condition. The terrain slopes down rather sharply from Onota Street to the West Branch of the Housatonic River, where there is a dumping ground several acres in extent. The best part of the area is on the high ground around Lakeway Drive where the houses are of a somewhat more substantial character and pride of home ownership seems more apparent. Values range from $2,700 to $7,000 representing about 85% of 1929 levels. Rentals are now from $11 ro $30 a month although the higher figure is the exception rather than the rule. These are reported to be about 85% of 1929, and the demand is fair to good.

This is known as the Peck’s Mill section. Inhabitants are principally Polish mill workers of the poorer classes, and there are some Jewish and Greek families. Favorable features are: proximity of the area to Pontoosuc Lake and the woolen mills; and the improved condition of Highland Avenue as the result of a recent W.P.A project. There are some single houses and summer cottages at Pontoosuc Lake of a fair character and condition, near the  Pontoosuc Lake Golf Club. Elsewhere in the area one family houses predominate, 10 to 25 years old, in poor to fair condition. About 75% of the area is undeveloped and no new construction is reported. Values of from $2,000 to $3,500 are about 80% of the high. Summer cottages near the Lake, rent at a somewhat higher rate than this. It is generally held that this lake is less desirable than the section near Onota Lake to the South-west.

This area is inhabited mostly by Greek and Polish mill workers. Practically 90% of the area is undeveloped. Small singles predominate 10 to 40 years old in poor to fair condition. The majority of streets are unpaved, and the location of houses more or less haphazard. Values are from $2,500 to $4,000 which is about 80% of 1929. No demand is reported and sales difficult. Property has always rented at low figures and there is now only a fair demand at from $15 to $25 a month.

This is known as the Silver Lake, or Lower Elm Street area. The terrain is low-lying, but level. The East Branch of the Housatonic River overflows its banks at certain seasons of the year. Efforts to overcome this by deepening the channel and straightening the river course have met with failure because landowners have been unwilling to accept a reasonable figure for their property which would be taken in the project. Italian laborers and unskilled factory workers predominate. Frame one to four family houses 10 to 60 years old. The majority are in poor condition, but some rehabilitation has taken place. High tension wires of the Turners Falls Electric Company cross the area. Newell Street is the best in the section. Values from $2,500 to $5,000 are about 80% of 1929. Demand is reported to be slow to fait, and sales poor. On the other hand, the rental demand is reported good at prices from $13 to $32 a month, which are about 20% under 1929 values.

This terrain is flat and located near the railroad yards. About half the people are Italian unskilled workers in the General Electric plant, and the other half native born white people, many of whom also work in the mills. Small single homes predominate 20 to 40 years old in poor to fair condition. No new construction is reported. There is a fair demand for rentals at $20 to $25 a month, but sales of property are poor.

Goodrich Pond area. Low-lying ground and near the railroad yards. Frequently flooded from the overflowing of the Housatonic River, sometimes up to the first floor of the houses. Italian laborers and mill workers predominate. Small single houses from 20 to 35 years old, and in poor condition; values of $2,000 to $3,000 have not declined very much since 1929. The vacancy percentage is very small due to the low rents prevailing of from $10 to $20 a month.

This is known as the Wahconah Park area. It is adjacent to the dumping ground and the swampy area bordering the West Branch of the Housatonic River. Inhabited by the poorer classes of native whites and there are some colored people. Frame two and four family houses predominate built 30 to 50 years old, and in poor condition. Values are $2,000 to $3,200 and the demand nil. There is practically no demand for rentals although rents are low at $11 to $17 a month.

"Jubilee Hill” is inhabited by a mixture of foreign races including Italians and Poles and some negroes. Frame multi-family houses predominate with a few two family dwellings, from 40 to 75 years old, in a poor to dilapidated condition. The people are mostly of the poorer laboring class and unskilled mill workers. A steep hill in the western portion of the area slopes down to the river flats which are muddy and unsightly. Values are estimated at from $2,000 to $6,000 with small demand and no sales reported. Low rental values of from $10 to $20 a month prevail and there is poor demand.
High and rolling land zoned for single family homes.
Attractiveness of development and convenience of location.

A section of extremely  large, modern homes many of which are occupied only during the summer season. Properties are large, beautifully landscaped and evidence marked pride of ownership. Because of size and expensive up-keep, the market is extremely thin; hence, stability of inhabitant notwithstanding, institutional lenders are somewhat wary of this area.
High, rolling and wooded ground which is restricted to one family homes.
Attractive location with country club to the south.
Distance from center of Bridgeport and lack of schools and sewers.

This has become a very desirable residential section for Bridgeport executives who prefer to live beyond the city limits. Dwellings are of fair size and in many cases, large with land in proportion. Architecture is varied and pleasing and grounds are well landscaped. Everywhere pride of ownership is evident. Expensive up-keep and high values have created a thin sales market yet it is a favorite of the lenders.
High, rolling and wooded land restricted to one family dwellings.
Attractive location with country club to the west.
None, save lack of schools and sewers.

A development of large homes and proportional plots with a special appeal to those who work in Bridgeport but desire to reside beyond the city limits. Architecture is varied but pleasing and landscaping attractive. Pride of ownership is everywhere in evidence. High values and up-keep have created a thin market and lenders practice precaution.
Ideal location for its present use.
Distance from schools, churches and shopping center.

This is a sparsely settled section containing fair sized estates and large attractive homes. These are, for the most part, occupied by New York commuters and many are used only during the summer months. Mortgagors look with decided favor on this area.
High ridgeland overlooking the Sound and a golf course.

This is an area of large, attractive homes surrounded by spacious and well kept grounds, as well as others much smaller. Occupants are commuters to New York and reside here only during summer months. High values and expensive up-keep have practically eliminated any market. Wide variation eliminates any predominating type.
Ground rises to the north. Zoned for one and two family homes.
Attractiveness of location and excellence of transportation, making area easily accessible to the business section.

A somewhat newer development which still continues. Homes are of moderate size on small plots, both showing pride of ownership. In the west there is a considerable amount of vacant land. Because of growth and character of owners, lenders like this section.

A residential section of cottages and bungalows used mostly during summer months only. Plots are in proportion to the size of dwelling. Area is a typical beach colony. Loans are carefully scrutinized.
High, rolling and wooden ground zoned for one family homes.
Lack of civic improvements, poor transportation and distance from schools, churches and center of Bridgeport.

This sparsely settled area has been improved with modest, single family homes of not too expensive construction. Grounds are not particularly large, but of sufficient size. Pride of ownership is noticeable.
High, rolling and wooded land restricted to single family construction.
Well located with a country club to the west.
Lack of sewers, schools and churches.
A small section containing modest sized homes and surrounding lots. Architecture is quite varied but pleasing and pride of ownership is evident.
Ground rises from the creek. Area is limited to one family homes.
An area occupied by those with places of business in Bridgeport. Neither homes nor grounds are large and both show pride of ownership.
Attractive to those who enjoy country property.
Inconveniently located and lack of sewers.
A slightly older section still only sparsely improved. Area includes quite a variation in type of dwelling and size of property. Some are fairly large, others are mere bungalows.
Generally flat, low land zoned for single family dwellings.
Attraction of a small, country town and waterfront.
None, save age of most structures.
The old section of Fairfield where still reside many families of wealth. Homes and Grounds are large. Interspersed are smaller dwellings and more particularly near the beach and to the  northeast.
Rolling and wooded land zoned for single family dwellings.
Conveniently located and with country atmosphere.
None, save two small manufacturing plants which are really not objectionable.
A sparsely improved section in which small homes and lots predominate. Two minor plants do not detract from the desirability of this neighborhood.
Rolling and well wooded land zoned for one family homes.
Attraction of a small town and pleasing location.
None, save size and age of many properties.

A somewhat older section in which properties are, for the most part, fairly large as are dwellings. Despite age they are well maintained and evidence a decided pride of ownership. This area rates a high Blue". Stability of home owners makes this a favorite with the lenders."
Land rises to the north. Area is zoned for one and two family dwellings.
None, other than that homes generally are not sufficiently modern.
Generally, an older section of the city in which the houses are built quite closely together and well maintained. Streets are lines with shade trees and pride of ownership is evidenced.
Generally low and wooded land now zoned for two family homes in the north and singles in the south.

Along the waterfront there are a number of large old homes on extensive plottages. Inland homes are more modern, smaller and built quite closely together. Properties are generally well cared for and show pride of ownership.
High, rolling ground generally well wooded. In the main, the area is zoned for single family homes.
A newer development which is still only sparsely improved in the north. Homes and plots are small, architecture is varied but pleasing and pride of ownership is in evidence.
Low, wooded land restricted to one family homes.

Originally, the prime residential section in which the city's leading citizens bought sizeable lots and erected thereon large and costly homes. Despite age, they are still well kept up. Size and cost of maintenance eliminates any sales or rental markets. With the passing of these older families, demolition must ultimately result.
Land rises steeply from the south. Area is now zoned for singles and doubles.
Topographical location and convenient to places of work.

This area contains a mixture of small singles and doubles located on comparatively small plots. Properties seem well cared for and pride of ownership is evident. Being small and surrounded by less desirable neighborhoods, this area will eventually seek their level  hence, lenders are wary.
Ground rises slightly from the river and then becomes rolling. Area is restricted to one family homes.
Attractiveness of location and convenience to small, central shopping district.
Distance from Bridgeport although most people employ their own cars.

This is a newer development created by a movement from the City of Bridgeport. Homes are small and located on plots of proportionate size. Architecture is not overly pleasing but pride of ownership is evident. This section rates a high Blue" and is so recognized by lending institutions."
Land rises from the river to become high and rolling in the north. Zoning restrictions permit of one and two family home.
Attractiveness of small town convenient to a small town and convenient to a small, central shopping district.
Distance from places of employment and center of Bridgeport. The northern portion lacks improvements.

A newer development in which small singles and bungalows predominate and is still only partly settled. Plots, though not large, are well maintained and show pride of ownership. Inhabitants are former residents of Bridgeport. Lenders practice cars in this section.
Low, wooded land which is zoned for single family homes.
Attractiveness of location and convenience to small town shopping center.
None, save distance from City of Bridgeport.
This is an older section of larger homes and extensive plots laid out around a village green. It has all the attractiveness of a small town and despite their age, are well maintained.
A rolling area of hills and ravines which is wooded in parts. This section is zoned for singles and doubles save the southern tip in which light industry will be permitted.
Lack of civic improvements as well as distance from center of the city and schools.

This should have been a most desirable residential section but cheapness of the land attracted the foreign element from hazardous section of the city. This class has erected a number of small, cheap homes including bungalows on equally small plots. As yet, the area remains only sparsely developed.
Land rising to the north where it becomes rolling. Zoning regulations permit of one and two family dwellings.
Distance from center of city and lack of improvements in the north.

A somewhat newer development which, in portions, particularly in the north, still remains only partially settled. Improvements consist of an equal amount of small singles and doubles situated on plots of proportionate size. Singles are generally small and of the bungalow type.
High and rolling land zoned for one and two family homes.
Distance from places of employment, poor transportation and lack of civic improvements.
This area becomes less and less improved in the north. Dwellings are, for the most part, doubles with a scattering of small bungalows. Plots are not large and pride of ownership is spotty.
Low, flat land which is surrounded on the south by swampland.

An intermingling of cheaply constructed, small singles and doubles in various states of repair. Plots are small and the whole area displays a very spotty pride of ownership. Lending precautions are always adopted.
Land rises slightly from the river.
This small area contains small, cheaply constructed dwellings which have been erected on plots of varying size. Pride of ownership is not much in evidence. Lenders do not favor placing money here.
Rough and irregular ground rising from the creek.
Appeal to laboring class desiring to move from the congested parts of Bridgeport.
An area of small, cheaply constructed one family homes and bungalows on plots of proportionate size. Portions, particularly to the northwest, are only partially improved.
Low, flat land which is treeless and near the beach.
A section of cottages and beach bungalows occupied for the most part only during summer months. The former have fair sized grounds, the latter almost none.
Land rises to the north and is zoned for singles, doubles and multi-family.
Convenient to the center of city and good transportation.
This area contains a mixture of singles, doubles and triples built closely together on very small plots. The western portion is only partly developed.
Flat ground zoned for business and multi-family dwellings.
Convenient to center of city and places of work.
Encroachment of business and obsolescence of dwellings.
An older section of the city containing closely built dwellings ranging from doubles to small apartment houses.
Low, flat land. Water front is largely zoned for light industry and the balance for doubles and multi-family.
Convenience to places of work and good transportation to center of city.

This is an area which includes a range from singles to four family dwellings but in which the former predominate. Dwellings for the most part, are built quite closely together. Mortgagors exercise care in landing.
Low, flat land zoned entirely for multi-family dwellings, heavy and light industry.
Convenience of location- nearness to center of city and places of work.

This is an old section of the city containing a mixture of closely built homes of which two and three family predominate. Most attractive are the row houses built by the Government during the war. There is also a scattering of small factories.
High, rolling ground which is zoned for singles and doubles.
Distance from center of city and poor transportation, as well as lack of civic improvements.
A somewhat newer section of generally small singles, many of which are of the bungalow type. Plots are small and pride of ownership is spotty. In sections, the area is only sparsely settled.
Flat land rising slightly in the north. The area is zoned for business and multi-family dwellings.
Convenience of location - nearness to center of city and places of employment.

A section in which old, two and three family homes built very closely together which, because of convenience of its location, retains its desirability from the factory workers standpoint. Although, there were less foreclosures in this area than in any other, lenders are now taking precautionary measures in making new loans. Some mortgages still bear civil war stamps.
Land rising steeply from the southwest and east and zoned for multi-family homes.
Convenient to places of work and attractive topography.
This area contains a mixture of some small singles, but doubles and triples predominate. The most attractive are company built row house. Plots are of fair size but pride of ownership is only spotty.
Low, flat land now entirely zoned for multi-family residences.
Only fair transportation and distance from center of city. Soot from coal being unloaded from barges.

This area contains a mixture of singles, doubles, triples, and four family dwellings as well as some flats all built closely together. Doubles and triples predominate. Company row house are the most attractive. Negros are confined to the sections designated in red" on the map. Lenders steer clear of this area and are inclined to dump properties."
Ground rises slightly to the north west. From Madison Avenue to Main Street is zoned for light industry, the balance for business.
Nearness to heart of city and good transportation.
Obsolescence of old dwellings and encroachment of business.

This is an old and densely built up section of the city containing a mixture varying from doubles to flats and a scattering of small plants. Sections has been entirely given over to the poorer classes.
Low, flat land which is swampy in parts and is now entirely zoned for both heavy and light industry.

An older section of the city in which sixes predominate and which houses unskilled factory labor. There is all the appearance of a slum area. Dwellings are in poor condition and pride of ownership is completely absent.
Low, flat land which is now entirely zoned for light industry.
Character of area as well as smoke from the railroad and harbor traffic.

An old and densely built up portion of the city containing almost every conceivable type of dwelling all in rather delapidated condition. There is no pride of ownership and the entire section constitutes a slum area.

Populated by well-to-do class of people, with homes averaging 5M to 15M- single (small) to large, equally divided, all attractive and substantial - approximately 50% brick and 50% frame construction, in very good condition, none over 10 years old, well maintained, averaging in age 5 years. Average rent $50.00 to $75.00 per month.

Wealthy class, homes valued at from $7500.00 to $30,000 - large, single, elaborate, 50% of brick and frame, excellent condition, some 25 years old, average 13 years, well maintained. Average rent $50.00 to $75.00 per month.

Homes owned in this section by thrifty well-to-do Bohemians, from $5,000 to 6,000 ordinary one and two-story single homes, solidly built, two to four bedrooms with bath, some 25 years old, average 15 years, in good condition and kept so. These people take great pride in their homes and grounds - mostly frame construction. As these Bohemians are of the older class, it is believed that as they die out, the younger will intermarry and leave that section for other parts of the city. Property here is mostly owned and can be sold only to Bohemians. Average rental $20.00 to $27.00 per month.

Homes here consist of 95% frame construction costing $4000.00 to $10,000 - occupied by business men, managers, clerks, all drawing good salaries, who own their homes - average home age 13 years, some 25 years, well maintained. Average rental $30.00 to $40.00 per month.

Consists in North as farm land valued at $100-$150 per acre. Suitable for acreage sub-divisions on east, small homes in poor shape averaging $2000.00. Average rental $15.00 to $20.00 per month.

Some farm land, the Sacred Heart Academy ground of approximately 35 acres, and some five and six-room cottages of one and two stories valued at approximately $2000.00, also a private golf course. The National Oats Company, One Minute Cereal Company, Cedar Rapids Engineering Company (tool-makers) , and Holland Furnace Company plant are all on the southern outskirts and are somewhat detrimental. The people are mostly native-born Americans, own homes, and earn from poor wages (in case of oatmeal mills) to medium and high wages in these industrial plants. Property age 20 years, mostly frame, and in fair shape. These buildings grew up with the plants and have not suffered much shrinkage in value, probably approximately 20% since 1929. Real estate sales are made - average price $3000.00. Very few new homes - slight rent increase. The Tool Company and Iowa Mfg. Company doubled their plants here during the past five years.

Some farm land, the Sacred Heart Academy ground of approximately 35 acres, and some five and six-room cottages of one and two stories valued at approximately $2000.00, also a private golf course.
